Name: Dwarf Galaxy Leo IV
Description: Leo IV is one of more than a dozen ultra-faint dwarf galaxies near the Milky Way. These galaxies are dominated by dark matter, an invisible substance that makes up most of the universe's mass.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 3982
Description: This image captures the face-on spiral galaxy NGC 3982. Its arms are lined with pink star-forming regions of glowing hydrogen, blue newborn star clusters, and dark dust lanes that provide the raw material for future generations of stars.

Name: Reflection Nebula NGC 1333
Description: NGC 1333 is a nearby star-forming region. Glowing gases and pitch-black dust are stirred up and blown around by several hundred newly forming stars embedded within this dark cloud.

Name: Omega Centauri

Name: Irregular Galaxy UGC 4459
Description: Irregular dwarf galaxies, such as UGC 4459, are one of the most common types of galaxy in the universe. UGC 4459’s diffused and disorganized appearance is characteristic of an irregular dwarf galaxy.

Name: Galaxy Cluster SDSS J1004+4112
Description: This picture captures a galaxy cluster called SDSS J1004+4112 that's so massive that its gravity bends and magnifies light from galaxies behind it. The light of a distant quasar (the brilliant core of an active galaxy) has been bent around the cluster, appearing in five places in this image.

Name: Spiral Galaxies NGC 4302 and NGC 4298

Name: Dwarf Galaxy Leo A
Description: This image features the nearby dwarf irregular galaxy Leo A. Astronomers study dwarf galaxies like Leo A because they are numerous and may offer clues to how galaxies grow and evolve.

Name: Globular Cluster Caldwell 73
Description: C73, or NGC 1851, is a globular cluster that may be the result of a collision of two star clusters. Unlike many globular clusters, C73 hosts stellar populations with different ages.

Name: Cosmic Reef

Description: The galaxy NGC 5427 is interacting gravitationally with a companion galaxy located outside the image. The effects show in the galactic distortion and cosmic bridge of stars seen in the lower-right.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 5584
Description: The brilliant, blue glow of young stars traces the graceful spiral arms of galaxy NGC 5584. Thin, dark dust lanes appear to be flowing from the yellowish core, where older stars reside.

Name: Mars
Description: This image captures springtime in the northern hemisphere of Mars. The northern polar ice cap has receded to its core of solid water-ice several hundred miles across. Morning clouds appear along the planet's western (left) limb.

Name: Interacting Galaxy ESO 507-70
Description: ESO 507-70 is an odd-looking galaxy that is probably the remnant of an earlier merger process. It is a chaotic swirl of gas, dust, and stars with no sign of its likely original spiral or elliptical structure.

Name: Globular Cluster NGC 6397
Description: This ancient stellar jewelry box, globular cluster NGC 6397, glitters with the light from hundreds of thousands of stars. The cluster is 13.4 billion years old, born shortly after the Big Bang.

Name: Triangulum Galaxy
Description: This mosaic captures the nearby Triangulum galaxy. Striking areas of star birth glow bright blue throughout the galaxy.

Name: AG Carinae
Description: The star AG Carinae is living on the edge! This petulant star is prone to outbursts, and will likely only survive a few million years – much shorter than the expected lifetime of our Sun, which is about 10 billion years.

Name: Bubble Nebula
Description: An enormous bubble is being blown into space by a super-hot, massive star. The Bubble Nebula is roughly seven light-years across and is located 7,100 light-years away in the constellation Cassiopeia.

Name: Globular Cluster 47 Tucanae
Description: This image of the heart of the giant globular star cluster 47 Tucanae reveals the glow of 200,000 stars. Young white dwarfs ― the burned-out relics of stars that have used up their nuclear fuel, cooled down, and lost most of their mass ― are beginning to migrate outward.

Name: SWEEPS Star Field
Description: Hubble peered into the crowded central bulge of our galaxy 26,000 light-years away and collected information for 180,000 stars as part of a survey called the Sagittarius Window Eclipsing Extrasolar Planet Search (SWEEPS).

Name: Stellar Object IRAS 05506+2414
Description: This bright young stellar object, which is known to astronomers as IRAS 05506+2414, may be an example of an explosive event caused by the disruption of a massive young star system.

Name: Elliptical Galaxy Messier 87
Description: This image of the giant galaxy M87 shows a 3,000-light-year-long jet of plasma blasting from the galaxy's 6.5-billion-solar-mass central black hole. The jet seems to cause stars to erupt along its trajectory.

Name: Little Ghost Nebula
Description: The Little Ghost Nebula appears as a small, ghostly cloud surrounding a dying star. It is found in the constellation Ophiuchus between 2,000 and 5,000 light-years away.

Description: Galaxy AM 1054-325 has been distorted into an S-shape by the gravitational pull of a neighboring galaxy. Newborn clusters of stars form along a stretched-out tidal tail for thousands of light-years.

Name: Galaxy Cluster MACS J1141.6-1905
Description: Hubble observed MACS J1141.6-1905 as part of a survey that looked at massive clusters of galaxies. The cluster shines brightly in x-rays, but Hubble captured this scene in visible and infrared light.

Name: Dwarf Irregular Galaxy ESO 490-017
Description: This dwarf irregular galaxy lies some 23 million light-years away. Its low surface brightness makes it appear as a faint, starry swarm behind brighter foreground stars.

Name: Bubble Nebula
Description: An enormous bubble, also known as NGC 7635, is being blown into space by a super-hot, massive star. Stellar winds from a massive star sweep up the cold gas in front of it, forming the outer edge of the bubble.

Name: Galaxy Cluster RCS2 032727-132623
Description: The light from a distant galaxy, nearly 10 billion light-years away, has been warped into arcs and streaks by the gravity of galaxy cluster RCS2 032727-132623. The cluster acts as a gravitational lens, bending and amplifying light from the background galaxy.

Name: Saturn's Double Light Show
Description: Hubble captured this rare ultraviolet image of Saturn with its rings edge-on and aurorae glowing at the planet's north and south poles. It takes Saturn almost 30 years to orbit the Sun, with the opportunity to image both of its poles occurring only twice during that time.

Name: Pluto System
Description: This image, taken through a red filter, captures Pluto and three of its satellites. The largest object in the image is Pluto and the second largest is Charon. Two smaller moons appear below them.

Name: Elliptical Galaxy Fornax A
Description: The dust lanes and star clusters of this giant elliptical galaxy, known as Fornax A, give evidence that the galaxy formed from a past merger of two gas-rich galaxies. It is also one of the strongest sources of radio emission in the sky.

Name: Dwarf Galaxy NGC 1705
Description: The heart of the galaxy NGC 1705 blazes with the light of thousands of young and old stars. This galaxy has been forming new stars throughout its life, but a burst of star-formation occurred about 26 to 31 million years ago.

Name: Elliptical Galaxy NGC 4881
Description: The brightest object in this photo mosaic of distant galaxies is the central galaxy NGC 4881. This is an elliptical galaxy located in the outskirts of the Coma Cluster, a massive cluster of galaxies.

Name: Globular Cluster 47 Tucanae
Description: The ancient globular cluster 47 Tucanae is a dense swarm of up to a million stars, and this view captures a close-up of thousands of them. The large, bright stars in the image are red giants near the end of their lives.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 1512
Description: The core of the barred spiral galaxy NGC 1512 is unique for its stunning 2,400-light-year-wide circle of infant star clusters, called a "circumnuclear" starburst ring. Starbursts are episodes of vigorous star formation.

Name: Orion Nebula
Description: The Orion Nebula, a turbulent stellar nursery, is a perfect laboratory to study how stars are born because it is just 1,500 light-years away, a relatively short distance within our galaxy.

Name: Reflection Nebula IC 2631
Description: Reflection nebulae like IC 2631 are clouds of gas and dust that reflect the light from nearby stars. The starlight scatters through the gas and dust like a flashlight beam shining on mist and illuminates it.

Name: Supernova Remnant Cassiopeia A
Description: The tattered remains of a supernova explosion known as Cassiopeia A are located in the Milky Way some 10,000 light-years away from Earth.

Name: Nebula NGC 3603
Description: In this stunning picture of the giant galactic nebula NGC 3603, Hubble captures various stages of the life cycle of stars in one single view.

Name: Beta Pictoris Disk
Description: In 1984, Beta Pictoris was the very first star discovered to be surrounded by a bright disk of light-scattering dust and debris. Planets are thought to form in such disks, and astronomers have discovered two planets orbiting Beta Pictoris.

Name: Interacting Galaxy NGC 454
Description: This interacting galaxy pair holds a large red elliptical galaxy and an irregular gas-rich blue galaxy. The system is in the early stages of an interaction that severely distorted both galaxies.

Name: Planetary Nebula NGC 2346
Description: NGC 2346 is a planetary nebula, formed by Sun-like stars near the ends of their lives. Its central star is known to be actually a very close pair of stars, orbiting each other every 16 days.

Name: Omega Centauri

Name: Flame Nebula

Name: Saturn in Ultraviolet
Description: This false-color image of Saturn, taken in ultraviolet light, reveals details in the hazes and clouds of the planet's atmosphere that are not easy or possible to see in visible light.

Name: Active Galaxy IC 5063
Description: This Hubble image shows the heart of an active, relatively nearby galaxy called IC 5063. A mixture of bright rays of light and dark shadows emerge from the blazing core, which is home to a supermassive black hole.

Name: Star-forming Nebula G035.20-0.74
Description: This star-forming nebula, G035.20-0.74, is known for producing a kind of hot, young, blue star known as a B-Type star, which is up to five times hotter than our Sun.

Name: Elliptical Galaxy NGC 1316
Description: The dust lanes and star clusters of this giant elliptical galaxy, known as Fornax A, give evidence that the galaxy formed from a past merger of two gas-rich galaxies. It is also one of the strongest sources of radio emission in the sky.

Name: Flame Nebula

Name: Einstein Ring SDSS J120540
Description: Einstein rings like this form when two galaxies are almost perfectly aligned, one behind the other, and the gravitational field of the closer galaxy bends and magnifies the light from the more-distant galaxy into bright arcs around itself.

Name: Reflection Nebula NGC 1333
Description: NGC 1333 is a nearby star-forming region. Glowing gases and pitch-black dust are stirred up and blown around by several hundred newly forming stars embedded within this dark cloud.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 5584

Name: Interacting Pair Arp 94

Name: Galaxy Cluster Abell 2261
Description: The giant elliptical galaxy in the center of this image is the most massive and brightest member of galaxy cluster Abell 2261. More than a million light-years wide, the galaxy is about 10 times bigger than our Milky Way galaxy.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 3021
Description: Spiral galaxy NGC 3021 is home to Cepheid variable stars. These stars pulsate at a rate that is closely related to their intrinsic brightness. Astronomers use this information to calculate a galaxy’s distance.

Name: Globular Cluster Messier 22
Description: M22 is one of about 150 globular star clusters in the Milky Way. Located just 10,000 light-years away in the constellation Sagittarius, it is one of the closest globular clusters to Earth.

Name: Mars
Description: This stunning portrait of Mars was taken just before the planet made one of its closest approaches to Earth (passing about 60 million miles [97 million km] from us). This view was taken on the last day of spring in the planet's northern hemisphere.

Name: Interacting Galaxy NGC 6786
Description: The smaller of the two galaxies, dubbed LEDA 62867 and positioned to the left of the frame, will probably be eventually swallowed by the larger spiral galaxy, NGC 6786 (to the right).

Name: Galaxy Pair NGC 3314
Description: This image shows a pair of galaxies called NGC 3314. Through a chance alignment, a face-on spiral galaxy lies precisely in front of another, larger spiral. This provides a view of dark material within the front galaxy, seen because it is silhouetted against the galaxy behind it.

Name: Galaxy UGC 5460
Description: This image reveals UGC 5460’s central bar of stars, winding spiral arms, and bright blue star clusters. Also captured in the upper left-hand corner is a far closer object: a star just 577 light-years away in our own galaxy.

Name: Southern Crab Nebula
Description: An aging red giant star is shedding its outer layers to produce the Southern Crab Nebula. The "legs" are likely to be the places where the outflowing material slams into surrounding gas and dust.

Name: Comet Siding Spring
Description: This comet plunged toward the Sun along a roughly 1-million-year orbit. Hubble resolved two jets of dust coming from the solid icy nucleus.

Name: Globular Cluster Messier 19
Description: Messier 19 is a globular cluster, in which stars orbit about a common center of gravity. Globular clusters of stars are usually spherical, but some, like M19, have a slightly elongated shape.

Name: Butterfly Nebula
Description: This Hubble image shows NGC 6302, nicknamed the Butterfly Nebula. The "wings" are regions of heated gas that are tearing across space at more than 600,000 miles (965,600 km) an hour.

Name: Interacting Galaxies Arp 297
Description: Arp 297 is a pair of interacting galaxies that consists of NGC 5754, the large spiral at the top, and NGC 5752, the smaller companion at the bottom left. NGC 5754's internal structure has hardly been disturbed, but it does have some kinked arms just beyond its inner ring.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 5584

Name: Dark Nebula LDN 1165
Description: This image captures a portion of a dark nebula called LDN 1165. Dark or absorption nebulae are clouds of gas and dust that neither emit nor reflect light, instead blocking light coming from behind them.

Name: Spiral Galaxy IC 4633
Description: The spiral galaxy IC 4633 is rich in star-forming activity and also hosts an active galactic nucleus at its core. From our point of view, the galaxy is tilted mostly towards us, giving astronomers a good view of its billions of stars.

Name: Omega Centauri

Name: Interacting Galaxies Arp 81

Name: Spiral Galaxy UGC 9391
Description: This spiral galaxy, UGC 9391, contains two types of stars that astronomers use to calculate accurate distances to galaxies and refine the measurement for how fast the universe expands with time, called the Hubble constant.

Name: Interacting Galaxy Group LEDA 60847
Description: This group of interacting galaxies is called LEDA 60847. Galaxy mergers are relatively common occurrences, and most larger galaxies are the result of smaller galaxies merging.

Name: Star Cloud Messier 24
Description: This detailed view of M24 captures a huge number of stars in only a tiny portion of the region, which is also known as the Small Sagittarius Star Cloud.

Name: Globular Cluster Messier 4
Description: Peering deep inside a cluster of several hundred thousand stars uncovers the oldest burned-out stars in our Milky Way Galaxy. Located in the globular cluster M4, these small, dying stars are known as white dwarfs.

Name: Supernova Didius
Description: Supernova Didius, named after a Roman emperor, is the white dot in the center of this image. The bright blob at upper left is the core of the supernova's host galaxy. The supernova is so far away, we see it as it appeared 7 billion years ago.

Name: Globular Cluster 47 Tucanae
Description: The ancient globular cluster 47 Tucanae is a dense swarm of up to a million stars, and this view captures a close-up of thousands of them. The large, bright stars in the image are red giants near the end of their lives.

Name: Stars in the Galactic Core
Description: These colorful stars reside at the heart of our Milky Way galaxy, about 26,000 light-years from Earth. Aging red giant stars coexist with their more plentiful younger cousins, the smaller, white, Sun-like stars, in this crowded region of our galaxy's central hub.

Name: Globular Cluster ESO 591-12
Description: ESO 591-12, also called Palomar 8, is a globular cluster ― a spherical collection of tens of thousands of star bound together by gravity. Globular clusters generally form early in the galaxies’ histories in regions rich in gas and dust.

Name: Globular Cluster Messier 22
Description: M22 is one of about 150 globular star clusters in the Milky Way. Located just 10,000 light-years away in the constellation Sagittarius, it is one of the closest globular clusters to Earth.

Name: Red Rectangle Nebula
Description: This image reveals details of one of the most unusual nebulae known in our Milky Way. Cataloged as HD 44179, this nebula is more commonly called the "Red Rectangle" because of its unique shape and color.

Name: Spiral Galaxy Messier 83
Description: This image of spiral galaxy M83 captures thousands of star clusters, hundreds of thousands of individual stars, and "ghosts" of dead stars called supernova remnants.

Name: Omega Centauri

Name: Water Plumes on Europa
Description: This composite image shows a suspected plume of material erupting near the 9 o'clock position off the limb of Jupiter's icy moon Europa. The plume corresponds to the location of an unusually warm spot on the moon's icy crust.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 4258
Description: NGC 4258 is a large spiral galaxy undergoing vigorous star and star-cluster formation, which occurs along the dark filaments that make up the spiral arms.

Name: Pinwheel Galaxy
Description: The Pinwheel galaxy has a pancake-like shape that we view face-on. This perspective shows off the spiral structure that gives the galaxy its nickname.

Name: Colliding Galaxy NGC 6745
Description: This image captures the collision of two galaxies. The larger spiral galaxy, NGC 6745, boasts an intact nucleus as it interacts with the smaller, passing galaxy that is nearly out of the frame to the lower right.

Name: Interacting Galaxy NGC 3690
Description: This system consists of a pair of galaxies that made a close pass some 700 million years ago. As a result of this interaction, the system underwent a fierce burst of star formation.

Name: Elliptical Galaxy Messier 87

Name: Spiral Galaxy UGC 9684
Description: This image of the spiral galaxy UGC 9684 shows an impressive example of several classic galactic features, including a clear bar in the galaxy's center, and a halo surrounding its disk.

Name: Spiral Galaxy Messier 83
Description: This image of spiral galaxy M83 captures thousands of star clusters, hundreds of thousands of individual stars, and "ghosts" of dead stars called supernova remnants.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 3982
Description: Face-on spiral galaxy NGC 3982 has arms lined with pink star-forming regions of glowing hydrogen, blue newborn star clusters, and dark dust lanes that provide the raw material for future generations of stars.

Name: Interacting Galaxy ESO 593-8
Description: ESO 593-8 is an impressive pair of interacting galaxies. One feather-shaped galaxy is crossing a companion. The two components will probably merge to form a single galaxy in the future.

Description: Light from a distant galaxy was deflected on its way to Earth by the gravitational field of a massive object along its path that magnified and distorted the galaxy's light into the arcs we see here.
