Description: This image captures the collision of two galaxies. The larger spiral galaxy, NGC 6745, boasts an intact nucleus as it interacts with the smaller, passing galaxy that is nearly out of the frame to the lower right.

Name: Interacting Galaxy ESO 148-2
Description: The cores of the two colliding galaxies ― seen at the center of the image ― are embedded in hot dust and contain a large number of stars. Two large tidal tails of stars and gas were pulled from the disks of the galaxies.

Name: Core of Galaxy Messier 81
Description: M81's central bulge is significantly larger than that of our Milky Way. A black hole of 70 million solar masses ― 15 times the size of the Milky Way's black hole ― resides at its center.

Name: Snowman Nebula
Description: Sweeping curves of bright gas and dark knots of dust appear in a small section of the Snowman Nebula. The gas has become charged by the energy of nearby massive stars until it glows.

Name: Skewed Spiral Arp 184
Description: Arp 184 has a single broad, star-speckled spiral arm that appears to stretch toward us. The galaxy’s far side sports a few wisps of gas and stars, but it lacks a similarly impressive spiral arm.

Name: Saturn
Description: This image of Saturn captures details in the hazes and clouds of the planet's atmosphere. The view is so sharp that it also reveals individual ringlets in Saturn's ring system.

Name: Globular Cluster Messier 22
Description: M22 is one of about 150 globular star clusters in the Milky Way. Located just 10,000 light-years away in the constellation Sagittarius, it is one of the closest globular clusters to Earth.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 4395
Description: This image of dwarf spiral galaxy NGC 4395 looks at a small section of the galaxy. NGC 4395 is one of the closest and dimmest known Seyfert galaxies, which have very bright cores driven by supermassive black holes.

Name: Snowman Nebula
Description: Sweeping curves of bright gas and dark knots of dust appear in a small section of the Snowman Nebula. The gas has become charged by the energy of nearby massive stars until it glows.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 1559
Description: This magnificent barred spiral galaxy is NGC 1559. This picture is composed of 10 different Hubble images, from ultraviolet through visible light and into the near-infrared spectrum.

Name: Dwarf Galaxy Holmberg IX
Description: This loose collection of stars is actually a dwarf irregular galaxy, called Holmberg IX. Of the more than 20,000 stars that can be resolved in this image, only about 10 percent are considered to be old stars.

Name: Galaxy Cluster Abell 2218
Description: Galaxy cluster Abell 2218 is a gravitational lens, warping and magnifying galaxies that lie behind the cluster core. The orange arc, for instance, is an elliptical galaxy much farther away, behind the cluster.

Name: Spiral Galaxy Messier 81
Description: The arms of the "grand design" spiral galaxy M81 are filled with young, bluish, hot stars. The greenish regions in the image are bright, gaseous clouds where new stars are forming.

Name: Globular Cluster NGC 6397
Description: Looking like glittering jewels, the stars in this image are part of the ancient globular star cluster NGC 6397. Scattered among these brilliant stars are the faintest stars ever seen in a globular cluster.

Name: Elliptical Galaxy Messier 87
Description: This image of the giant galaxy M87 shows a 3,000-light-year-long jet of plasma blasting from the galaxy's 6.5-billion-solar-mass central black hole. The jet seems to cause stars to erupt along its trajectory.

Name: Galactic Center
Description: This infrared image of the center of our Milky Way galaxy reveals a population of massive stars and complex structures in the hot ionized gas that swirls around the galactic core.

Name: Shadow on TW Hydrae’s Disk
Description: This image reveals a shadow moving counterclockwise around a gas-and-dust disk encircling the young star TW Hydrae. The shadow may be caused by the gravitational effect of an unseen planet orbiting close to the star.

Name: Globular Cluster NGC 6397
Description: Looking like glittering jewels, the stars in this image are part of the ancient globular star cluster NGC 6397. Scattered among these brilliant stars are the faintest stars ever seen in a globular cluster.

Name: Galaxy NGC 4438
Description: Known as a peculiar galaxy because of its unusual shape, NGC 4438 is home to a supermassive black hole at its center that is blowing huge bubbles of hot gas into space.

Name: Omega Centauri
Description: Omega Centauri consists of roughly 10 million stars that are gravitationally bound. The cluster is about 10 times as massive as other big globular clusters – almost as massive as a small galaxy.

Name: Interstellar Bubble N44F
Description: This circular feature on the left side of this image is an interstellar bubble called N44F. It is being inflated by a torrent of fast-moving particles from an exceptionally hot star once buried inside this cold, dense cloud.

Name: Globular Cluster NGC 6397
Description: Looking like glittering jewels, the stars in this image are part of the ancient globular star cluster NGC 6397. Scattered among these brilliant stars are the faintest stars ever seen in a globular cluster.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 5468
Description: The galaxy NGC 5468 has hosted a number of observed supernovae. The orientation of the spiral galaxy with respect to us makes it easier to spot these exploding stars as they appear; we see it face on, meaning we can see the galaxy’s loose, open spiral pattern in beautiful detail.

Name: Veil Nebula
Description: The Veil Nebula is the remnant of a star roughly 20 times as massive as our Sun that exploded about 10,000 years ago. If you could see the entire nebula without the aid of a telescope, it would be as wide as six full Moons placed side-by-side.

Name: Barnard’s Galaxy
Description: NGC 6822 or Caldwell 57, also called Barnard’s Galaxy, lies more than 2 million light-years away, still within our corner of the cosmos. This image shows a field of stars in the galaxy’s outskirts. The long gap is an artifact of one of Hubble's old cameras.

Name: Star RS Puppis
Description: The bright star RS Puppis is swaddled in a cocoon of reflective dust illuminated by the glittering star. The star is 10 times more massive than our Sun and is 200 times larger.

Name: Globular Cluster Messier 22
Description: M22 is one of about 150 globular star clusters in the Milky Way. Located just 10,000 light-years away in the constellation Sagittarius, it is one of the closest globular clusters to Earth.

Name: Globular Cluster NGC 6397
Description: Looking like glittering jewels, the stars in this image are part of the ancient globular star cluster NGC 6397. Scattered among these brilliant stars are the faintest stars ever seen in a globular cluster.

Name: Quasar 3C 273
Description: Astronomers have peered into the throat of an energetic monster black hole powering a quasar called 3C 273. A quasar is a galactic center that glows brightly as the black hole consumes material in its immediate surroundings.

Name: Spiral Galaxy Messier 81
Description: The arms of the "grand design" spiral galaxy M81 are filled with young, bluish, hot stars. The greenish regions in the image are bright, gaseous clouds where new stars are forming.

Name: Spiral Galaxy Messier 81
Description: The arms of the "grand design" spiral galaxy M81 are filled with young, bluish, hot stars. The greenish regions in the image are bright, gaseous clouds where new stars are forming.

Name: Galaxy Cluster Abell 1351
Description: This image of the galaxy cluster Abell 1351 is filled with streaks of light that are actually images of distant galaxies. The light from these faraway galaxies is warped by the gravity of Abell 1351, which is so massive that it bends space-time!

Name: White Dwarf Stein 2051 B
Description: The white dwarf star Stein 2051 B and the smaller star below it appear to be close neighbors, but actually reside far away from each other. Stein 2051 B is 17 light-years from Earth; the other star is about 5,000 light-years away.

Name: Protostar in IC 2631
Description: This infrared image captures a protostar in the reflection nebula IC 2631. Eventually the core of a protostar becomes hot and dense enough for nuclear fusion to begin, transforming it into a star.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 5410 and Companion
Description: This pair of interacting galaxies is made up of larger spiral NGC 5410, which contains many young, blue star clusters, and smaller galaxy UGC 8932, which is likely distorted by NGC 5410’s gravitational pull.

Name: Ghost Head Nebula
Description: The Ghost Head Nebula is a star-forming region in a nearby galaxy called the Large Magellanic Cloud. The two bright areas (the "eyes of the ghost") are very hot, glowing blobs of hydrogen and oxygen.

Name: Dwarf Galaxy IC 4662
Description: This image captures a starburst region in the dwarf galaxy IC 4662. Starburst regions are areas of intense star formation.

Name: Infrared Jupiter and Moons
Description: Near-infrared Hubble observations show a rare alignment of three of Jupiter's largest moons - Io, Ganymede, and Callisto – scattering their shadows over the gas giant planet. While all three moons’ shadows are visible on the planet, Callisto is not visible in this picture.

Name: Jellyfish Galaxy JO175
Description: The jellyfish galaxy, JO175, appears to hang suspended in space. Jellyfish galaxies get their unusual name from the tendrils of star-forming gas and dust that trail behind them like the tentacles of a jellyfish.

Name: Herbig-Haro Object HH111
Description: This striking image features a relatively rare phenomenon known as a Herbig-Haro object, in this case HH111. These objects develop when streams of ionized gas collide with clouds of gas and dust that surround newly formed stars at speeds of hundreds of miles per second.

Name: Starburst Galaxy Messier 82
Description: Galaxy M82 is remarkable for its bright blue disk, webs of shredded clouds, and fiery-looking plumes of glowing hydrogen blasting out of its central region. In M82, stars are being born 10 times faster than they are inside our Milky Way galaxy.

Name: Spiral Galaxy Messier 61
Description: The luminous heart of the spiral galaxy M61 is framed by its winding spiral arms, threaded with dark tendrils of dust. In addition to bright bands of stars, the spiral arms of M61 are studded with ruby-red patches of light.

Name: Interacting Galaxies IRAS 18090
Description: This system consists of two interacting spiral galaxies. The galaxy to the left displays a dim plume of luminosity that extends to the right in the direction of the second spiral.

Name: Globular Cluster Messier 4
Description: Peering deep inside a cluster of several hundred thousand stars uncovers the oldest burned-out stars in our Milky Way Galaxy. Located in the globular cluster M4, these small, dying stars are known as white dwarfs.

Name: Elliptical Galaxy Messier 84
Description: M84 is an elliptical galaxy, one of over a thousand galaxies that make up the Virgo cluster. This image combines observations taken at visible, infrared, and ultraviolet wavelengths.

Name: Four Faces of Mars
Description: Four sides of Mars are captured in these Hubble images taken over the course of a day. Mars has rotated about ninety degrees between each view.

Name: Globular Cluster NGC 6397
Description: Looking like glittering jewels, the stars in this image are part of the ancient globular star cluster NGC 6397. Scattered among these brilliant stars are the faintest stars ever seen in a globular cluster.

Name: Globular Cluster Messier 107
Description: M107 is one of more than 150 globular star clusters found around the disk of our Milky Way Galaxy. These spherical collections each contain hundreds of thousands of extremely old stars and are among the oldest objects in the galaxy.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 5584
Description: The brilliant, blue glow of young stars traces the graceful spiral arms of galaxy NGC 5584. Thin, dark dust lanes appear to be flowing from the yellowish core, where older stars reside.

Name: Orion Nebula
Description: The Orion Nebula, a turbulent stellar nursery, is a perfect laboratory to study how stars are born because it is just 1,500 light-years away, a relatively short distance within our galaxy.

Name: Interacting Galaxies AM 0500-620
Description: AM 0500-620 includes a pair of galaxies, with one spiral galaxy seen nearly face-on that is partially backlit by a background galaxy. These interacting galaxies are located 350 million light-years away in the constellation Dorado.

Name: Globular Cluster NGC 6397
Description: Looking like glittering jewels, the stars in this image are part of the ancient globular star cluster NGC 6397. Scattered among these brilliant stars are the faintest stars ever seen in a globular cluster.

Name: Orion Nebula
Description: The Orion Nebula is the nearest star-forming region to Earth. Massive, young stars are shaping the nebula with their winds and radiation. Pillars of dense gas may be the homes of budding stars. The bright central region is the home of the four heftiest stars in the nebula.

Name: Spiral Galaxy UGC 9391
Description: This spiral galaxy, UGC 9391, contains two types of stars that astronomers use to calculate accurate distances to galaxies and refine the measurement for how fast the universe expands with time, called the Hubble constant.

Name: Spiral Galaxy Messier 96
Description: M96 is a spiral galaxy about the same mass and size as our own Milky Way. It is very asymmetrical because of the gravitational pull of its neighboring galaxies.

Name: Eagle Nebula Pillars
Description: Hubble's view of the "Pillars of Creation" in the Eagle Nebula displays three giant columns of cold gas giving birth to new stars. The pillars are bathed in the scorching ultraviolet light from a cluster of young, massive stars beyond the top of the image.

Name: Comet P/2019 LD2
Description: Hubble snapped this image of a young comet as it orbited near Jupiter's gravitationally captured ancient asteroids, called the Trojans. This is the first comet astronomers spotted near the Trojans.

Name: Tadpole Galaxy
Description: This odd-looking galaxy with the long streamer of stars, dubbed the "tadpole" and also known as UGC 10214, appears to be racing through space like a runaway pinwheel firework.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 1961
Description: The galaxy NGC 1961 unfurls magnificent spiral arms. Glittering, blue regions of bright young stars dot the dusty spiral arms, winding around the galaxy’s glowing center.

Name: Symbiotic Star Mira HM Sge
Description: Located 3,400 light-years away, the symbiotic star Mira HM Sge consists of a red giant and a white dwarf companion. The stars are too close together to be resolved by Hubble in this image.

Name: Interacting Galaxies Arp 274
Description: Arp 274 is a system of three galaxies that appear to be partially overlapping. Two of the galaxies are rapidly forming new stars, evident in the bright blue knots strung along the arms of the galaxy on the right and along the small galaxy on the left.

Name: Globular Cluster NGC 6397
Description: Looking like glittering jewels, the stars in this image are part of the ancient globular star cluster NGC 6397. Scattered among these brilliant stars are the faintest stars ever seen in a globular cluster.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 3982
Description: Face-on spiral galaxy NGC 3982 has arms lined with pink star-forming regions of glowing hydrogen, blue newborn star clusters, and dark dust lanes that provide the raw material for future generations of stars.

Name: Omega Nebula
Description: This hotbed of newly formed stars is known as the Omega Nebula. The region of the nebula seen here by Hubble is 3,500 times wider than our entire solar system.

Name: Elliptical Galaxy Messier 87
Description: This image of the giant galaxy M87 shows a 3,000-light-year-long jet of plasma blasting from the galaxy's 6.5-billion-solar-mass central black hole. The jet seems to cause stars to erupt along its trajectory.

Name: Jupiter
Description: This image of Jupiter was taken when the planet was closest to Earth in 2017. The Great Red Spot appears on the left side, along with a smaller, reddish storm in the lower right dubbed "Red Spot Jr."

Name: Globular Cluster Messier 22
Description: M22 is one of about 150 globular star clusters in the Milky Way. Located just 10,000 light-years away in the constellation Sagittarius, it is one of the closest globular clusters to Earth.

Name: Planetary Nebula Hubble 12
Description: The hourglass shape of this bipolar planetary nebula known as PN Hb 12 (a.k.a. Hubble 12) was formed as a Sun-like star approached the end of its life and puffed its outer layers into the surrounding space.

Name: Jellyfish Galaxy JO206
Description: The jellyfish galaxy JO206 showcases a colorful star-forming disk surrounded by a pale, luminous cloud of dust. The tendrils of jellyfish galaxies are formed by the interaction between galaxies and galaxy clusters.

Name: Stars in the Galactic Core
Description: These colorful stars reside at the heart of our Milky Way galaxy, about 26,000 light-years from Earth. Aging red giant stars coexist with their more plentiful younger cousins, the smaller, white, Sun-like stars, in this crowded region of our galaxy's central hub.

Name: Galaxy Pair NGC 3314
Description: This image shows a pair of galaxies called NGC 3314. Through a chance alignment, a face-on spiral galaxy lies precisely in front of another, larger spiral. This provides a view of dark material within the front galaxy, seen because it is silhouetted against the galaxy behind it.

Name: Open Cluster NGC 6530
Description: A portion of the open cluster NGC 6530 appears as a roiling wall of smoke studded with stars. The cluster is set within the larger Lagoon Nebula, a gigantic interstellar cloud of gas and dust.

Name: White Dwarf Stein 2051 B
Description: The white dwarf star Stein 2051 B and the smaller star below it appear to be close neighbors, but actually reside far away from each other. Stein 2051 B is 17 light-years from Earth; the other star is about 5,000 light-years away.

Name: Comet 252P/LINEAR
Description: This image was taken roughly two weeks after the icy visitor Comet 252P/LINEAR made its closest approach to Earth on March 21 while traveling away from Earth and the Sun in one of the closest encounters between a comet and our planet.

Name: Jellyfish Galaxy JO206
Description: The jellyfish galaxy JO206 showcases a colorful star-forming disk surrounded by a pale, luminous cloud of dust. The tendrils of jellyfish galaxies are formed by the interaction between galaxies and galaxy clusters.

Name: Galactic Center
Description: This infrared image of the center of our Milky Way galaxy reveals a population of massive stars and complex structures in the hot ionized gas that swirls around the galactic core.

Name: Globular Cluster 47 Tucanae
Description: This image shows the core of the globular star cluster 47 Tucanae. The entire cluster contains about a million stars, with many packed tightly in the core.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 3368
Description: NGC 3368 is a large spiral galaxy about 35 million light-years from Earth. It is undergoing vigorous star and star cluster formation, which occurs along the dark filaments that make up the spiral arms.

Name: Globular Cluster Messier 80
Description: This stellar swarm is one of the densest of the 147 known globular star clusters in the Milky Way galaxy. M80, also called NGC 6093, contains hundreds of thousands of stars, all held together by their mutual gravitational attraction.

Name: Open Cluster Pismis 24
Description: The small open star cluster Pismis 24 lies in the core of the large emission nebula NGC 6357. Some of the stars in this cluster are extremely massive and emit intense ultraviolet radiation.

Name: Galaxy ESO 510-G13
Description: Usually, when a spiral galaxy appears edge-on, its dust and spiral arms appear flat. The warping of the disk in ESO 510-G13 suggests this galaxy has recently undergone a collision with a nearby galaxy and is in the process of swallowing it.

Name: Galaxy RX J1504
Description: This galaxy shows chains of star formation in ultraviolet light. This star formation is a product of the action of the jets from a central black hole that controls infalling gas from the galaxy's halo.

Name: Orion Nebula
Description: The Orion Nebula is the nearest star-forming region to Earth. Massive young stars are shaping the nebula with their winds and radiation. Pillars of dense gas may be the homes of budding stars. The bright central region is the home of the four heftiest stars in the nebula.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 1559
Description: This magnificent barred spiral galaxy is NGC 1559. This picture is composed of 10 different Hubble images, from ultraviolet through visible light and into the near-infrared spectrum.

Name: Mile-Wide Asteroid Streak
Description: While performing a detailed study of the Sun's nearest stellar neighbor, Proxima Centauri, Hubble captured an asteroid streak (upper right), seen here as a curved blue line against the backdrop of stars.

Name: 30 Doradus Nebula
Description: Glowing hydrogen clouds and dark filamentary dust structures are visible in this close-up view of a star-birth region called the 30 Doradus Nebula. The giant stellar factory lies 170,000 light-years away inside the Large Magellanic Cloud.

Name: Orion Nebula
Description: The Orion Nebula is the nearest star-forming region to Earth. Massive young stars are shaping the nebula with their winds and radiation. Pillars of dense gas may be the homes of budding stars. The bright central region is the home of the four heftiest stars in the nebula.

Name: Interacting Galaxy IC 4687
Description: IC 4687 (left) forms a triplet with two other galaxies. It has a chaotic body of stars, gas, and dust and a large curly tail to the left. The two companions are partially obscured by dark bands of dust.

Name: Irregular Galaxy PGC 18431
Description: The sphere of space surrounding our galaxy is known as the Local Volume, a region 35 million light-years in diameter and home to several hundred known galaxies. The beautiful dwarf irregular galaxy known as PGC 18431 is one of them.

Name: Elliptical Galaxy Fornax A
Description: This beautiful silhouette of dark dust clouds against the glowing nucleus of the elliptical galaxy Fornax A may represent the aftermath of a 100-million-year-old cosmic collision between the elliptical and a smaller companion galaxy.

Name: Polar-Ring Galaxy NGC 4650A
Description: About 130 million light-years away, NGC 4650A is one of only 100 known polar-ring galaxies, which feature a ring of stars encircling a disk. Polar rings might form when two galaxies collide, with one galaxy becoming the inner disk and the other forming the ring.

Name: Black Eye Galaxy
Description: Messier 64, formed by a collision of two galaxies, has a spectacular dark band of dust in front of the galaxy's bright nucleus, giving rise to its nicknames of the "Black Eye" or "Evil Eye" galaxy.

Name: Interacting Galaxy ESO 69-6
Description: The galaxies of this interacting pair, called ESO 69-6, bear some resemblance to musical notes. Long tidal tails of gas and stars torn away from the outer regions sweep out from the two galaxies.

Name: Orion Nebula
Description: The Orion Nebula is the nearest star-forming region to Earth. Massive young stars are shaping the nebula with their winds and radiation. Pillars of dense gas may be the homes of budding stars. The bright central region is the home of the four heftiest stars in the nebula.

Name: Jupiter's Junior Red Spot
Description: Astronomers witnessed the birth of a new red spot on the planet Jupiter, which is located half a billion miles away. Dubbed "Red Spot Jr.," the storm is roughly one-half the diameter of its bigger and legendary cousin, the Great Red Spot.

Name: Jupiter and Ganymede
Description: This image shows Jupiter and its large moon Ganymede as the moon peeks out from behind the planet. Composed of rock and ice, Ganymede is the largest moon in our solar system.

Name: Proxima Centauri
Description: Shining brightly in this image is our closest stellar neighbor: Proxima Centauri, just over four light-years from Earth. Although it looks bright through the eye of Hubble, Proxima Centauri is not visible to the naked eye.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 5584
Description: The brilliant, blue glow of young stars traces the graceful spiral arms of galaxy NGC 5584. Thin, dark dust lanes appear to be flowing from the yellowish core, where older stars reside.

Name: 30 Doradus Nebula
Description: Glowing hydrogen clouds and dark filamentary dust structures are visible in this close-up view of a star-birth region called the 30 Doradus Nebula. The giant stellar factory lies 170,000 light-years away inside the Large Magellanic Cloud.

Name: Polar-Ring Galaxy NGC 4650A
Description: Located about 130 million light-years away, NGC 4650A is one of only 100 known polar-ring galaxies. Their unusual disk-ring structure is not yet fully understood.

Name: Circinus Galaxy
Description: Resembling a swirling witch's cauldron of glowing vapors, the black-hole-powered core of the Circinus galaxy appears in this image. Much of the gas in the spiral galaxy's disk is concentrated in two rings.

Name: Comet ISON
Description: This image of Comet C/2012 S1 (ISON) was taken when the comet was slightly closer than Jupiter's orbit. Even at that great distance, the comet was already active as sunlight warmed the surface and caused frozen volatiles to sublimate.

Name: Diffuse Galaxy GAMA 526784
Description: The ultra-diffuse galaxy GAMA 526784 appears as a tenuous patch of light in this image. One oddity of this class of galaxies is their unusual abundance of bright globular star clusters, something not observed in other types of galaxies.

Name: Globular Cluster 47 Tucanae
Description: The ancient globular cluster 47 Tucanae is a dense swarm of up to a million stars, and this view captures a close-up of thousands of them. The large, bright stars in the image are red giants near the end of their lives.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 4414
Description: This Hubble image reveals the central regions of the dusty spiral galaxy NGC 4414. The galaxy’s arms are very rich in clouds of interstellar dust, visible as dark patches and streaks silhouetted against the starlight.

Name: Galactic Center
Description: This infrared image of the center of our Milky Way galaxy reveals a population of massive stars and complex structures in the hot ionized gas that swirls around the galactic core.

Name: Galaxy Hydra A
Description: This galaxy shows chains of star formation in ultraviolet light. This star formation in each galaxy is a product of the action of the jets from a central black hole that controls infalling gas from the galaxy's halo.

Name: Orion Nebula
Description: The Orion Nebula is the nearest star-forming region to Earth. Massive young stars are shaping the nebula with their winds and radiation. Pillars of dense gas may be the homes of budding stars. The bright central region is the home of the four heftiest stars in the nebula.

Name: Brown Dwarf 2M1207A and Companion
Description: This brown dwarf, no more than 30 times the mass of Jupiter, is too small to become a star. When its glow is removed, a smaller and fainter companion becomes visible. No more that four times the mass of Jupiter, this companion is called a "super-Jupiter."

Name: 30 Doradus Nebula
Description: Glowing hydrogen clouds and dark filamentary dust structures are visible in this close-up view of a star-birth region called the 30 Doradus Nebula. The giant stellar factory lies 170,000 light-years away inside the Large Magellanic Cloud.

Name: Hanny's Voorwerp
Description: This image shows a ghostly green blob of gas that appears to float near a normal-looking spiral galaxy. The bizarre object, dubbed Hanny's Voorwerp, is the visible part of a 300,000-light-year-long streamer of gas stretching around the galaxy, called IC 2497.

Name: Globular Cluster 47 Tucanae
Description: This image shows the core of the globular star cluster 47 Tucanae. The entire cluster contains about a million stars, with many packed tightly in the core.

Name: Orion Nebula
Description: The Orion Nebula, a turbulent stellar nursery, is a perfect laboratory to study how stars are born because it is just 1,500 light-years away, a relatively short distance within our galaxy.

Name: Dwarf Galaxy Leo A
Description: This image features the nearby dwarf irregular galaxy Leo A. Astronomers study dwarf galaxies like Leo A because they are numerous and may offer clues to how galaxies grow and evolve.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 4414
Description: This Hubble image reveals the central regions of the dusty spiral galaxy NGC 4414. The galaxy’s arms are very rich in clouds of interstellar dust, visible as dark patches and streaks silhouetted against the starlight.

Name: Galaxy Cluster Abell 2261
Description: The giant elliptical galaxy in the center of this image is the most massive and brightest member of galaxy cluster Abell 2261. More than a million light-years wide, the galaxy is about 10 times bigger than our Milky Way galaxy.

Name: Globular Cluster 47 Tucanae
Description: This image shows the core of the globular star cluster 47 Tucanae. The entire cluster contains about a million stars, with many packed tightly in the core.

Name: Stellar Jet in the Running Man Nebula
Description: A jet from a newly formed star flares into the shining depths of reflection nebula NGC 1977. The jet (orange object at bottom center) is being emitted by the young star Parengo 2042, which is embedded in a disk of debris that could give rise to planets.

Name: De Mairan's Nebula
Description: A massive star is illuminating this small region, called Messier 43 or De Mairan's Nebula, and sculpting the landscape of dust and gas.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 6956
Description: Against an inky black backdrop, the blue swirls of spiral galaxy NGC 6956 stand out radiantly. NGC 6956 is a barred spiral galaxy, a common type of spiral galaxy with a bar-shaped structure of stars in its center.

Name: Interacting Galaxy ESO 99-4
Description: ESO 99-4 is a galaxy with a highly peculiar shape. It is probably the remnant of an earlier merger process that has deformed it, leaving the main body largely obscured by dark bands of dust.

Name: Sunburst Arc
Description: The Sunburst Arc is a galaxy almost 11 billion light-years from Earth. Its warped, arced appearance is because it's been gravitationally lensed into multiple images by a massive foreground cluster of galaxies that's 4.6 billion light-years away.

Name: Orion Nebula
Description: The Orion Nebula, a turbulent stellar nursery, is a perfect laboratory to study how stars are born because it is just 1,500 light-years away, a relatively short distance within our galaxy.

Name: Interacting Galaxy II Zw 96
Description: This is a system of merging galaxies with a bizarre shape called II Zw 96. Powerful young starburst regions hang as long threadlike structures between the main galaxy cores.

Name: Interacting Galaxy IRAS 20351
Description: IRAS 20351+2521 is a galaxy with a sprawling structure of gas, dust, and numerous blue star knots. It's located about 450 million light-years away from Earth.

Name: Veil Nebula
Description: In this small piece of the Veil Nebula, wisps of gas are part of what remains of a star that was once 20 times more massive than our Sun. A fast-moving blast wave from the star's explosion is plowing into a wall of interstellar gas, causing it to glow.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 5584
Description: The brilliant, blue glow of young stars traces the graceful spiral arms of galaxy NGC 5584. Thin, dark dust lanes appear to be flowing from the yellowish core, where older stars reside.

Name: Planetary Nebula NGC 6891
Description: NGC 6891 is a bright, asymmetrical planetary nebula. Hubble captures the central white dwarf star, a spherical outer halo that is expanding faster than the inner nebula, and at least two ellipsoidal shells that are oriented differently.

Name: Globular Cluster Messier 4
Description: M4 is a dense collection of several hundred thousand stars. Astronomers suspect that an intermediate-mass black hole, weighing as much as 800 times the mass of our Sun, lurks unseen at its core.

Name: Orion Nebula
Description: The Orion Nebula is the nearest star-forming region to Earth. Massive young stars are shaping the nebula with their winds and radiation. Pillars of dense gas may be the homes of budding stars. The bright central region is the home of the four heftiest stars in the nebula.

Name: Veil Nebula
Description: In this small piece of the Veil Nebula, wisps of gas are part of what remains of a star that was once 20 times more massive than our Sun. A fast-moving blast wave from the star's explosion is plowing into a wall of interstellar gas, causing it to glow.

Name: Jupiter's Junior Red Spot
Description: Astronomers witnessed the birth of a new red spot on the planet Jupiter, which is located half a billion miles away. Dubbed "Red Spot Jr.," the storm is roughly one-half the diameter of its bigger and legendary cousin, the Great Red Spot.

Name: Galaxy Abell 1664
Description: This galaxy shows chains of star formation in ultraviolet light. This star formation is a product of the action of the jets from a central black hole that controls infalling gas from the galaxy's halo.

Name: Globular Cluster Messier 2
Description: M2 is one of the largest globular star clusters, a spherical group of stars bound together by their mutual gravitational attraction. Most of the cluster’s mass is concentrated at its center, with shimmering streams of stars extending outward into space.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 3370
Description: The majestic dusty spiral galaxy, NGC 3370, shows intricate spiral arm structure spotted with hot areas of new star formation. In 1994, it hosted an exploding star called SN 1994ae, which briefly outshone the tens of billions of other stars in its galaxy.

Name: Galaxy Cluster Abell 2261
Description: The giant elliptical galaxy in the center of this image is the most massive and brightest member of galaxy cluster Abell 2261. More than a million light-years wide, the galaxy is about 10 times bigger than our Milky Way galaxy.

Name: Galaxy Cluster IDCS J1426.5+3508
Description: The light we observe from this rare, extremely massive young galaxy cluster, IDCS 1426, left the cluster when the universe was less than a third of its current age.

Name: Medusa Merger
Description: The galaxy pictured in this image, called NGC 4194 and nicknamed the Medusa merger, was not always one entity, but two. An early galaxy consumed a smaller, gas-rich system, throwing out streams of stars and dust into space.

Name: Spiral Galaxy UGC 5460
Description: This image reveals UGC 5460’s central bar of stars, winding spiral arms, and bright blue star clusters. Also captured in the upper left-hand corner is a far closer object: a star just 577 light-years away in our own galaxy.

Name: Interacting Galaxies Arp 195
Description: Taking center stage in this image is a system known as Arp 195, a clashing triplet of interacting galaxies caught in a dramatic gravitational tug-of-war.

Name: Globular Cluster Messier 79
Description: The globular star cluster M79 is located 41,000 light-years from Earth. It contains about 150,000 stars packed into an area measuring only 118 light-years across. Its stars are some of the oldest in our galaxy.

Name: Globular Cluster Messier 22
Description: M22 is one of about 150 globular star clusters in the Milky Way. Located just 10,000 light-years away in the constellation Sagittarius, it is one of the closest globular clusters to Earth.

Name: Carina Nebula
Description: Previously unseen details of a mysterious, complex structure within the Carina Nebula, or NGC 3372, are revealed by this image of the "Keyhole Nebula," located about 8,000 light-years from Earth.

Name: Interacting Galaxies ESO 255-7
Description: ESO 255-7 consists of a quartet of interacting galaxies. Three or four galaxies are embedded in a common structure with an arc-like shape. The upper part of this structure appears almost like a single galaxy but is, in fact, two galaxies.

Name: Comet 73P/Schwassmann-Wachmann 3
Description: Astronomers got an extraordinary view of comet 73P/Schwassmann-Wachmann 3 as it fell apart. Hubble images uncovered many more fragments than were reported by ground-based observers.

Name: Asteroid P/2010 A2
Description: Hubble imaged a tail flowing from this peculiar asteroid, dubbed P/2010 A2. Scientists suspect the debris was produced by a collision with another asteroid.

Name: Colliding Galaxies Arp 143
Description: A spectacular head-on collision between two galaxies fueled the unusual triangular-shaped star-birthing frenzy seen in this image of Arp 143, a galaxy pair about 191 million light-years away!

Name: Dense Core CB 130-3
Description: CB 130-3 is an object known as a dense core, a compact agglomeration of gas and dust. Dense cores like this are the birthplaces of stars. A compact object teetering on the brink of becoming a star is embedded deep within CB 130-3.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 1559
Description: This magnificent barred spiral galaxy is NGC 1559. This picture is composed of 10 different Hubble images, from ultraviolet through visible light and into the near-infrared spectrum.

Name: Globular Cluster Messier 55
Description: This image shows just a portion of globular cluster M55. The cluster as a whole appears spherical because the stars’ intense gravitational attraction pulls them together.

Name: Galactic Center
Description: This infrared image of the center of our Milky Way galaxy reveals a population of massive stars and complex structures in the hot ionized gas that swirls around the galactic core.

Name: Galaxy Cluster IDCS J1426.5+3508
Description: The light we observe from this rare, extremely massive young galaxy cluster, IDCS 1426, left the cluster when the universe was less than a third of its current age.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 6956
Description: Against an inky black backdrop, the blue swirls of spiral galaxy NGC 6956 stand out radiantly. NGC 6956 is a barred spiral galaxy, a common type of spiral galaxy with a bar-shaped structure of stars in its center.

Name: Comet 73P/Schwassmann-Wachmann 3
Description: Astronomers got an extraordinary view of comet 73P/Schwassmann-Wachmann 3 as it fell apart. Hubble images uncovered many more fragments than were reported by ground-based observers.

Name: Omega Centauri
Description: Omega Centauri consists of roughly 10 million stars that are gravitationally bound. The cluster is about 10 times as massive as other big globular clusters – almost as massive as a small galaxy.

Name: Jupiter
Description: This image of Jupiter was taken by the Outer Planet Atmospheres Legacy (OPAL) program, a long-term project that uses Hubble to capture global maps of the outer planets every year. The Great Red Spot appears in the lower right.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 6503
Description: Most galaxies are clumped together in groups or clusters. A neighboring galaxy is never far away. But this galaxy, known as NGC 6503, has found itself in a lonely position, at the edge of a strangely empty patch of space called the Local Void.

Name: Globular Cluster Messier 22
Description: M22 is one of about 150 globular star clusters in the Milky Way. Located just 10,000 light-years away in the constellation Sagittarius, it is one of the closest globular clusters to Earth.

Name: Planetary Nebula NGC 6751
Description: This strikingly unusual planetary nebula, NGC 6751, is a cloud of gas ejected several thousand years ago from the hot star visible in its center.

Name: Jellyfish Galaxy JW39
Description: Despite jellyfish galaxy JW39’s serene appearance, it is adrift in a ferociously hostile environment: a galaxy cluster. Galaxies in galaxy clusters are often distorted by the gravitational pull of larger neighbors, twisting them into a variety of shapes.

Name: 30 Doradus Nebula
Description: This is the inner part of the 30 Doradus Nebula, a turbulent star-birth region in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a satellite galaxy of our Milky Way. The bright cluster of stars at left is known as R136.

Name: Crab Nebula
Description: The glow of a dead star, which exploded long ago as a supernova, reveals itself in this image of the Crab Nebula. At its center is a rotating neutron star, or pulsar, which has about the same mass as the Sun squeezed into a sphere only a few miles wide.

Name: Galaxy Cluster Abell S1063
Description: The immense galaxy cluster Abell S1063 is surrounded by magnified images of galaxies much farther away. The huge mass of the cluster distorts and magnifies the light from galaxies that lie far behind it due to an effect called gravitational lensing.

Name: Elliptical Galaxy Messier 87
Description: This image of the giant galaxy M87 shows a 3,000-light-year-long jet of plasma blasting from the galaxy's 6.5-billion-solar-mass central black hole. The jet seems to cause stars to erupt along its trajectory.

Name: Interacting Galaxies Arp 300
Description: Arp 300 consists of two interacting galaxies, UGC 05028 (the smaller galaxy) and UGC 05029 (the larger spiral). Likely due to its gravitational dance with its larger partner, UGC 05028 has an asymmetric, irregular structure.

Name: Galactic Center
Description: This infrared image of the center of our Milky Way galaxy reveals a population of massive stars and complex structures in the hot ionized gas that swirls around the galactic core.

Name: Galaxy Cluster Abell S1063
Description: The immense galaxy cluster Abell S1063 is surrounded by magnified images of galaxies much farther away. The huge mass of the cluster distorts and magnifies the light from galaxies that lie far behind it due to an effect called gravitational lensing.

Name: Comet ATLAS
Description: Hubble observed the Comet ATLAS disintegrating into multiple pieces. Before its breakup, the comet's nucleus was likely about the length of two football fields.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 3982
Description: Face-on spiral galaxy NGC 3982 has arms lined with pink star-forming regions of glowing hydrogen, blue newborn star clusters, and dark dust lanes that provide the raw material for future generations of stars.

Name: Lenticular Galaxy NGC 3489
Description: Lenticular galaxies like NGC 3489 exhibit traits of both spirals and ellipticals. They have a central bulge and a thin, circular disk, like spiral galaxies, but they lack arms. And like elliptical galaxies, they have older stars and little ongoing star formation.

Name: Cygnus Loop Supernova Remnant
Description: This image captures a small portion of the Cygnus Loop supernova remnant. The Cygnus Loop marks the edge of a bubble-like, expanding blast wave from a colossal stellar explosion that occurred about 15,000 years ago.

Name: Galaxy ZwCl 8193
Description: This galaxy shows chains of star formation in ultraviolet light. This star formation in each galaxy is a product of the action of the jets from a central black hole that controls infalling gas from the galaxy's halo.

Name: Globular Cluster Messier 22
Description: M22 is one of about 150 globular star clusters in the Milky Way. Located just 10,000 light-years away in the constellation Sagittarius, it is one of the closest globular clusters to Earth.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 4414
Description: This Hubble image reveals the central regions of the dusty spiral galaxy NGC 4414. The galaxy’s arms are very rich in clouds of interstellar dust, visible as dark patches and streaks silhouetted against the starlight.

Name: Tucana Dwarf
Description: Tucana Dwarf is a dwarf spheroidal galaxy, much smaller and less luminous than most other dwarf galaxies. Dust is sparse and the stellar population skews towards the older range, giving them a dimmer look.

Name: Two Red Spots on Jupiter
Description: This image captures a second "red spot" (lower left) that emerged alongside the bigger and more famous Great Red Spot (right) on Jupiter. The new storm is roughly one-half the size of the Great Red Spot.

Name: Omega Centauri
Description: Omega Centauri consists of roughly 10 million stars that are gravitationally bound. The cluster is about 10 times as massive as other big globular clusters – almost as massive as a small galaxy.

Name: Herbig-Haro 110
Description: Herbig-Haro 110 is a mystery – a stellar jet with no star found. Herbig-Haro objects are twin jets of heated gas, ejected in opposite directions away from a forming star. This one may result from a dark, dense cloud interrupting and diverting a different jet.

Name: Tucana Dwarf
Description: Tucana Dwarf is a dwarf spheroidal galaxy, much smaller and less luminous than most other dwarf galaxies. Dust is sparse and the stellar population skews towards the older range, giving them a dimmer look.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 5068
Description: NGC 5068 is a barred spiral galaxy. At the top center of this image lies NGC 5068’s bright central bar of mature stars. The bright pinkish-red splotches are regions of ionized hydrogen gas where young star clusters lie.

Name: Galactic Center
Description: This infrared image of the center of our Milky Way galaxy reveals a population of massive stars and complex structures in the hot ionized gas that swirls around the galactic core.

Name: Tucana Dwarf
Description: Tucana Dwarf is a dwarf spheroidal galaxy, much smaller and less luminous than most other dwarf galaxies. Dust is sparse and the stellar population skews towards the older range, giving them a dimmer look.

Name: Globular Cluster NGC 2419
Description: Globular star clusters like NGC 2419 are both beautiful and fascinating. These spherical groups of stars orbit the center of a galaxy. The stars populating globular clusters are very similar because they formed at roughly the same time, from the same collapsing cloud of gas.

Name: Orion Nebula
Description: The Orion Nebula is the nearest star-forming region to Earth. Massive young stars are shaping the nebula with their winds and radiation. Pillars of dense gas may be the homes of budding stars. The bright central region is the home of the four heftiest stars in the nebula.

Name: Galaxy Cluster Abell S1063
Description: The immense galaxy cluster Abell S1063 is surrounded by magnified images of galaxies much farther away. The huge mass of the cluster distorts and magnifies the light from galaxies that lie far behind it due to an effect called gravitational lensing.

Name: Supernova Remnant N 49
Description: N 49 is a supernova remnant in a neighboring galaxy called the Large Magellanic Cloud. The delicate filaments are sheets of debris from a stellar explosion whose light would have reached Earth thousands of years ago.

Name: Omega Centauri
Description: Omega Centauri consists of roughly 10 million stars that are gravitationally bound. The cluster is about 10 times as massive as other big globular clusters – almost as massive as a small galaxy.

Name: NaSt1 Wolf-Rayet Star
Description: A pancake-shaped disk of gas surrounds an extremely bright star nicknamed "Nasty 1," derived from its catalog name of NaSt1. Nasty 1 is thought to be a Wolf-Rayet star, a massive, rapidly evolving star well over 10 times the mass of our Sun.

Name: Makemake and its Moon
Description: This image reveals the first moon discovered around dwarf planet Makemake. The tiny moon, located just above Makemake in this image, is almost lost in the glare of the bright dwarf planet.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 5068
Description: NGC 5068 is a barred spiral galaxy. At the top center of this image lies NGC 5068’s bright central bar of mature stars. The bright pinkish-red splotches are regions of ionized hydrogen gas where young star clusters lie.

Name: Galaxy Cluster SDSS J1004+4112
Description: This picture captures a galaxy cluster called SDSS J1004+4112 that's so massive that its gravity bends and magnifies light from galaxies behind it. The light of a distant quasar (the brilliant core of an active galaxy) has been bent around the cluster, appearing in five places in this image.

Name: Elliptical Galaxy NGC 4993
Description: In this galaxy, called NGC 4993, two neutron stars collided, creating gravitational waves discovered in 2017. The event produced a flash of light, called a kilonova, which appears to the upper left of center.

Name: Saturn Nebula
Description: The planetary nebula Caldwell 55, also called the Saturn Nebula and NGC 7009, formed when the dying star at the nebula’s heart cast off its outer layers. The resulting gaseous shells make it resemble a piece of wrapped cosmic candy.

Name: Galaxy Pair Arp 116
Description: The giant elliptical galaxy Messier 60 and a much smaller spiral galaxy, NGC 4647, make up the galaxy pair Arp 116. It’s unclear whether these two galaxies are interacting gravitationally – they may just overlap from our viewpoint on Earth. NGC 4647 is about the size of our Milky Way, while M60 has the mass of about a trillion times that of the Sun.

Name: Omega Centauri
Description: Omega Centauri consists of roughly 10 million stars that are gravitationally bound. The cluster is about 10 times as massive as other big globular clusters – almost as massive as a small galaxy.

Name: Nebula N 180B
Description: N 180B is an active region of star formation in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a dwarf galaxy orbiting our Milky Way. This particular region contains some of the brightest known star clusters.

Name: Omega Centauri
Description: Omega Centauri consists of roughly 10 million stars that are gravitationally bound. The cluster is about 10 times as massive as other big globular clusters – almost as massive as a small galaxy.

Name: White Dwarf Stein 2051 B
Description: The white dwarf star Stein 2051 B and the smaller star below it appear to be close neighbors, but actually reside far away from each other. Stein 2051 B is 17 light-years from Earth; the other star is about 5,000 light-years away.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 3972
Description: In galaxy NGC 3972, astronomers examine pulsating stars called Cepheid variables, which blink at a rate matched closely by their intrinsic brightness, making them ideal for measuring accurate distances to relatively nearby galaxies.

Name: Makemake and its Moon
Description: This image reveals the first moon discovered around the dwarf planet Makemake. The tiny moon, located just above Makemake in this image, is almost lost in the glare of the bright dwarf planet.

Name: Star V838 Monocerotis
Description: In 2002, a dim star suddenly became 600,000 times more luminous than our Sun, temporarily making it the brightest star in our Milky Way galaxy. This image of V838 Monocerotis captures its "light echo."

Name: Comet ISON
Description: The Sun-approaching Comet ISON floats against a backdrop of numerous galaxies and a handful of foreground stars. The icy visitor, with its long tail, appears to be swimming through a deep pond of celestial wonders.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 5068
Description: NGC 5068 is a barred spiral galaxy. At the top center of this image lies NGC 5068’s bright central bar of mature stars. The bright pinkish-red splotches are regions of ionized hydrogen gas where young star clusters lie.

Name: Neptune
Description: This image of the distant planet Neptune shows a dynamic atmosphere and captures the fleeting orbits of its moons. Neptune is the most distant giant planet in our solar system, orbiting the Sun every 165 years.

Name: Globular Cluster Messier 22
Description: M22 is one of about 150 globular star clusters in the Milky Way. Located just 10,000 light-years away in the constellation Sagittarius, it is one of the closest globular clusters to Earth.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 3982
Description: This image captures the face-on spiral galaxy NGC 3982. Its arms are lined with pink star-forming regions of glowing hydrogen, blue newborn star clusters, and dark dust lanes that provide the raw material for future generations of stars.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 3370
Description: The majestic dusty spiral galaxy, NGC 3370, shows intricate spiral arm structure spotted with hot areas of new star formation. In 1994, it hosted an exploding star called SN 1994ae, which briefly outshone the tens of billions of other stars in its galaxy.

Name: Globular Cluster NGC 6397
Description: This ancient stellar jewelry box, a globular cluster called NGC 6397, glitters with the light from hundreds of thousands of stars. The cluster is 13.4 billion years old, which means it was born shortly after the Big Bang.

Name: Mars Near Opposition
Description: The orbits of the planets Earth and Mars provide a geometric line up that is out of this world. Every 26 months, Mars is opposite the Sun in our nighttime sky.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 5068
Description: NGC 5068 is a barred spiral galaxy. At the top center of this image lies NGC 5068’s bright central bar of mature stars. The bright pinkish-red splotches are regions of ionized hydrogen gas where young star clusters lie.

Name: Globular Cluster Messier 15
Description: This dense cluster of stars is known as Messier 15 (or M15) and is located about 35,000 light-years away. The fuzzy, blue area to the left of the cluster's core is a planetary nebula, a cloud of gas that has been cast off by a dying, medium-sized star.

Name: Irregular Galaxy NGC 5408
Description: Most galaxies possess a majestic spiral or elliptical structure. About a quarter of galaxies, though, defy such conventional aesthetics and instead sport a messy, indefinable shape. Known as irregular galaxies, this group includes NGC 5408.

Name: Galaxy Cluster MACS 1206
Description: Galaxy cluster MACS J1206.2-0847 is a cosmic lens; its immense gravity bends and magnifies the light of more-distant galaxies beyond it. The distorted shapes are distant galaxies whose light has been magnified.

Name: Galaxy Pair NGC 3314
Description: The two overlapping galaxies that make up NGC 3314 look as if they are colliding, but they are actually separated by about 10 times the distance between our Milky Way and the neighboring Andromeda galaxy. The alignment gives a unique look at the silhouetted spiral arms in the closer face-on spiral, NGC 3314A.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 6956
Description: Against an inky black backdrop, the blue swirls of spiral galaxy NGC 6956 stand out radiantly. NGC 6956 is a barred spiral galaxy, a common type of spiral galaxy with a bar-shaped structure of stars in its center.

Name: Interacting Galaxy ESO 239-2
Description: ESO 239-2 is the result of a cosmic collision between galaxies that will eventually result in a larger "elliptical" galaxy. The intermediate stage captured here shows a galaxy with long tails of dust and gas that envelope the galaxy's core.

Name: Active Galaxy UGC 7342
Description: Extending from this active galaxy are bizarre, greenish knots of gas and dust glowing from the light of high-energy particles, blasted by powerful ultraviolet radiation from a supermassive black hole at the galaxy's center.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 3370
Description: The majestic dusty spiral galaxy, NGC 3370, shows intricate spiral arm structure spotted with hot areas of new star formation. In 1994, it hosted an exploding star called SN 1994ae, which briefly outshone the tens of billions of other stars in its galaxy.

Name: Globular Cluster 47 Tucanae
Description: The ancient globular cluster 47 Tucanae is a dense swarm of up to a million stars, and this view captures a close-up of thousands of them. The large, bright stars in the image are red giants near the end of their lives.

Name: Galaxy Pair Arp 303
Description: Two spiral galaxies, IC 563 (bottom right) and IC 564 (top left), collectively known as Arp 303, are very bright at infrared wavelengths and host many bright star-forming regions.

Name: Cat's Eye Nebula
Description: Produced by a dying star, the Cat's Eye Nebula is one of the most complex planetary nebulae known. This image reveals a pattern of concentric rings around the central star. Each "ring" is actually the edge of a spherical bubble of material ejected by the star.

Name: Globular Cluster 47 Tucanae
Description: This image of the heart of the giant globular star cluster 47 Tucanae reveals the glow of 200,000 stars. Young white dwarfs ― the burned-out relics of stars that have used up their nuclear fuel, cooled down, and lost most of their mass ― are beginning to migrate outward.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 5068
Description: NGC 5068 is a barred spiral galaxy. At the top center of this image lies NGC 5068’s bright central bar of mature stars. The bright pinkish-red splotches are regions of ionized hydrogen gas where young star clusters lie.

Name: Globular Cluster Messier 22
Description: M22 is one of about 150 globular star clusters in the Milky Way. Located just 10,000 light-years away in the constellation Sagittarius, it is one of the closest globular clusters to Earth.

Name: Interacting Galaxies Arp 105
Description: Arp 105 is a dazzling ongoing merger between an elliptical galaxy (NGC 3561B) and a spiral galaxy (NGC 3561A) drawn together by gravity, characterized by a long, drawn out tidal tail of stars and gas.

Name: Galactic Center
Description: This infrared image of the center of our Milky Way galaxy reveals a population of massive stars and complex structures in the hot ionized gas that swirls around the galactic core.

Name: Globular Cluster NGC 2808
Description: This dense swarm of stars lies at the center of the globular star cluster NGC 2808. Of the about 150 known globular clusters in our Milky Way galaxy, NGC 2808 is one of the most massive, containing more than a million stars.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 3583
Description: NGC 3583 is a barred spiral galaxy with two arms that twist out into the universe. This galaxy is located 98 million light-years away. Two supernovae were observed in this galaxy, one in 1975 and another in 2015.

Name: Globular Cluster Messier 30
Description: This image of globular cluster M30 captures a dense swarm of several hundred thousand stars bound together by gravity. M30 is about 90 light-years across and formed 13 billion years ago.

Name: Stars in the Galactic Core
Description: These colorful stars reside at the heart of our Milky Way galaxy, about 26,000 light-years from Earth. Aging red giant stars coexist with their more plentiful younger cousins, the smaller, white, Sun-like stars, in this crowded region of our galaxy's central hub.

Name: R Aquarii
Description: The binary star system called R Aquarii undergoes violent eruptions that blast out huge filaments of glowing gas, weaving a spiral pattern among the stars.

Name: Galaxy Pair Arp 116
Description: The giant elliptical galaxy Messier 60 and a much smaller spiral galaxy, NGC 4647, make up the galaxy pair Arp 116. It’s unclear whether these two galaxies are interacting gravitationally – they may just overlap from our viewpoint on Earth. NGC 4647 is about the size of our Milky Way, while M60 has the mass of about a trillion times that of the Sun.

Name: FrEGGs
Description: This image shows knots of cold, dense interstellar gas where new stars are forming. These Free-floating Evaporating Gaseous Globules (frEGGs) are dark and rarely seen by telescopes. This image also features a giant O-type star and an even more massive supergiant B-type star to the right.

Name: Globular Cluster Pismis 26
Description: This glittering gathering of stars is Pismis 26, a globular star cluster located about 23,000 light-years away. Many thousands of stars gleam brightly against the black backdrop of the image, with some brighter red and blue stars located along the outskirts of the cluster.

Name: Galaxy Cluster SDSS J1531+3414
Description: This dense galaxy cluster, made up of mostly giant elliptical galaxies with a few spirals and irregular galaxies mixed in, has a powerful gravitational pull that warps and magnifies the image of background galaxies into blue streaks and arcs.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 3982
Description: This image captures the face-on spiral galaxy NGC 3982. Its arms are lined with pink star-forming regions of glowing hydrogen, blue newborn star clusters, and dark dust lanes that provide the raw material for future generations of stars.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 3370
Description: The majestic dusty spiral galaxy, NGC 3370, shows intricate spiral arm structure spotted with hot areas of new star formation. In 1994, it hosted an exploding star called SN 1994ae, which briefly outshone the tens of billions of other stars in its galaxy.

Name: Elliptical Galaxy Messier 87
Description: This image of the giant galaxy M87 shows a 3,000-light-year-long jet of plasma blasting from the galaxy's 6.5-billion-solar-mass central black hole. The blowtorch-like jet seems to cause stars to erupt along its trajectory.

Name: R Aquarii
Description: The binary star system called R Aquarii undergoes violent eruptions that blast out huge filaments of glowing gas, weaving a spiral pattern among the stars.

Name: Veil Nebula
Description: The Veil Nebula is the remnant of a star roughly 20 times as massive as our Sun that exploded about 10,000 years ago. If you could see the entire nebula without the aid of a telescope, it would be as wide as six full Moons placed side-by-side.

Name: Comet ISON
Description: At the time Hubble took this image, comet ISON (C/2012 S1) was hurtling toward the Sun at a whopping 48,000 miles (77,000 km) per hour. The comet was 403 million miles (649 million km) from Earth, between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter.

Name: Globular Cluster Messier 30
Description: This image of globular cluster M30 captures a dense swarm of several hundred thousand stars bound together by gravity. M30 is about 90 light-years across and formed 13 billion years ago.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 3972
Description: In galaxy NGC 3972, astronomers examine pulsating stars called Cepheid variables, which blink at a rate matched closely by their intrinsic brightness, making them ideal for measuring accurate distances to relatively nearby galaxies.

Name: Globular Cluster NGC 6441
Description: Globular clusters like NGC 6441 are roughly spherical groupings of stars held together by gravity. This is one of the most massive and luminous globular clusters in our Milky Way Galaxy; it's estimated that its stars are about 1.6 million times the mass of our Sun.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 4680
Description: NGC 4680 is actually a rather tricky galaxy to classify. It is sometimes referred to as a spiral galaxy, but it is also sometimes classified as a lenticular galaxy. Lenticular galaxies are "lens-shaped" and fall somewhere in between spiral galaxies and elliptical galaxies.

Name: Red Spots on Jupiter
Description: This image captures three red spots in Jupiter's atmosphere. The famous Great Red Spot appears on the right, while "Red Spot Jr." is to the lower left and an even smaller "baby red spot" appears at left.

Name: Active Galaxy NGC 5252
Description: Extending from this active galaxy are bizarre, greenish knots of gas and dust glowing from the light of high-energy particles, blasted by powerful ultraviolet radiation from a supermassive black hole at the galaxy's center.

Name: Galaxy Cluster MACS J1720.2+3536
Description: The heart of a vast cluster of galaxies called MACS J1720+35 is shown in this image. The galaxy cluster is so massive that its gravity distorts, brightens, and magnifies light from more-distant objects behind it, an effect called gravitational lensing.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 3370
Description: The majestic dusty spiral galaxy, NGC 3370, shows intricate spiral arm structure spotted with hot areas of new star formation. In 1994, it hosted an exploding star called SN 1994ae, which briefly outshone the tens of billions of other stars in its galaxy.

Name: Omega Centauri
Description: Omega Centauri consists of roughly 10 million stars that are gravitationally bound. The cluster is about 10 times as massive as other big globular clusters – almost as massive as a small galaxy.

Name: Red Spots on Jupiter
Description: This image captures three red spots in Jupiter's atmosphere. The famous Great Red Spot appears on the right, while "Red Spot Jr." is to the lower left and an even smaller "baby red spot" appears at left.

Name: Globular Cluster Messier 22
Description: M22 is one of about 150 globular star clusters in the Milky Way. Located just 10,000 light-years away in the constellation Sagittarius, it is one of the closest globular clusters to Earth.

Name: Interacting Galaxy UGC 8058
Description: The extraordinary galaxy UGC 8058, also known as Markarian 231, has long tidal tails and a disturbed shape. It shows clear signs of the presence of a powerful quasar in its center.

Name: Tucana Dwarf
Description: Tucana Dwarf is a dwarf spheroidal galaxy, much smaller and less luminous than most other dwarf galaxies. Dust is sparse and the stellar population skews towards the older range, giving them a dimmer look.

Name: Interacting Galaxy UGC 8335
Description: UGC 8335 is a strongly interacting pair of spiral galaxies. The interaction unites the galaxies via a bridge of material and has yanked two strongly curved tails of gas and stars from the outer parts of the galaxies.

Name: Cone Nebula
Description: This image shows the tip of the Cone Nebula, a star-forming region in the constellation Monoceros. This conical pillar stretches over seven light-years and is just a small portion of a much larger star-formation complex.

Name: Stars in the Galactic Core
Description: These colorful stars reside at the heart of our Milky Way galaxy, about 26,000 light-years from Earth. Aging red giant stars coexist with their more plentiful younger cousins, the smaller, white, Sun-like stars, in this crowded region of our galaxy's central hub.

Name: Tucana Dwarf
Description: Tucana Dwarf is a dwarf spheroidal galaxy, much smaller and less luminous than most other dwarf galaxies. Dust is sparse and the stellar population skews towards the older range, giving them a dimmer look.

Name: Jupiter
Description: An image of Jupiter in visible light examines cloud activity, showing the turbulent pattern generated by the two plumes at the upper left part of Jupiter.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 4414
Description: This Hubble image reveals the central regions of the dusty spiral galaxy NGC 4414. The galaxy’s arms are very rich in clouds of interstellar dust, visible as dark patches and streaks silhouetted against the starlight.

Name: Star-Forming Region N11B
Description: This panoramic view captures an iridescent tapestry of star birth, filled with glowing gas, dark dust clouds, and young, hot stars. The star-forming region, cataloged as N11B, lies in a nearby galaxy, the Large Magellanic Cloud.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 3982
Description: This image captures the face-on spiral galaxy NGC 3982. Its arms are lined with pink star-forming regions of glowing hydrogen, blue newborn star clusters, and dark dust lanes that provide the raw material for future generations of stars.

Name: Globular Cluster Messier 71
Description: This is the center of the globular cluster M71, a great ball of ancient stars on the edge of our galaxy. This group of stars, known as the Angelfish Cluster, is one of the smallest of its kind.

Name: Mars and Phobos
Description: Mars's tiny moon Phobos appears star-like in this image. The little moon completes an orbit in just 7 hours and 39 minutes, which is faster than Mars rotates. Rising in the Martian west, it runs three laps around the Red Planet in the course of one Martian day.

Name: Emission Nebula NGC 261
Description: The ionized gas blazing from within this diffuse region marks NGC 261 as an emission nebula. It is home to numerous stars hot enough to irradiate surrounding hydrogen gas, causing the cloud to emit a pinkish-red glow.

Name: Interacting Galaxies IRAS 19297-0406
Description: This image shows a tumultuous collision between four galaxies located 1 billion light-years from Earth. The tangled-up galaxies, called IRAS 19297-0406, are crammed together in the center of the picture.

Name: Supernova Remnant 1E 0102
Description: This portrait reveals the gaseous remains of an exploded massive star that erupted approximately 1,700 years ago. The stellar corpse is a supernova remnant named 1E 0102.2-7219, located in the Small Magellanic Cloud.

Name: Interacting Galaxies Arp 283
Description: In this pair of gravitationally interacting galaxies, known as Arp 283, the galaxy NGC 2799 (left) is seemingly being pulled into the center of the galaxy NGC 2798 (right).

Name: R Aquarii
Description: The binary star system called R Aquarii undergoes violent eruptions that blast out huge filaments of glowing gas, weaving a spiral pattern among the stars.

Name: Spiral Galaxy Messier 95
Description: The barred spiral galaxy M95 contains around 40 billion stars. Its spiral arms host a flurry of star birth activity and sparkle with the light of countless young, blue stars. The arms themselves are very tightly wound around the galaxy’s core and are nearly circular.

Name: Galaxy Cluster Abell 2744
Description: Located 3.5 billion light-years away, Abell 2744 contains several hundred galaxies and might be a pile-up of at least four smaller galaxy clusters. Abell 2744's strong gravitational field acts as a lens, brightening and magnifying the light of nearly 3,000 distant background galaxies.

Name: Galactic Center
Description: Peering deep into the heart of our Milky Way galaxy reveals a tapestry of more than half a million stars. Except for a few blue foreground stars, the rest are part of the Milky Way's nuclear star cluster, the most massive and densest star cluster in our galaxy.

Name: Asteroid Vesta
Description: Hubble's sharp vision saw features as small as about 37 miles (60 kilometers) across on the asteroid Vesta's surface, revealing differences in brightness and color later investigated by the Dawn mission.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 3583
Description: NGC 3583 is a barred spiral galaxy with two arms that twist out into the universe. This galaxy is located 98 million light-years away. Two supernovae were observed in this galaxy, one in 1975 and another in 2015.

Name: Supernova Remnant 1E 0102
Description: This portrait reveals the gaseous remains of an exploded massive star that erupted approximately 1,700 years ago. The stellar corpse is a supernova remnant named 1E 0102.2-7219, located in the Small Magellanic Cloud.

Name: Red Spots on Jupiter
Description: This image captures three red spots in Jupiter's atmosphere. The famous Great Red Spot appears on the right, while "Red Spot Jr." is to the lower left and an even smaller "baby red spot" appears at left.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 3370
Description: The majestic dusty spiral galaxy, NGC 3370, shows intricate spiral arm structure spotted with hot areas of new star formation. In 1994, it hosted an exploding star called SN 1994ae, which briefly outshone the tens of billions of other stars in its galaxy.

Name: Dark Spot on Neptune
Description: A dark vortex appears in the atmosphere of Neptune. Though similar features were seen in 1989 and 1994, this vortex is the first one observed on the planet in the 21st century.

Name: Molten Ring Galaxy
