Description: NGC 7674 is a spiral galaxy tilted nearly face-on to Earth. Faint streamers below and to the left of the galaxy have been created by gravitational interactions with companion galaxies.

Name: Globular Cluster Messier 80
Description: M80 is one of the densest of the approximately 150 known globular clusters in the Milky Way galaxy. The cluster contains hundreds of thousands of stars held together by their mutual gravitational attraction.

Name: Diffuse Galaxy UGC 477
Description: UGC 477 is a low surface brightness (LSB) galaxy. LSB galaxies like UGC 477 are more diffusely distributed than galaxies such as our Milky Way. With surface brightnesses up to 250 times fainter than the night sky, these galaxies can be incredibly difficult to detect.

Name: 30 Doradus Nebula
Description: Glowing hydrogen clouds and dark filamentary dust structures are visible in this close-up infrared view of a star-birth region called the 30 Doradus Nebula. The giant stellar factory lies 170,000 light-years away inside the Large Magellanic Cloud.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 4414
Description: This Hubble image reveals the central regions of the dusty spiral galaxy NGC 4414. The galaxy’s arms are rich in clouds of interstellar dust, visible as dark patches and streaks silhouetted against the starlight.

Name: Omega Centauri
Description: This view shows about 50,000 stars at the heart of Omega Centauri, a huge globular star cluster 17,000 light-years from Earth. Omega Centauri is the biggest and brightest globular cluster in the Milky Way, and one of the few that can be seen by the unaided eye.

Name: Interacting Galaxy NGC 7469
Description: This pair of interacting galaxies includes the barred spiral galaxy NGC 7469, also called Arp 298 or Mrk 1514, and its smaller companion IC 5283. This system is located about 200 million light-years away in the constellation Pegasus.

Name: Globular Cluster Messier 22
Description: M22 is one of about 150 globular star clusters in the Milky Way. Located just 10,000 light-years away in the constellation Sagittarius, it is one of the closest globular clusters to Earth.

Name: Elliptical Galaxy Messier 87
Description: This image of the giant galaxy M87 shows a 3,000-light-year-long jet of plasma blasting from the galaxy's 6.5-billion-solar-mass central black hole. The jet seems to cause stars to erupt along its trajectory.

Name: Galaxy Cluster Abell 2744
Description: Abell 2744 contains several hundred galaxies and might be a pile-up of at least four smaller galaxy clusters. Abell 2744's strong gravitational field acts as a lens, distorting and magnifying the light of nearly 3,000 distant background galaxies.

Name: Galaxy Cluster Abell 1689
Description: This image shows the center of Abell 1689, an immense cluster of galaxies located 2.2 billion light-years away. Astronomers used Hubble to map the distribution of dark matter in the galaxy cluster.

Name: Globular Cluster 47 Tucanae
Description: The ancient globular cluster 47 Tucanae is a dense swarm of up to a million stars, and this view captures a close-up of thousands of them. The large, bright stars in the image are red giants near the end of their lives.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 3509
Description: Like most spiral galaxies, NGC 3509 is actively creating new stars. The color red in this image represents near-infrared wavelengths of light and showcases star-forming regions along the galaxy’s spiral arms.

Name: Globular Cluster NGC 2298
Description: Globular clusters like NGC 2298, a sparkling collection of thousands of stars held together by mutual gravitational attraction, are typically home to older populations of stars.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 3972
Description: In galaxy NGC 3972, astronomers examine pulsating stars called Cepheid variables, which blink at a rate matched closely by their intrinsic brightness, making them ideal for measuring accurate distances to relatively nearby galaxies.

Name: Star VY Canis Majoris
Description: The hypergiant star VY Canis Majoris is surrounded by clouds of gas that it has cast off in a long series of outbursts. These eruptions have formed loops, arcs, and knots of material moving at various speeds and in many different directions.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 6217
Description: The barred spiral galaxy NGC 6217 has been characterized as a starburst galaxy, which means it is undergoing a high rate of star formation compared to a typical galaxy.

Name: Teacup Galaxy
Description: Extending from this active galaxy are bizarre, greenish knots of gas and dust glowing from the light of high-energy particles, blasted by powerful ultraviolet radiation from a supermassive black hole at the galaxy's center.

Name: Gamma-Ray Burst 130603B
Description: This image reveals a new type of stellar explosion produced from the merger of two compact objects. This created a short-duration gamma-ray burst, a mysterious flash of intense high-energy radiation.

Name: Crescent Nebula
Description: Also called Caldwell 27 or NGC 6888, the Crescent Nebula holds a massive, incredibly hot star at its heart. This stellar demolition zone lies within our own galaxy, about 4,700 light-years from Earth.

Name: Galaxy Cluster Abell 1689
Description: This image shows the inner region of Abell 1689, an immense cluster of galaxies located 2.2 billion light-years away. Astronomers used Hubble to map the distribution of dark matter in the galaxy cluster.

Name: Sombrero Galaxy
Description: The Sombrero galaxy's hallmark is a brilliant white core encircled by thick lanes of dust. As seen from Earth, the spiral galaxy is tilted nearly edge-on.

Name: Active Galaxy NGC 5972
Description: Extending from this active galaxy are bizarre, greenish knots of gas and dust glowing from the light of high-energy particles, blasted by powerful ultraviolet radiation from a supermassive black hole at the galaxy's center.

Name: Interacting Galaxies NGC 7764A
Description: In this group of three galaxies, collectively known as NGC 7764A, the two galaxies in the upper right of the image appear to be interacting. It's unclear whether the galaxy to the lower left is interacting with the other two.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 4603
Description: Spiral galaxy NGC 4603 is the most distant galaxy in which a special class of pulsating stars called Cepheid variables have been found. Cepheid variable stars can be used to determine the distance to galaxies.

Name: Globular Cluster Messier 22
Description: M22 is one of about 150 globular star clusters in the Milky Way. Located just 10,000 light-years away in the constellation Sagittarius, it is one of the closest globular clusters to Earth.

Name: Spiral Galaxy Messier 74
Description: M74, also called NGC 628, is a stunning example of a "grand-design" spiral galaxy that is viewed from Earth nearly face-on. Its perfectly symmetrical spiral arms emanate from the central nucleus and are dotted with clusters of young stars.

Name: Andromeda's Double Nucleus
Description: Hubble zeroed in on the nucleus of spiral galaxy M31, or Andromeda, our closest neighboring galaxy. Andromeda’s "double nucleus" appearance is caused by an elliptical ring of old, reddish stars in orbit around the galaxy’s black hole.

Name: Galaxy Cluster Abell 2744
Description: Abell 2744 contains several hundred galaxies and might be a pile-up of at least four smaller galaxy clusters. Abell 2744's strong gravitational field acts as a lens, distorting and magnifying the light of nearly 3,000 distant background galaxies.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 7456
Description: This image reveals fine detail in the galaxy NGC 7456’s patchy spiral arms, followed by clumps of dark, obscuring dust. Blossoms of glowing pink are rich reservoirs of gas where new stars are forming.

Name: Galaxy Cluster Abell 1689
Description: This image shows the center of Abell 1689, an immense cluster of galaxies located 2.2 billion light-years away. Astronomers used Hubble to map the distribution of dark matter in the galaxy cluster.

Name: Spiral Galaxy Messier 74
Description: M74, also called NGC 628, is a stunning example of a "grand-design" spiral galaxy that is viewed from Earth nearly face-on. Its perfectly symmetrical spiral arms emanate from the central nucleus and are dotted with clusters of young stars.

Name: Galaxy Cluster Abell 2744
Description: Abell 2744 contains several hundred galaxies and might be a pile-up of at least four smaller galaxy clusters. Abell 2744's strong gravitational field acts as a lens, distorting and magnifying the light of nearly 3,000 distant background galaxies.

Name: Omega Centauri
Description: Omega Centauri consists of roughly 10 million stars that are gravitationally bound. The cluster is about 10 times as massive as other big globular clusters – almost as massive as a small galaxy.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 1546
Description: NGC 1546 is a nearby galaxy in the constellation Dorado. Its orientation gives us a good view of its dust lanes from slightly above and backlit by the galaxy's core.

Name: Stephan's Quintet
Description: This close-up shows four of the five galaxies that make up Stephan's Quintet. The image reveals bright, blue clusters of stars, born from the violent interactions between some of the member galaxies.

Name: Emission Nebula N11
Description: The sprawling filaments of emission nebula N11 weave stellar matter in and out of each other like sparkling candy floss. These cotton-spun clouds of gas are ionized by a host of young and massive stars, giving the complex a cherry-pink appearance.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 2008
Description: The spiral galaxy NGC 2008 sits center stage, with its ghostly spiral arms spreading out toward us. Spiral galaxies are common across the cosmos, comprising over 70% of all observed galaxies—including our own, the Milky Way.

Name: Spiral Galaxy Markarian 1337
Description: Mrk 1337 is a weakly barred spiral galaxy, with its arms emerging from a central bar of gas and stars. Bars occur in roughly half of spiral galaxies, including our own galaxy, the Milky Way.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 1385
Description: This jewel-bright image shows a luminous tangle of stars and dust called the barred spiral galaxy NGC 1385, located about 68 million light-years from Earth.

Name: Hubble-V Nebula
Description: Hubble-V is an active star-forming region within galaxy NGC 6822. The cloud is about 200 light-years across and contains a dense knot of dozens of ultra-hot stars, each 100,000 times brighter than our Sun.

Name: Circumstellar Disk HD 61005
Description: This dust disk around a young star is about 22 billion miles (35 billion km) across. Its shape is produced by starlight scattering off dust.

Name: Trifid Nebula
Description: The Trifid Nebula is a stellar nursery criss-crossed by huge, dark lanes of dust. This close-up view of the center of the nebula, near the intersection of the dust bands, shows a group of recently formed, massive, bright stars.

Name: Core of the Andromeda Galaxy
Description: This Hubble image looks at the heart of one of our closest galactic neighbors, the Andromeda Galaxy (M31). Astronomers believe the two bright objects are a ring of red stars and a disk of blue stars.

Name: Lenticular Galaxy NGC 4753
Description: This is a nearly edge-on view of the lenticular galaxy NGC 4753. Lenticular galaxies have an elliptical shape and ill-defined spiral arms. NGC 4753’s distinct dust lanes around its center likely came from a previous merge with another galaxy.

Name: Interacting Galaxies AM 2026-424
Description: The colliding galaxies AM 2026-424 resemble a face. Each "eye" is the bright core of a galaxy, one of which slammed into another. The outline of the face is a ring of young blue stars. Other clumps of new stars form a nose and mouth.

Name: Globular Cluster NGC 6397
Description: This ancient stellar jewelry box, a globular cluster called NGC 6397, glitters with the light from hundreds of thousands of stars. The cluster is 13.4 billion years old, which means it was born shortly after the Big Bang.

Name: Globular Cluster 47 Tucanae
Description: This image of the heart of the giant globular star cluster 47 Tucanae reveals the glow of 200,000 stars. Young white dwarfs ― the burned-out relics of stars that have used up their nuclear fuel, cooled down, and lost most of their mass ― are beginning to migrate outward.

Name: Galaxy Pair Arp 116
Description: The giant elliptical galaxy Messier 60 and a much smaller spiral galaxy, NGC 4647, make up the galaxy pair Arp 116. It’s unclear whether these two galaxies are interacting gravitationally – they may just overlap from our viewpoint on Earth. NGC 4647 is about the size of our Milky Way, while M60 has the mass of about a trillion times that of the Sun.

Name: Omega Centauri
Description: Omega Centauri consists of roughly 10 million stars that are gravitationally bound. The cluster is about 10 times as massive as other big globular clusters – almost as massive as a small galaxy.

Name: Galaxy Cluster Abell 1689
Description: This image shows the center of Abell 1689, an immense cluster of galaxies located 2.2 billion light-years away. Astronomers used Hubble to map the distribution of dark matter in the galaxy cluster.

Name: Core of the Andromeda Galaxy
Description: This Hubble image looks at the heart of one of our closest galactic neighbors, the Andromeda Galaxy (M31). Astronomers believe the two bright objects are a ring of red stars and a disk of blue stars.

Name: Omega Centauri
Description: Omega Centauri consists of roughly 10 million stars that are gravitationally bound. The cluster is about 10 times as massive as other big globular clusters – almost as massive as a small galaxy.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 4603
Description: Spiral galaxy NGC 4603 is the most distant galaxy in which a special class of pulsating stars called Cepheid variables have been found. Cepheid variable stars can be used to determine the distance to galaxies.

Name: Veil Nebula
Description: The Veil Nebula is the remnant of a star roughly 20 times as massive as our Sun that exploded about 10,000 years ago. If you could see the entire nebula without the aid of a telescope, it would be as wide as six full Moons placed side-by-side.

Name: Galaxy Cluster Abell 1689
Description: This image shows the center of Abell 1689, an immense cluster of galaxies located 2.2 billion light-years away. Astronomers used Hubble to map the distribution of dark matter in the galaxy cluster.

Name: Lenticular Galaxy NGC 4660
Description: This lenticular galaxy holds galactic winds that were discovered as outflowing gas associated with star formation around its core.

Name: Compact Galaxy ESO 185-IG013
Description: ESO 185-IG013 is a luminous blue compact galaxy, a nearby galaxy that shows an intense burst of star formation. They are unusually blue in visible light, which sets them apart from other high-starburst galaxies that emit more infrared light.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 4603
Description: Spiral galaxy NGC 4603 is the most distant galaxy in which a special class of pulsating stars called Cepheid variables have been found. Cepheid variable stars can be used to determine the distance to galaxies.

Name: Star WR 124 and Nebula M1-67
Description: The star Hen 2-427, more commonly known as WR 124, shines brightly at the center of the nebula M1-67 that surrounds it, forming a spectacular cosmic pairing.

Name: Interacting Galaxies Arp 142
Description: The interacting galaxy duo near the bottom of this image is Arp 142. The pair contains the disturbed, star-forming spiral galaxy NGC 2936 along with its elliptical companion NGC 2937 at lower left. Above them is an unrelated, bluish galaxy called UGC 5130.

Name: Trifid Nebula
Description: The Trifid Nebula is a stellar nursery criss-crossed by huge, dark lanes of dust. This close-up view of the center of the nebula, near the intersection of the dust bands, shows a group of recently formed, massive, bright stars.

Name: Galaxy Cluster Abell 2744
Description: Abell 2744 contains several hundred galaxies and might be a pile-up of at least four smaller galaxy clusters. Abell 2744's strong gravitational field acts as a lens, distorting and magnifying the light of nearly 3,000 distant background galaxies.

Name: Lensed Quasar RXJ1131-1231
Description: The gravity from the central core of a massive galaxy magnifies and distorts the light from a quasar behind it. Quasars are extremely distant cosmic streetlights produced by active black holes.

Name: Diffuse Galaxy NGC 1052-DF2
Description: NGC 1052-DF2, or DF2, is an unusual "see-through" galaxy. The giant cosmic cotton ball is so diffuse and its ancient stars so spread out that distant galaxies in the background can be seen through it.

Name: Galaxies in the Groth Strip
Description: This field of galaxies is just a small part of a cosmic tapestry Hubble imaged as part of the All-wavelength Extended Groth Strip International Survey. In it are galaxies of all shapes, sizes, colors, and distances. Larger ones are nearby, while the smallest ones are far away.

Name: Galaxy Abell 2597
Description: This galaxy shows chains of star formation in ultraviolet light. This star formation is a product of the action of the jets from a central black hole that controls infalling gas from the galaxy's halo.

Name: Stingray Nebula
Description: Hen-1357, named the "Stingray Nebula" because its shape resembles a stingray fish, is the youngest known planetary nebula, and is merely one-tenth the size of other planetary nebulae.

Name: Diffuse Galaxy NGC 1052-DF2
Description: NGC 1052-DF2, or DF2, is an unusual "see-through" galaxy. The giant cosmic cotton ball is so diffuse and its ancient stars so spread out that distant galaxies in the background can be seen through it.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 3081
Description: NGC 3081 is seen here nearly face-on. Compared to other spiral galaxies, it looks a little different. The galaxy's barred spiral center is surrounded by a bright loop known as a resonance ring. This ring is full of bright clusters and bursts of new star formation.

Name: Supernova 2002dd
Description: This image captures a stellar explosion called a supernova in a small part of the sky known as the Hubble Deep Field. The supernova, designated SN 2002dd, appears as a red dot near the center of the image.

Name: Galaxy Cluster Abell 1689
Description: This image shows the center of Abell 1689, an immense cluster of galaxies located 2.2 billion light-years away. Astronomers used Hubble to map the distribution of dark matter in the galaxy cluster.

Name: Kuiper Belt Object 1110113Y
Description: This Kuiper Belt Object is no bigger than 19 to 28 miles (30 to 45 km) across, and it is a deep-freeze relic of what the outer solar system was like 4.6 billion years ago, during the period when the Sun formed.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 1672
Description: Shining stars fill the disk of barred spiral galaxy NGC 1672, giving the galaxy a beautiful glow. At the galaxy’s very center sits an active galactic nucleus, which forms as a result of heated matter swirling in the accretion disk around NGC 1672’s supermassive black hole.

Name: Vega's Circumstellar Disk
Description: The summer star Vega is encircled by a nearly 100-billion-mile-diameter disk of debris, known as a circumstellar disk, that's far more smooth than those we see in many other young star systems.

Name: Neptune
Description: Neptune is the most distant major planet in our solar system. This image reveals high-altitude clouds in the northern and southern hemispheres of the planet. These clouds are composed of methane ice crystals.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 922
Description: Bright pink nebulae almost completely encircle spiral galaxy NGC 922. The ring structure and the galaxy's distorted spiral shape result from a smaller galaxy scoring a cosmic bull's-eye, hitting the center of NGC 922 some 330 million years ago.

Name: Omega Centauri
Description: Omega Centauri consists of roughly 10 million stars that are gravitationally bound. The cluster is about 10 times as massive as other big globular clusters – almost as massive as a small galaxy.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 1672
Description: Shining stars fill the disk of barred spiral galaxy NGC 1672, giving the galaxy a beautiful glow. At the galaxy’s very center sits an active galactic nucleus, which forms as a result of heated matter swirling in the accretion disk around NGC 1672’s supermassive black hole.

Name: Galaxy Cluster Abell 2744
Description: Abell 2744 contains several hundred galaxies and might be a pile-up of at least four smaller galaxy clusters. Abell 2744's strong gravitational field acts as a lens, distorting and magnifying the light of nearly 3,000 distant background galaxies.

Name: Seyfert's Sextet
Description: At first, Seyfert's Sextet looks like six galaxies grouped closely together. However, the small galaxy with the prominent spiral arms (right of center) is much farther away than the others, and a bright clump to the lower right is material torn from one of the other galaxies.

Name: Dust Storm on Mars
Description: This Hubble image of the Sinus Meridiani region on Mars shows evidence of a dust storm about 930 miles (1500 km) long.

Name: Galaxy Pair Arp 116
Description: The giant elliptical galaxy Messier 60 and a much smaller spiral galaxy, NGC 4647, make up the galaxy pair Arp 116. It’s unclear whether these two galaxies are interacting gravitationally – they may just overlap from our viewpoint on Earth. NGC 4647 is about the size of our Milky Way, while M60 has the mass of about a trillion times that of the Sun.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 922
Description: Bright pink nebulae almost completely encircle spiral galaxy NGC 922. The ring structure and the galaxy's distorted spiral shape result from a smaller galaxy scoring a cosmic bull's-eye, hitting the center of NGC 922 some 330 million years ago.

Name: Omega Centauri
Description: Omega Centauri consists of roughly 10 million stars that are gravitationally bound. The cluster is about 10 times as massive as other big globular clusters – almost as massive as a small galaxy.

Name: Galaxy Cluster RDCS 1252.9-2927
Description: This image captures the massive galaxy cluster RDCS 1252.9-2927. The galaxies in the cluster already existed when the universe was just 5 billion years old, or about 35 percent of its present age.

Name: Omega Centauri
Description: The core of this globular cluster glitters with the light of 2 million stars. The entire cluster contains 10 million stars, and is among the biggest and most massive of some 200 globular clusters orbiting the Milky Way galaxy.

Name: Globular Cluster Messier 2
Description: M2 is one of the largest globular star clusters, a spherical group of stars bound together by their mutual gravitational attraction. Most of the cluster’s mass is concentrated at its center, with shimmering streams of stars extending outward into space.

Name: Comet C/2017 K2
Description: This image shows a fuzzy cloud of dust, called a coma, surrounding the comet C/2017 K2 PANSTARRS (K2), taken when the frozen visitor was just beyond Saturn's orbit. It's the farthest active comet ever observed entering the solar system.

Name: Spiral Galaxy Caldwell 45
Description: Hubble captured reddish-pink clouds of star-forming regions in spiral galaxy Caldwell 45, also called NGC 5248. It's a "grand design" spiral, with prominent spiral arms that reach from near the core out through the disk.

Name: Quasar MC2 1635+119
Description: This image shows shells of stars around a quasar known as MC2 1635+119. Quasars are among the brightest objects in the universe. They reside in the centers of galaxies and are powered by supermassive black holes.

Name: Galaxy Cluster Abell 209
Description: This image of a massive, spacetime-warping cluster of galaxies, called Abell 209, shows more than a hundred galaxies. They are separated by millions of light-years, and the seemingly-empty space between the galaxies is filled with hot, diffuse gas.

Name: Retina Nebula
Description: This Hubble image reveals a dying star, nicknamed the Retina Nebula. It got its name from the intricate tendrils of dust seen in this edge-on view.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 4603
Description: Spiral galaxy NGC 4603 is the most distant galaxy in which a special class of pulsating stars called Cepheid variables have been found. Cepheid variable stars can be used to determine the distance to galaxies.

Name: Globular Cluster NGC 6397
Description: This ancient stellar jewelry box, globular cluster NGC 6397, glitters with the light from hundreds of thousands of stars. The cluster is 13.4 billion years old, born shortly after the Big Bang.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 3783
Description: While the focus of this image is the bright barred spiral galaxy NGC 3783, which lies about 130 million light-years from Earth, the eye is equally drawn to the very bright object in the lower right part of this image. This is the star HD 101274.

Name: Supernova Remnant 0509-68.7
Description: Supernova remnant SNR 0509-68.7 is the irregularly shaped dust cloud at the upper center of the image. The gas in the lower half of the image and the dense concentration of stars in the lower left are the outskirts of the star cluster NGC 1850.

Name: Globular Cluster NGC 1850
Description: This 100 million-year-old globular cluster is a spherical collection of densely packed stars held together by gravity. Unlike most globular clusters, however, the stars of NGC 1850 are relatively young. Globular clusters with young stars such are not present in our own Milky Way galaxy.

Name: Andromeda Galaxy
Description: Over 100 million stars are on display in this portion of the Andromeda galaxy, located over 2 million light-years away. This portrait of our galactic neighbor uses 7,398 exposures taken over 411 individual pointings of the telescope.

Name: Omega Centauri
Description: The core of this globular cluster glitters with the light of 2 million stars. The entire cluster contains 10 million stars, and is among the biggest and most massive of some 200 globular clusters orbiting the Milky Way galaxy.

Name: Ant Nebula
Description: The Ant Nebula displays intriguing symmetrical patterns in the lobes of gas being ejected from a dying Sun-like star at its center.

Name: Omega Centauri
Description: The core of this globular cluster glitters with the light of 2 million stars. The entire cluster contains 10 million stars, and is among the biggest and most massive of some 200 globular clusters orbiting the Milky Way Galaxy.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 1309
Description: Looking like a child's pinwheel ready to be set spinning by a gentle breeze, this dramatic spiral galaxy is home to multiple notable stellar explosions, called supernovae, including SN 2002fk and SN 2012Z.

Name: Comet 9P/Tempel 1
Description: This image of Comet 9P/Tempel 1 reveals the dusty inner coma around the nucleus. The image was taken just days before the Deep Impact spacecraft rendezvoused with the comet, releasing an 820 pound "Smart Impactor" that slammed into the comet.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 1015
Description: NGC 1015 is a barred spiral galaxy, so called because the higher concentration of stars near the galaxy's center forms a bar or rod through the center.

Name: Comet Shoemaker-Levy 9 Fragments
Description: This image captures the brightest "nucleus" in a string of approximately 20 objects that comprised the broken-up comet Shoemaker-Levy 9. The image reveals that this bright segment is actually a group of at least four separate pieces.

Name: Active Galaxy NGC 5972
Description: Extending from this active galaxy are bizarre, greenish knots of gas and dust glowing from the light of high-energy particles, blasted by powerful ultraviolet radiation from a supermassive black hole at the galaxy's center.

Name: Globular Cluster NGC 6652
Description: The core of the globular star cluster NGC 6652 is suffused with the pale blue light of countless stars. Globular clusters are stable, tightly gravitationally bound clusters containing anywhere from tens of thousands to millions of stars.

Name: Veil Nebula
Description: The Veil Nebula is the remnant of a star roughly 20 times as massive as our Sun that exploded about 10,000 years ago. If you could see the entire nebula without the aid of a telescope, it would be as wide as six full Moons placed side-by-side.

Name: Stars in the Galactic Core
Description: These colorful stars reside at the heart of our Milky Way galaxy, about 26,000 light-years from Earth. Aging red giant stars coexist with their more plentiful younger cousins, the smaller, white, Sun-like stars, in this crowded region of our galaxy's central hub.

Name: Necklace Nebula
Description: The Necklace Nebula contains the glowing remains of an ordinary, Sun-like star shedding material at the end of its life. The nebula consists of a bright ring, measuring 12 trillion miles (19 trillion km) across, dotted with dense, bright knots of gas that resemble diamonds in a necklace.

Name: Andromeda Galaxy
Description: This panoramic view of the neighboring Andromeda galaxy, located 2.5 million light-years away, captures the glow of 200 million stars. It took over 10 years to make this vast and colorful portrait of the galaxy, requiring over 600 overlapping snapshots that were challenging to stitch together.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 5559
Description: NGC 5559 is a spiral galaxy, with spiral arms filled with gas and dust sweeping out around the bright galactic bulge. These arms are a rich environment for star formation, dotted with a festive array of colors.

Name: Dwarf Galaxy Kiso 5639
Description: Dwarf galaxy Kiso 5639 is a member of a class of "tadpole" galaxies, so named because of their bright heads and elongated tails.

Name: Open Cluster NGC 460
Description: The NGC 460 star cluster resides in a complex of stellar clusters and nebulae. Open clusters like NGC 460 are made of anywhere from a few dozen to a few thousand stars loosely knitted together by gravity.

Name: Globular Cluster 47 Tucanae
Description: This image shows the core of the globular star cluster 47 Tucanae. The entire cluster contains about a million stars, with many packed tightly in the core.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 428
Description: Although a spiral shape in this messy barred spiral galaxy is still just about visible in this close-up shot, overall, NGC 428’s structure appears to be quite distorted and warped, thought to be a result of a collision between two galaxies.

Name: Pluto's Moon Kerberos
Description: While searching for rings around the dwarf planet Pluto, Hubble discovered the previously unseen, tiny moon P4, later named Kerberos. Kerberos has a diameter of only about 8 to 21 miles (13 to 34 km).

Name: Gamma-ray Burst 130603B
Description: This image reveals a new type of stellar explosion produced from the merger of two compact objects. This created a short-duration gamma-ray burst, a mysterious flash of intense high-energy radiation.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 613
Description: NGC 613 is a lovely example of a barred spiral galaxy. It is easily distinguishable as such because of its well-defined central bar and long arms, which spiral loosely around its nucleus.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 7678
Description: NGC 7678 is a galaxy with one particularly prominent arm. With a diameter of around 115,000 light-years, this bright spiral galaxy is a similar size to our own Milky Way Galaxy.

Name: Galaxy Pair NGC 3314
Description: The two overlapping galaxies that make up NGC 3314 look as if they are colliding, but they are actually separated by about 10 times the distance between our Milky Way and the neighboring Andromeda galaxy. The alignment gives a unique look at the silhouetted spiral arms in the closer face-on spiral, NGC 3314A.

Name: Open Cluster NGC 460
Description: The NGC 460 star cluster resides in a complex of stellar clusters and nebulae. Open clusters like NGC 460 are made of anywhere from a few dozen to a few thousand stars loosely knitted together by gravity.

Name: Saturn
Description: Saturn has a slight reddish haze over its northern hemisphere in this color composite, perhaps due to heating from increased sunlight. Two of its icy moons are clearly visible: Mimas at right, and Enceladus at bottom.

Name: Globular Cluster Ruprecht 106
Description: Almost all globular clusters contain at least two groups of stars with distinct chemical compositions. Ruprecht 106 is one of a small number that do not possess these multiple populations of stars.

Name: Trifid Nebula
Description: The Trifid Nebula is a stellar nursery criss-crossed by huge, dark lanes of dust. This close-up view of the center of the nebula, near the intersection of the dust bands, shows a group of recently formed, massive, bright stars.

Name: Carina Nebula
Description: This close-up view shows only a three-light-year-wide portion of the Carina Nebula, which has a diameter of over 200 light-years. Dramatic dark dust knots and complex structures are sculpted by stellar winds and radiation from the star Eta Carinae (located outside the picture).

Name: Globular Cluster NGC 2031
Description: This dense group of thousands of stars, the globular cluster NGC 2031, is held together in a spherical shape by its stars’ mutual gravitational attraction. NGC 2031 lives in an extremely dense and starry region of the Large Magellanic Cloud.

Name: Galaxy Cluster Abell 1689
Description: This image shows the center of Abell 1689, an immense cluster of galaxies located 2.2 billion light-years away. Astronomers used Hubble to map the distribution of dark matter in the galaxy cluster.

Name: Jupiter in Ultraviolet
Description: Jupiter shown in a color composite of ultraviolet wavelengths features the iconic, massive storm called the “Great Red Spot,” which appears blue in this image.

Name: Planetary Nebula NGC 5189
Description: The knotty, filamentary structure of NGC 5189 formed as a dying star shed its outer layers. Interestingly, this planetary nebula has two nested structures tilted with respect to each other.

Name: Black Eye Galaxy
Description: Messier 64, formed by a collision of two galaxies, has a spectacular dark band of dust in front of the galaxy's bright nucleus, giving rise to its nicknames of the "Black Eye" or "Evil Eye" galaxy.

Name: Galaxy Cluster Abell 1689
Description: This image shows the center of Abell 1689, an immense cluster of galaxies located 2.2 billion light-years away. Astronomers used Hubble to map the distribution of dark matter in the galaxy cluster.

Name: Dual Quasar J0749+2255
Description: J0749+2255 is a pair of quasars that existed when the universe was just 3 billion years old. Quasars are bright objects powered by supermassive black holes. They blast out energy as they devour material within their gravitational grasp.

Name: Elliptical Galaxy Messier 87
Description: This image of the giant galaxy M87 shows a 3,000-light-year-long jet of plasma blasting from the galaxy's 6.5-billion-solar-mass central black hole. The jet seems to cause stars to erupt along its trajectory.

Name: Galaxy Cluster Abell 1689
Description: This image shows the center of Abell 1689, an immense cluster of galaxies located 2.2 billion light-years away. Astronomers used Hubble to map the distribution of dark matter in the galaxy cluster.

Name: Globular Cluster 47 Tucanae
Description: This image shows the core of the globular star cluster 47 Tucanae. The entire cluster contains about a million stars, with many packed tightly in the core.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 4051
Description: The subject of this image, a spiral galaxy named NGC 4051, has hosted multiple supernova explosions in past years. These explosive events were seen scattered throughout the center and spiral arms of the galaxy.

Name: Omega Centauri
Description: Omega Centauri consists of roughly 10 million stars that are gravitationally bound. The cluster is about 10 times as massive as other big globular clusters – almost as massive as a small galaxy.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 4603
Description: Spiral galaxy NGC 4603 is the most distant galaxy in which a special class of pulsating stars called Cepheid variables have been found. Cepheid variable stars can be used to determine the distance to galaxies.

Name: Jupiter's Spots
Description: This image provides a close look at Jupiter's famous Great Red Spot and a smaller storm dubbed "Red Spot Jr." below it. To the right of the Great Red Spot is the remnant of an even smaller spot that has faded and is being consumed by the much larger storm.

Name: Galaxy Cluster IDCS J1426.5+3508
Description: The light we observe from this rare, extremely massive young galaxy cluster, IDCS 1426, left the cluster when the universe was less than a third of its current age.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 6217
Description: The barred spiral galaxy NGC 6217 has been characterized as a starburst galaxy, which means it is undergoing a high rate of star formation compared to a typical galaxy.

Name: Galaxy Cluster Abell 1689
Description: This image shows the center of Abell 1689, an immense cluster of galaxies located 2.2 billion light-years away. Astronomers used Hubble to map the distribution of dark matter in the galaxy cluster.

Name: Omega Centauri
Description: Omega Centauri consists of roughly 10 million stars that are gravitationally bound. The cluster is about 10 times as massive as other big globular clusters – almost as massive as a small galaxy.

Name: Hoag's Object
Description: A nearly perfect ring of hot, blue stars pinwheels about the yellow nucleus of an unusual galaxy known as Hoag's Object. Curiously, a background object that bears an uncanny resemblance to Hoag's Object can be seen in the gap at the one o'clock position.

Name: Galaxy Cluster TN J1338-1942
Description: This galaxy cluster contains a massive embryonic galaxy surrounded by smaller developing galaxies. The central galaxy has spectacular radio-emitting jets, fueled by a supermassive black hole in the galaxy's nucleus.

Name: Dwarf Galaxy NGC 4449
Description: NGC 4449 is a dwarf galaxy, which means that it is far smaller and contains fewer stars than the Milky Way. This galaxy is currently forming new stars at a much faster rate than expected for its size, which makes it a starburst galaxy.

Name: Star Cluster NGC 346
Description: The dazzling young star cluster NGC 346 is home to more than 2,500 newborn stars. The cluster’s most massive stars, which are many times more massive than our Sun, blaze with an intense blue light in this image.

Name: Andromeda Galaxy
Description: Over 100 million stars are on display in this portion of the Andromeda galaxy, located over 2 million light-years away. This portrait of our galactic neighbor uses 7,398 exposures taken over 411 individual pointings of the telescope.

Name: Dwarf Galaxy NGC 4068
Description: This image captures a starburst region in the dwarf galaxy NGC 4068. Starburst regions are areas of intense star formation.

Name: Andromeda Galaxy
Description: Over 100 million stars are on display in this portion of the Andromeda galaxy, located over 2 million light-years away. This portrait of our galactic neighbor uses 7,398 exposures taken over 411 individual pointings of the telescope.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 1015
Description: NGC 1015 is a barred spiral galaxy, so called because the higher concentration of stars near the galaxy's center forms a bar or rod through the center.

Name: Spiral Galaxy D100
Description: The spiral galaxy D100, on the far right of this Hubble image, is being stripped of its gas as it plunges toward the center of the giant Coma galaxy cluster. The dark brown streaks near D100's central region are silhouettes of dust escaping from the galaxy.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 4666
Description: This majestic spiral galaxy is undergoing a particularly intense episode of star formation. Astronomers refer to galaxies that rapidly form stars as starburst galaxies; NGC 4666’s starburst is likely due to gravitational interactions with its unruly galaxy neighbors.

Name: Interacting Galaxies UGC 06471 and UGC 06472
Description: This image shows a cosmic collision between two galaxies, UGC 06471 and UGC 06472. The colliding galaxies are 145 million light-years from Earth. Such collisions distort the shapes of the galaxies as they merge and eventually form a larger galaxy.

Name: Galaxy NGC 6744
Description: NGC 6744 is a large spiral galaxy about 31 million light-years from Earth. It is undergoing vigorous star and star cluster formation along the dark filaments that make up the spiral arms.

Name: Open Cluster NGC 2660
Description: NGC 2660 is an open cluster, a type of star cluster that can contain anywhere from tens to a few hundreds of stars loosely bound together by gravity.

Name: Supernova SN 2005cs
Description: Hubble captured images of an exploding star, called Supernova (SN) 2005cs, 12 days after its discovery. Comparing those photos with Hubble images of the same region taken before the supernova pinpointed the star that exploded.

Name: Interacting Galaxy IC 1623
Description: IC 1623 is an interacting galaxy system that is very bright when observed in infrared light. One of the two galaxies, the infrared-bright galaxy VV 114E, has a substantial amount of warm and dense gas.

Name: Galaxy Cluster TN J1338-1942
Description: The galaxy cluster TN J1338-1942 contains a massive embryonic galaxy surrounded by smaller developing galaxies. The central galaxy has spectacular radio-emitting jets, fueled by a supermassive black hole deep within the galaxy's nucleus.

Name: Andromeda Galaxy
Description: Over 100 million stars are on display in this portion of the Andromeda galaxy, located over 2 million light-years away. This portrait of our galactic neighbor uses 7,398 exposures taken over 411 individual pointings of the telescope.

Name: Galaxy Pair NGC 3314
Description: The two overlapping galaxies that make up NGC 3314 look as if they are colliding, but they are actually separated by about 10 times the distance between our Milky Way and the neighboring Andromeda galaxy. The alignment gives a unique look at the silhouetted spiral arms in the closer face-on spiral, NGC 3314A.

Name: Galaxy Cluster Abell 2744
Description: Abell 2744 contains several hundred galaxies and might be a pile-up of at least four smaller galaxy clusters. Abell 2744's strong gravitational field acts as a lens, distorting and magnifying the light of nearly 3,000 distant background galaxies.

Name: Omega Centauri
Description: Omega Centauri consists of roughly 10 million stars that are gravitationally bound. The cluster is about 10 times as massive as other big globular clusters – almost as massive as a small galaxy.

Name: Star Cluster NGC 346
Description: This image captures a dynamic star-forming region in a nearby dwarf galaxy called the Small Magellanic Cloud. At the center is a brilliant star cluster called NGC 346.

Name: Globular Cluster 47 Tucanae
Description: This image shows the core of the globular star cluster 47 Tucanae. The entire cluster contains about a million stars, with many packed tightly in the core.

Name: Spiral Galaxy ESO 420-G013
Description: ESO 420-G013 is a face-on spiral galaxy and a Seyfert galaxy, a type of galaxy with a bright nucleus powered by a supermassive black hole. Dark lanes of dust are visible against the background glow of the galaxy’s many stars.

Name: Open Cluster NGC 6791
Description: NGC 6791 is an "open cluster" of stars loosely bound by gravity. This image is filled with stars estimated to be 8 billion years old. Two background galaxies are visible at upper left.

Name: Omega Centauri
Description: Omega Centauri consists of roughly 10 million stars that are gravitationally bound. The cluster is about 10 times as massive as other big globular clusters – almost as massive as a small galaxy.

Name: Supernova Remnant N 49
Description: N 49 is a supernova remnant in a neighboring galaxy called the Large Magellanic Cloud. The delicate filaments are sheets of debris from a stellar explosion whose light would have reached Earth thousands of years ago.

Name: Galaxy HIPASS J1131–31
Description: The tiny galaxy HIPASS J1131–31 peeks out from behind the glare of star TYC 7215-199-1, a star within our Milky Way that's positioned between Hubble and the galaxy.

Name: Star Cluster NGC 602
Description: This image depicts bright, blue, newly formed stars that are blowing a cavity in the center of a star-forming region in the Small Magellanic Cloud. At the heart of the star-forming region lies star cluster NGC 602, also called N90.

Name: Galaxy IC 1954
Description: Spiral galaxy IC 1954, located 45 million light-years from Earth, sports a glowing bar in its core, majestically winding spiral arms, and clouds of dark dust.

Name: Swan Nebula
Description: Messier 17, also known as the Omega Nebula or Swan Nebula, is one of the largest star-forming regions in the Milky Way galaxy. It contains one of our galaxy’s youngest star clusters, only 1 million years old.

Name: Core of Star Cluster Omega Centauri
Description: This view shows stars at the heart of Omega Centauri, one of roughly 150 globular clusters in our Milky Way galaxy. The behemoth stellar grouping is the biggest and brightest globular cluster in the Milky Way, and one of the few that can be seen by the unaided eye.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 4100
Description: This sparkling spiral galaxy looks almost stretched across the sky in this image. Known as NGC 4100, the galaxy boasts a neat spiral structure and swirling arms speckled with the bright blue hue of newly formed stars.

Name: Galaxy Cluster Abell 209
Description: This image of a massive, spacetime-warping cluster of galaxies, called Abell 209, shows more than a hundred galaxies. They are separated by millions of light-years, and the seemingly-empty space between the galaxies is filled with hot, diffuse gas.

Name: Star Cluster NGC 346
Description: This image captures a dynamic star-forming region in a nearby dwarf galaxy called the Small Magellanic Cloud. At the center is a brilliant star cluster called NGC 346.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 1559
Description: This barred spiral galaxy is NGC 1559. This picture is composed of 10 different Hubble images in a number of wavelengths of light, from ultraviolet through visible light and into the near-infrared spectrum.

Name: Interacting Galaxy ESO 239-2
Description: ESO 239-2 is the result of a cosmic collision between galaxies that will eventually result in a larger "elliptical" galaxy. The intermediate stage captured here shows a galaxy with long tails of dust and gas that envelope the galaxy's core.

Name: Andromeda Galaxy
Description: This panoramic view of the neighboring Andromeda galaxy, located 2.5 million light-years away, captures the glow of 200 million stars. It took over 10 years to make this vast and colorful portrait of the galaxy, requiring over 600 overlapping snapshots that were challenging to stitch together.

Name: Open Cluster NGC 6791
Description: NGC 6791 is an "open cluster" of stars loosely bound by gravity. This image is filled with stars estimated to be 8 billion years old. Two background galaxies are visible at upper left.

Name: Elliptical Galaxy Messier 87
Description: This image of the giant galaxy M87 shows a 3,000-light-year-long jet of plasma blasting from the galaxy's 6.5-billion-solar-mass central black hole. The jet seems to cause stars to erupt along its trajectory.

Name: Globular Cluster NGC 6397
Description: This ancient stellar jewelry box, globular cluster NGC 6397, glitters with the light from hundreds of thousands of stars. The cluster is 13.4 billion years old, born shortly after the Big Bang.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 300
Description: NGC 300 is a spiral galaxy similar to our own Milky Way galaxy. Some of the bright blue specks in this image are young, massive stars called blue supergiants, and they are among the brightest stars seen in spiral galaxies.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 4603
Description: Spiral galaxy NGC 4603 is the most distant galaxy in which a special class of pulsating stars called Cepheid variables have been found. Cepheid variable stars can be used to determine the distance to galaxies.

Name: Star Cluster NGC 346
Description: This image captures a dynamic star-forming region in a nearby dwarf galaxy called the Small Magellanic Cloud. At the center is a brilliant star cluster called NGC 346.

Name: Sculpted Landscape of the Carina Nebula
Description: Violent stellar winds and powerful radiation from massive stars are sculpting these one-light-year-tall pillars in the surrounding Carina Nebula. Inside the dense structures, new stars may be born.

Name: Star Cluster Trumpler 14
Description: Called Trumpler 14, this cluster of stars is located 8,000 light-years away in a huge star-forming region known as the Carina Nebula. The cluster is only 500,000 years old and has one of the highest concentrations of bright, massive stars in the Milky Way.

Name: Interacting Galaxies AM 1316-241
Description: AM 1316-241 is made up of two interacting galaxies: a spiral galaxy (on the left) in front of an elliptical galaxy (on the right). The starlight from the background elliptical galaxy is partially obscured by bands and filaments of dust in the foreground spiral galaxy.

Name: Fomalhaut and Fomalhaut b
Description: This image shows the debris disk around the star Fomalhaut. These disks often give rise to planets. Fomalhaut b, originally thought to be a planet when observed in 2015, was later discovered to be a rarely-seen collision between icy objects in the disk.

Name: Bok Globule: The Caterpillar
Description: A Bok globule nicknamed the "caterpillar" appears at the right in this image of the Carina Nebula. Its glowing edge indicates that it is being photoionized by the hottest stars in the cluster.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 4603
Description: Spiral galaxy NGC 4603 is the most distant galaxy in which a special class of pulsating stars called Cepheid variables have been found. Cepheid variable stars can be used to determine the distance to galaxies.

Name: Star Cluster NGC 602
Description: This image depicts bright, blue, newly formed stars that are blowing a cavity in the center of a star-forming region in the Small Magellanic Cloud. At the heart of the star-forming region lies star cluster NGC 602, also called N90.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 300
Description: NGC 300 is a spiral galaxy similar to our own Milky Way galaxy. Some of the bright blue specks in this image are young, massive stars called blue supergiants, and they are among the brightest stars seen in spiral galaxies.

Name: Globular Cluster 47 Tucanae
Description: This image of the heart of the giant globular star cluster 47 Tucanae reveals the glow of 200,000 stars. Young white dwarfs ― the burned-out relics of stars that have used up their nuclear fuel, cooled down, and lost most of their mass ― are beginning to migrate outward.

Name: Fomalhaut and Fomalhaut b
Description: This image shows the debris disk around the star Fomalhaut. These disks often give rise to planets. Fomalhaut b, originally thought to be a planet when observed in 2015, was later discovered to be a rarely-seen collision between icy objects in the disk.

Name: Hickson Compact Group 87
Description: This troupe of galaxies, known as Hickson Compact Group 87, is performing an intricate dance orchestrated by the mutual gravitational forces acting between them. The small spiral near the center could either be a member or an unrelated background object.

Name: Ant Nebula
Description: The Ant Nebula displays intriguing symmetrical patterns in the lobes of gas being ejected from a dying Sun-like star at its center.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 1015
Description: NGC 1015 is a barred spiral galaxy, so called because the higher concentration of stars near the galaxy's center forms a bar or rod through the center.

Name: Galaxy Cluster MACS J2129-0741
Description: This is a wide view of galaxy cluster MACS J2129-0741. The massive galaxy cluster magnifies, brightens, and distorts the images of remote background galaxies, including the far-distant, dead disk galaxy MACS2129-1.

Name: Antennae Galaxies
Description: The two merging spiral galaxies that comprise the Antennae galaxies began their interaction only a few hundred million years ago. Over the course of the merger, billions of stars will be formed.

Name: Planetary Nebula Hen 2-437
Description: Hen 2-437 is a planetary nebula, one of around 3,000 such objects known to reside within the Milky Way. Planetary nebulae such as Hen 2-437 form when an aging low-mass star, such as the Sun, reaches the final stages of life.

Name: Galaxy Abell 2597
Description: This galaxy shows chains of star formation in ultraviolet light. This star formation is a product of the action of the jets from a central black hole that controls infalling gas from the galaxy's halo.

Name: Globular Cluster NGC 1466
Description: NGC 1466 is an ancient, glimmering ball of stars, roughly spherical and bound together by gravity. This is called a globular cluster.

Name: Comet 3I/ATLAS
Description: Interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS was photographed when it was 277 million miles (365 million km) from Earth. The comet has a teardrop-shaped cocoon of dust coming off its solid, icy nucleus.

Name: Protostar IRAS 20324+4057
Description: This caterpillar-shaped knot, called IRAS 20324+4057, is a protostar that is in the process of growing from the dust and gas surrounding it. However, other bright stars are blasting ultraviolet radiation at this "wanna-be" star and sculpting the gas and dust into its long shape.

Name: Globular Cluster Messier 30
Description: This image of globular cluster M30 captures a dense swarm of several hundred thousand stars bound together by gravity. M30 is about 90 light-years across and formed 13 billion years ago.

Name: Irregular Galaxy NGC 4214
Description: Nearby galaxy NGC 4214 is forming clusters of new stars from its interstellar gas and dust. Young, hot stars have a whitish to bluish color in this image because of their high surface temperatures.

Name: Jupiter and Io
Description: While hunting for volcanic plumes on Io, astronomers captured this image of the volatile moon sweeping across the giant face of Jupiter. Io is roughly the size of Earth's Moon, but 2,000 times farther away from its planet.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 5643
Description: The glorious spiral galaxy NGC 5643 is a grand design spiral, which refers to the galaxy’s symmetrical form with two large, winding spiral arms that are clearly visible.

Name: Impact Scar on Jupiter
Description: This image of Jupiter reveals an elongated, dark spot. The unexpected blemish was created when an asteroid plunged into Jupiter and exploded, scattering debris into the giant planet's cloud tops.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 4680
Description: NGC 4680 is actually a rather tricky galaxy to classify. It is sometimes referred to as a spiral galaxy, but it is also sometimes classified as a lenticular galaxy. Lenticular galaxies are "lens-shaped" and fall somewhere in between spiral galaxies and elliptical galaxies.

Name: Lensed Quasar WFI2033-4723
Description: The gravity from the central core of a massive galaxy magnifies and distorts the light from a quasar behind it. Quasars are extremely distant cosmic streetlights produced by active black holes.

Name: Andromeda Galaxy Tendril
Description: Swaths of ionized gas glow in a tendril of the Milky Way's neighboring galaxy, Andromeda. These regions, which are common in spiral and irregular galaxies, often indicate the presence of recent star formation.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 4395
Description: This image of dwarf spiral galaxy NGC 4395 looks at a small section of the galaxy. NGC 4395 is one of the closest and dimmest known Seyfert galaxies, which have very bright cores driven by supermassive black holes.

Name: Jupiter and Io
Description: This image shows Jupiter's volcanic moon Io passing above the turbulent clouds of the giant planet. The conspicuous black spot on Jupiter is Io's shadow. The shadow sweeps across the face of Jupiter at 17 kilometers per second.

Name: Globular Cluster 47 Tucanae
Description: This image shows the core of the globular star cluster 47 Tucanae. The entire cluster contains about a million stars, with many packed tightly in the core.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 1309
Description: Looking like a child's pinwheel ready to be set spinning by a gentle breeze, this dramatic spiral galaxy is home to multiple notable stellar explosions, called supernovae, including SN 2002fk and SN 2012Z.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 6956
Description: Against an inky black backdrop, the blue swirls of spiral galaxy NGC 6956 stand out radiantly. NGC 6956 is a barred spiral galaxy, a common type of spiral galaxy with a bar-shaped structure of stars in its center.

Name: Andromeda Galaxy Tendril
Description: Swaths of ionized gas glow in a tendril of the Milky Way's neighboring galaxy, Andromeda. These regions, which are common in spiral and irregular galaxies, often indicate the presence of recent star formation.

Description: This troupe of galaxies, known as Hickson Compact Group 87, is performing an intricate dance orchestrated by the mutual gravitational forces acting between them. The small spiral near the center could either be a member or an unrelated background object.

Name: Eta Carinae
Description: The giant, petulant star Eta Carinae is prone to violent explosions. It's the largest of a double-star system located about 7,500 light-years away.

Name: Stephan's Quintet
Description: A clash among members of a famous galaxy group called Stephan's Quintet, also known as Hickson Compact Group 92, reveals an assortment of stars across a wide color range, from young, blue stars to aging, red stars.

Name: Uranus and Ariel
Description: This is the first time astronomers observed a moon and its shadow passing together over the face of Uranus. The 700-mile-diameter (1127 km) moon, Ariel (white dot), is casting a shadow onto the cloud tops of Uranus.

Name: Galaxy Cluster Abell 370
Description: The galaxy cluster Abell 370 contains several hundred galaxies tied together by the mutual pull of gravity. Entangled among the galaxies are arcs of blue light, actually distorted and magnified images of remote galaxies behind the cluster.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 7678
Description: NGC 7678 is a galaxy with one particularly prominent arm. With a diameter of around 115,000 light-years, this bright spiral galaxy is a similar size to our own Milky Way Galaxy.

Name: Pillar in the Carina Nebula
Description: Composed of gas and dust, this pillar of star birth resides in a tempestuous stellar nursery called the Carina Nebula. Within this pillar is Herbig Haro 666, a young star that is shooting out narrow jets in opposite directions.

Name: Triangulum Galaxy
Description: This mosaic captures the nearby Triangulum galaxy. Striking areas of starbirth glow bright blue throughout the galaxy, particularly in beautiful nebulae of hot gas like star-forming region NGC 604 in the upper left.

Name: Planetary Nebula NGC 5307
Description: NGC 5307, about 10,000 light-years away, is an example of a planetary nebula with a pinwheel or spiral structure. Each blob of gas ejected from the central star has a counterpart on the opposite side of the star.

Name: Star Cluster Trumpler 14
Description: Called Trumpler 14, this cluster of stars is located 8,000 light-years away in a huge star-forming region known as the Carina Nebula. The cluster is only 500,000 years old and has one of the highest concentrations of bright, massive stars in the entire Milky Way.

Name: Active Galaxy NGC 1275
Description: Fine, thread-like filamentary structures in the gas surrounding this galaxy mark the feedback process through which energy is transferred from the central massive black hole to the surrounding gas.

Name: Galaxy Cluster Abell 370
Description: The galaxy cluster Abell 370 contains several hundred galaxies tied together by the mutual pull of gravity. Entangled among the galaxies are arcs of blue light, actually distorted and magnified images of remote galaxies behind the cluster.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 5861
Description: The beautiful NGC 5861 is an intermediate spiral galaxy. Two supernovae, SN 1971D and SN 2017erp, have been observed in the galaxy. Supernovae are powerful and luminous explosions created by massive, dying stars.

Name: Globular Cluster NGC 6440
Description: NGC 6440 is a globular cluster, a roughly spherical, tightly packed collection of hundreds of thousands to millions of stars. The stars average about one light-year apart, but can be as close together as the size of our solar system.

Name: Hourglass Nebula
Description: The Hourglass Nebula has been formed by a dying Sun-like star shedding its outer layers of gas. One theory suggests that the hourglass shape is produced as a fast stellar wind encounters a slowly expanding cloud that is more dense near the star's equator than near its poles.

Name: Galaxy Cluster Abell 370
Description: The galaxy cluster Abell 370 contains several hundred galaxies tied together by the mutual pull of gravity. Entangled among the galaxies are arcs of blue light, actually distorted and magnified images of remote galaxies behind the cluster.

Name: Triple Star System in a Cocoon of Gas
Description: A trio of dazzling stars blaze from the hollowed-out cavity of a reflection nebula. The triple-star system is made up of the variable star HP Tau, HP Tau G2, and HP Tau G3.

Name: Active Galaxy NGC 1275
Description: Fine, thread-like filamentary structures in the gas surrounding this galaxy mark the feedback process through which energy is transferred from the central massive black hole to the surrounding gas.

Name: Diffuse Galaxy NGC 1052-DF2
Description: NGC 1052-DF2, or DF2, is an unusual "see-through" galaxy. The giant cosmic cotton ball is so diffuse and its ancient stars so spread out that distant galaxies in the background can be seen through it.

Name: Triangulum Galaxy
Description: This mosaic captures the nearby Triangulum galaxy. Striking areas of star birth glow bright blue throughout the galaxy, particularly in beautiful nebulae of hot gas like star-forming region NGC 604 in the upper left.

Name: Galaxy Cluster MACS J0416.1-2403
Description: Massive galaxy cluster MACS J0416.1-2403 weighs as much as a million billion suns. The cluster's gravitational field magnifies and distorts the light from galaxies far behind it, a phenomenon called gravitational lensing.

Name: Globular Cluster Messier 72
Description: M72 is a collection of stars formally known as a globular cluster. The intense gravitational attraction between the closely packed stars gives globular clusters their regular, spherical shape.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 2276
Description: The lopsided galaxy NGC 2276's uneven appearance is due to a neighboring galaxy to the right (not seen here) gravitationally tugging on its disk of blue stars, pulling the stars on one side of the galaxy outward.

Name: Elliptical Galaxy Messier 87
Description: This image of the giant galaxy M87 shows a 3,000-light-year-long jet of plasma blasting from the galaxy's 6.5-billion-solar-mass central black hole. The jet seems to cause stars to erupt along its trajectory.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 1672
Description: NGC 1672 is a barred spiral galaxy. Its arms do not twist all the way to the galaxy's center but attach to the ends of a bar of stars that extends from the nucleus. Clusters of hot, young, blue stars form along the spiral arms, while surrounding clouds of hydrogen gas glow red.

Name: Trifid Nebula
Description: The Trifid Nebula is a stellar nursery criss-crossed by huge, dark lanes of dust. This close-up view of the center of the nebula, near the intersection of the dust bands, shows a group of recently formed, massive, bright stars.

Name: Galaxy Cluster MACS J0416.1-2403
Description: Massive galaxy cluster MACS J0416.1-2403 weighs as much as a million billion suns. The cluster's gravitational field magnifies and distorts the light from galaxies far behind it, a phenomenon called gravitational lensing.

Name: Globular Cluster NGC 6397
Description: This ancient stellar jewelry box, globular cluster NGC 6397, glitters with the light from hundreds of thousands of stars. The cluster is 13.4 billion years old, born shortly after the Big Bang.

Name: Triangulum Galaxy
Description: This mosaic captures the nearby Triangulum galaxy. Striking areas of star birth glow bright blue throughout the galaxy.

Name: Hubble-V Nebula
Description: Hubble-V is an active star-forming region within galaxy NGC 6822. The cloud is about 200 light-years across and contains a dense knot of dozens of ultra-hot stars, each 100,000 times brighter than our Sun.

Name: Twin Jet Nebula
Description: The Twin Jet Nebula, also known as M2-9, is a striking example of a "butterfly" or a bipolar planetary nebula. If the nebula is sliced across the star, each side of it appears much like a pair of exhausts from jet engines.

Name: Spiral Galaxy ESO 137-001
Description: The spiral galaxy ESO 137-001 is zooming toward the upper right of this image so rapidly that much of its own gas is caught and torn away. The galaxy's stars remain intact due to the gravity tying them together.

Name: Spiral Galaxy Messier 33
Description: Reddish clouds of ionized hydrogen are interspersed with dark lanes of dust in the center of spiral galaxy Messier 33. The apparent graininess of the image is actually swarms of countless stars.

Description: This mosaic captures the nearby Triangulum galaxy. Striking areas of star birth glow bright blue throughout the galaxy.

Name: Impact Scar on Jupiter
Description: This image shows a scar on Jupiter. The unexpected blemish was created when an object (likely an asteroid) plunged into Jupiter and exploded, scattering debris into the giant planet's cloud tops.

Name: Triangulum Galaxy
Description: This mosaic captures the nearby Triangulum galaxy. Striking areas of star birth glow bright blue throughout the galaxy.

Name: Planetary Nebula IC 3568
Description: IC 3568, a round planetary nebula, lies at a distance of about 9,000 light-years away from Earth. Its bright yellow-green inner shell and faint, smooth, circular outer envelope gives it the appearance of a lime.

Name: Galaxy Cluster MACS J2129-0741
Description: This is a wider view of galaxy cluster MACS J2129-0741. The massive galaxy cluster magnifies, brightens, and distorts the images of remote background galaxies, including the far-distant, dead disk galaxy MACS2129-1.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 1637
Description: The spiral galaxy NGC 1637 holds evidence of star formation scattered throughout its disk, if you know where to look. The galaxy’s spiral arms have pockets of pink clouds, many with bright blue stars.

Name: Herbig-Haro 24
Description: A partially obscured, newborn star near the center of this image is shooting twin jets into the surrounding gas and dust. The shocks from the collision light up patches of nebulosity collectively called Herbig-Haro 24.

Name: Galaxy Cluster Abell 370
Description: The galaxy cluster Abell 370 contains several hundred galaxies tied together by the mutual pull of gravity. Entangled among the galaxies are arcs of blue light, actually distorted and magnified images of remote galaxies behind the cluster.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 3982
Description: This image captures the face-on spiral galaxy NGC 3982. Its arms are lined with pink star-forming regions of glowing hydrogen, blue newborn star clusters, and dark dust lanes that provide the raw material for future generations of stars.

Name: Object TMR-1C
Description: An unusual object called TMR-1C, initially suspected to be the first directly detected planet outside our solar system, is now believed to be a background star whose light has been dimmed by interstellar dust.

Name: Active Galaxy NGC 1275
Description: Fine, thread-like filamentary structures in the gas surrounding this galaxy mark the feedback process through which energy is transferred from the central massive black hole to the surrounding gas.

Name: Andromeda Galaxy
Description: Over 100 million stars are on display in this portion of the Andromeda galaxy, located over 2 million light-years away. This portrait of our galactic neighbor uses 7,398 exposures taken over 411 individual pointings of the telescope.

Name: Globular Cluster 47 Tucanae

Name: Egg Nebula

Description: Dozens of hot, blue, and high-mass stars shine within star cluster NGC 346. Astronomers believe this cluster contains more than half of the known high-mass stars in the whole Small Magellanic Cloud.

Name: Saturn and its Moons
Description: This image captures the moons Titan and Tethys. Titan chases its own shadow across Saturn's disk. The planet's rings are tilted nearly edge-on toward the Sun, an event that occurs once every 15 years.

Name: Planetary Nebula NGC 2022
Description: NGC 2022 is a vast orb of gas in space, cast off by an aging star. The star is visible in the orb's center, shining through the gases it held onto for most of its stellar life.

Name: Diffuse Galaxy NGC 1052-DF2
Description: NGC 1052-DF2, or DF2, is an unusual "see-through" galaxy. The giant cosmic cotton ball is so diffuse and its ancient stars so spread out that distant galaxies in the background can be seen through it.

Name: Star Cluster NGC 346
Description: Nested within the Small Magellanic Cloud is this spectacular star cluster, known as NGC 346. Its hot stars unleash a torrent of radiation and energetic outflows, which erode the denser portions of gas and dust in the surrounding nebula, N66.

Name: Center of the Crab Nebula
Description: At the center of the Crab Nebula sits a stellar remnant called a neutron star that has about the same mass as the Sun compressed into a sphere only a few miles across. Spinning 30 times a second, the neutron star shoots out beams of energy that make it look like it's pulsating.

Name: Interacting Galaxies Arp 295
Description: One of the galaxies from galactic group Arp 295 is visible in this image, along with part of the 250,000-light-year-long bridge of stars and gas that stretches between two of the galaxies.

Name: Stephan's Quintet

Name: Supernova in Galaxy NGC 2403

Name: Star Cluster Liller 1
Description: Liller 1 is a particularly interesting globular cluster, because unlike most of its kind, it contains a mix of very young and very old stars: the oldest is 12 billion years old, and the youngest component is just 1-2 billion years old.

Name: Galactic Center
Description: Peering deep into the heart of our Milky Way galaxy reveals a tapestry of more than half a million stars. Except for a few blue foreground stars, the rest are part of the Milky Way's nuclear star cluster, the most massive and densest star cluster in our galaxy.

Name: Asteroid Trail Past Sagittarius Dwarf Irregular Galaxy

Name: Lensed Quasar HE0435-1223

Name: Elliptical Galaxy NGC 4993
Description: In this galaxy, called NGC 4993, two neutron stars collided, creating gravitational waves discovered in 2017. The event produced a flash of light, called a kilonova, which appears to the upper left of center.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 6956
Description: Against an inky black backdrop, the blue swirls of spiral galaxy NGC 6956 stand out radiantly. NGC 6956 is a barred spiral galaxy, a common type of spiral galaxy with a bar-shaped structure of stars in its center.

Name: Galaxy Cluster Abell 520
Description: The merging galaxy cluster Abell 520 formed from a violent collision of massive galaxy clusters.

Name: Saturn in Multiple Wavelengths
Description: Hubble observed Saturn with a wide array of different light filters on the visible and ultraviolet scale to learn more about the behavior and composition of its atmosphere.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 7331
Description: The spiral galaxy known as NGC 7331 faces us partially edge-on, showcasing its beautiful arms, which swirl like a whirlpool around its bright central region. NGC 7331 is similar in size, shape, and mass to our Milky Way Galaxy.

Name: Abell 2744 Parallel Field

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 695

Name: Open Cluster NGC 2002
Description: NGC 2002 is an open cluster, a type of star cluster that has low star density and an irregular shape due to the weak mutual gravitational attraction of its stars. It is more spherical than a typical open cluster, and is relatively young at 18 million years old.

Name: Dark Spot on Uranus
