Name: Interacting Galaxy ESO 550-2
Description: ESO 550-2 shows a pair of spiral galaxies, with the larger viewed nearly face-on and accompanied by a smaller, highly tilted partner. Tidal interaction from the smaller companion has clearly deformed one arm of the larger galaxy.

Name: Globular Cluster NGC 6652
Description: The core of the globular star cluster NGC 6652 is suffused with the pale blue light of countless stars. Globular clusters are stable, tightly gravitationally bound clusters containing anywhere from tens of thousands to millions of stars.

Name: Hubble Ultra Deep Field
Description: This image of the Hubble Ultra Deep Field includes infrared observations that allowed Hubble to peer deeper into the universe than it ever had before. The faintest and reddest objects in the image are galaxies that formed 600 million years after the Big Bang.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 1015
Description: NGC 1015 is a barred spiral galaxy, so called because the higher concentration of stars near the galaxy's center forms a bar or rod through the center.

Name: Ghost Nebula IC 63
Description: Powerful gushers of energy from seething stars can sculpt eerie-looking figures with long flowing veils of gas and dust. One striking example is "the Ghost of Cassiopeia," officially known as IC 63.

Name: Galaxy Cluster MACS J0416.1-2403
Description: Massive galaxy cluster MACS J0416.1-2403 weighs as much as a million billion suns. The cluster's gravitational field magnifies and distorts the light from galaxies far behind it, a phenomenon called gravitational lensing.

Name: Spiral Galaxy Messier 83
Description: This image of spiral galaxy M83 captures thousands of star clusters, hundreds of thousands of individual stars, and "ghosts" of dead stars called supernova remnants.

Name: Hubble Ultra Deep Field
Description: This image of the Hubble Ultra Deep Field includes infrared observations that allowed Hubble to peer deeper into the universe than it ever had before. The faintest and reddest objects in the image are galaxies that formed 600 million years after the big bang.

Name: Pillars of Creation in Infrared Light
Description: By observing near-infrared light, we can see through much of the gas and dust in the Eagle Nebula's Pillars of Creation, revealing stars behind the nebula and hidden away inside the pillars.

Name: Binary Asteroid System 288P
Description: Two asteroids orbiting each other as a pair, collectively known as 2006 VW139/288P, have comet-like features. These include a bright halo of material, called a coma, and a long tail of dust.

Name: Galaxy Cluster MACS J0416.1-2403
Description: Massive galaxy cluster MACS J0416.1-2403 weighs as much as a million billion suns. The cluster's gravitational field magnifies and distorts the light from galaxies far behind it, a phenomenon called gravitational lensing.

Name: Abell 370 Parallel Field
Description: This is a view of a random patch of sky that reveals how the universe looks at large: a "wallpaper" of innumerable galaxies spread across space and time. They offer a wide assortment of majestic star cities that vary in age, shape, and stellar populations.

Name: Hubble Ultra Deep Field
Description: This image of the Hubble Ultra Deep Field includes infrared observations that allowed Hubble to peer deeper into the universe than it ever had before. The faintest and reddest objects in the image are galaxies that formed 600 million years after the big bang.

Name: Pillars of Creation in Infrared Light
Description: By observing near-infrared light, we can see through much of the gas and dust in the Eagle Nebula's Pillars of Creation, revealing stars behind the nebula and hidden away inside the pillars.

Name: Star Cluster Westerlund 2
Description: This image captures a giant cluster of about 3,000 stars called Westerlund 2. The cluster resides inside a vibrant stellar breeding ground known as Gum 29, located 20,000 light-years away.

Name: Star V838 Monocerotis
Description: This image captures a light echo from the star V838 Monocerotis. After the star brightened temporarily, light from that eruption began propagating outward through a dusty cloud around the star. The light reflects or "echoes" off the dust and then travels to Earth.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 1309
Description: Looking like a child's pinwheel ready to be set spinning by a gentle breeze, this dramatic spiral galaxy is home to multiple notable stellar explosions, called supernovae, including SN 2002fk and SN 2012Z.

Name: Galaxy HUDF-JD2
Description: The small red object at the center of this image (just above the large spiral galaxy) is one of the most distant galaxies ever seen. Called HUDF-JD2, it is one of about 10,000 galaxies found in the Hubble Ultra Deep Field.

Name: Star Cluster Westerlund 2
Description: This image captures a giant cluster of about 3,000 stars called Westerlund 2. The cluster resides inside a vibrant stellar breeding ground known as Gum 29, located 20,000 light-years away.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 1309
Description: Looking like a child's pinwheel ready to be set spinning by a gentle breeze, this dramatic spiral galaxy is home to multiple notable stellar explosions, called supernovae, including SN 2002fk and SN 2012Z.

Name: Interacting Galaxy MCG02-001
Description: MCG+12-02-001 consists of a pair of galaxies visibly affected by gravitational interaction as material is flung out in opposite directions. The larger galaxy is at the top and a smaller galaxy, resembling an erupting volcano, is at the bottom.

Name: Spiral Galaxy Messier 83
Description: This image of spiral galaxy M83 captures thousands of star clusters, hundreds of thousands of individual stars, and "ghosts" of dead stars called supernova remnants.

Name: Nebula N 81
Description: This image shows a newborn star cluster cradled within a nebula, or glowing cloud of gas, called N 81. This stellar nursery lies about 200,000 light-years away within the Small Magellanic Cloud, a small galaxy orbiting our own Milky Way.

Name: Globular Cluster 47 Tucanae
Description: This image shows the core of the globular star cluster 47 Tucanae. The entire cluster contains about a million stars, with many packed tightly in the core.

Name: Spiral Galaxy UGC 10043
Description: Spiral galaxy UGC 10043 is one of the somewhat rare spiral galaxies that we see edge-on. This edge-on viewpoint makes the galaxy’s disk appear as a sharp line through space.

Name: Twin Jet Nebula
Description: The Twin Jet Nebula, also known as M2-9, is a striking example of a "butterfly" or a bipolar planetary nebula. If the nebula is sliced across the star, each side of it appears much like a pair of exhausts from jet engines.

Name: Interacting Galaxy MCG11-002
Description: MCG+08-11-002 is an odd-looking galaxy with a spectacular dark band of dust in front of the galaxy's center, making it resemble a "black eye." Scientists believe that it resulted from a collision of two galaxies.

Name: Hubble Ultra Deep Field
Description: This image of the Hubble Ultra Deep Field includes infrared observations that allowed Hubble to peer deeper into the universe than it ever had before. The faintest and reddest objects in the image are galaxies that formed 600 million years after the big bang.

Name: Pillars of Creation in Visible Light
Description: The towering Pillars of Creation are about 5 light-years tall. They are part of the Eagle Nebula, a vast star-forming region. Stars are being born deep inside the pillars, which are made of cold hydrogen gas laced with dust.

Name: Spiral Galaxy IC 758
Description: The serene spiral galaxy IC 758 appears peaceful, with its soft blue spiral arms curving gently around its hazy barred center. However, in 1999, astronomers spotted a powerful explosion in this galaxy. The supernova SN 1999bg marked the dramatic end of a massive star.

Name: Newly Forming Star FS Tau
Description: Jets of energized material emerge from the cocoon of newly forming star FS Tau B to blast across space, slicing through the gas and dust of a shining nebula.

Name: Nebula N159
Description: This Hubble view of a turbulent starbirth region reveals ridges, arcs, and filaments sculpted by torrential stellar winds from hot, newborn, massive stars.

Name: Hubble Ultra Deep Field
Description: This image of the Hubble Ultra Deep Field includes infrared observations that allowed Hubble to peer deeper into the universe than it ever had before. The faintest and reddest objects in the image are galaxies that formed 600 million years after the big bang.

Name: Globular Cluster 47 Tucanae
Description: This image of the heart of the giant globular star cluster 47 Tucanae reveals the glow of 200,000 stars. Young white dwarfs ― the burned-out relics of stars that have used up their nuclear fuel, cooled down, and lost most of their mass ― are beginning to migrate outward.

Name: Interacting Galaxies 2MASX J06094582-2140234
Description: Here we see two spiral galaxies engaged in a cosmic tug-of-war, but in this contest, there will be no winner. The structures of both objects are slowly distorted to resemble new forms, and in some cases, merge together to form new, super galaxies.

Name: Center of the Crab Nebula
Description: At the center of the Crab Nebula sits a stellar remnant called a neutron star that has about the same mass as the Sun compressed into a sphere only a few miles across. Spinning 30 times a second, the neutron star shoots out beams of energy that make it look like it's pulsating.

Name: Spiral Galaxy Messier 81
Description: The arms of the "grand design" spiral galaxy M81 are filled with young, bluish, hot stars. The greenish regions in the image are bright, gaseous clouds where new stars are forming.

Name: Hubble-X Nebula
Description: Hubble-X is a glowing gas cloud, one of the most active star-forming regions within galaxy NGC 6822. The cloud is about 110 light-years across and contains many thousands of newly formed stars in a central cluster.

Name: Globular Cluster 47 Tucanae
Description: This image of the heart of the giant globular star cluster 47 Tucanae reveals the glow of 200,000 stars. Young white dwarfs ― the burned-out relics of stars that have used up their nuclear fuel, cooled down, and lost most of their mass ― are beginning to migrate outward.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 1309
Description: Looking like a child's pinwheel ready to be set spinning by a gentle breeze, this dramatic spiral galaxy is home to multiple notable stellar explosions, called supernovae, including SN 2002fk and SN 2012Z.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 5643
Description: The glorious spiral galaxy NGC 5643 is a grand design spiral, which refers to the galaxy’s symmetrical form with two large, winding spiral arms that are clearly visible.

Name: Spiral Galaxy Messier 81
Description: The arms of the "grand design" spiral galaxy M81 are filled with young, bluish, hot stars. The greenish regions in the image are bright, gaseous clouds where new stars are forming.

Name: Spiral Galaxy Messier 81
Description: The arms of the "grand design" spiral galaxy M81 are filled with young, bluish, hot stars. The greenish regions in the image are bright, gaseous clouds where new stars are forming.

Name: Star Cluster Westerlund 2
Description: This image captures a giant cluster of about 3,000 stars called Westerlund 2. The cluster resides inside a vibrant stellar breeding ground known as Gum 29, located 20,000 light-years away.

Name: Orion Nebula "Window Curtain"
Description: This image reveals the structure of a thin sheet of gas located at the edge of the famous "Great Nebula" in Orion, also known as Messier 42 or NGC 1976.

Name: Galaxy Cluster Abell 370
Description: The galaxy cluster Abell 370 contains several hundred galaxies tied together by the mutual pull of gravity. Entangled among the galaxies are arcs of blue light, actually distorted and magnified images of remote galaxies behind the cluster.

Name: Trifid Nebula
Description: The Trifid Nebula reveals a stellar nursery being torn apart by radiation from a nearby, massive star.

Name: V838 Monocerotis Light Echo
Description: This image captures a light echo from the star V838 Monocerotis. After the star brightened temporarily, light from that eruption began propagating outward through a dusty cloud around the star. The light reflects or "echoes" off the dust and then travels to Earth.

Name: Binary Asteroid System 288P
Description: Two asteroids orbiting each other as a pair, collectively known as 2006 VW139/288P, have comet-like features. These include a bright halo of material, called a coma, and a long tail of dust.

Name: Planetary Nebula Hubble 5
Description: Hubble 5, lying 2,200 light-years away, is a "butterfly" or bipolar (two-lobed) nebula. The heat generated by fast winds causes each of the lobes to expand, much like a pair of balloons with internal heaters.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 1559
Description: This magnificent barred spiral galaxy is NGC 1559. This picture is composed of a whopping 10 different Hubble images, from ultraviolet through visible light and into the near-infrared spectrum.

Name: Orion Nebula "Window Curtain"
Description: This image reveals the structure of a thin sheet of gas located at the edge of the famous "Great Nebula" in Orion, also known as Messier 42 or NGC 1976.

Name: Galaxy Behind Star Cluster NGC 6752
Description: This image shows stars in a small part of the globular cluster NGC 6752. Near the bottom appears a background galaxy, much farther away, that astronomers found while studying this image. It's a dwarf galaxy that is nearly as old as the universe.

Name: Crab Nebula
Description: The glow of a dead star, which exploded long ago as a supernova, reveals itself in this image of the Crab Nebula. At its center is a rotating neutron star, or pulsar, which has about the same mass as the Sun squeezed into a sphere only a few miles wide.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 6814
Description: The striking face-on spiral galaxy NGC 6814 has a luminous nucleus and spectacular sweeping arms, rippled with an intricate pattern of dark dust. Spiral galaxies make up about 60 percent of the galaxies in the local universe.

Name: Active Asteroid P/2013 P5
Description: This body in the asteroid belt, designated P/2013 P5, was first discovered as an unusually fuzzy-looking object. This image reveals a never-before-seen set of six comet-like tails radiating from the asteroid.

Name: Galaxy Cluster Abell 370
Description: The galaxy cluster Abell 370 contains several hundred galaxies tied together by the mutual pull of gravity. Entangled among the galaxies are arcs of blue light, actually distorted and magnified images of remote galaxies behind the cluster.

Name: GOODS South Field
Description: More than 12 billion years of cosmic history are shown in this panoramic view of thousands of galaxies in various stages of assembly. The view covers a portion of the southern field of a galaxy census called the Great Observatories Origins Deep Survey (GOODS).

Name: Spiral Galaxy UGC 3912
Description: UGC 3912 is classified as a spiral galaxy, but you wouldn’t know it from this detailed image. UGC 3912’s distorted shape typically indicates a gravitational encounter with another galaxy.

Name: Galaxy Cluster Abell 370
Description: The galaxy cluster Abell 370 contains several hundred galaxies tied together by the mutual pull of gravity. Entangled among the galaxies are arcs of blue light, actually distorted and magnified images of remote galaxies behind the cluster.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 1087
Description: New and old stars twinkle in the dusty arms of barred spiral galaxy NGC 1087. The elongated, bright-white bar structure at the galaxy’s center is shorter compared to other barred galaxies.

Name: Galaxy Cluster El Gordo
Description: This galaxy cluster, cataloged as ACT-CL J0102-4915 and nicknamed "El Gordo" ("the fat one" in Spanish), contains several hundred galaxies swarming around under the collective gravitational pull. The total mass of the cluster is estimated to weigh as much as 3 million billion stars like our Sun.

Name: Starburst Galaxy NGC 3310
Description: There are several hundred star clusters in the starburst galaxy NGC 3310. They appear in this image as the bright, blue clumps that trace the galaxy's spiral arms.

Name: Planetary Nebula Hubble 12
Description: This bipolar planetary nebula known as PN Hb 12 (a.k.a. Hubble 12), reminiscent of a butterfly or an hourglass, was formed as a Sun-like star approached the end of its life and puffed its outer layers into the surrounding space.

Name: Elliptical Galaxy UGC 10143
Description: The giant elliptical galaxy UGC 10143 is the biggest and brightest member of galaxy cluster Abell 2147. Ellipticals are often near the center of galaxy clusters, suggesting they may form when galaxies merge.

Name: Galaxy Behind Star Cluster NGC 6752
Description: This image shows stars in a small part of the globular cluster NGC 6752. Near the bottom appears a background galaxy, much farther away, that astronomers found while studying this image. It's a dwarf galaxy that is nearly as old as the universe.

Name: Hubble Ultra Deep Field
Description: This image of the Hubble Ultra Deep Field includes infrared observations that allowed Hubble to peer deeper into the universe than it ever had before. The faintest and reddest objects in the image are galaxies that formed 600 million years after the big bang.

Name: Arches Cluster
Description: The Arches cluster is the densest known star cluster in our galaxy and resides 25,000 light-years away. In this rough-and-tumble region, huge clouds of gas collide to form behemoth stars.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 253
Description: NGC 253 is one of the brightest spiral galaxies in the sky. This image captures a swath of its bright and dusty core, revealing individual stars.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 5921
Description: Much like our own galaxy, the Milky Way, the spiral galaxy NGC 5921 contains a prominent bar – a central linear band of stars. Roughly half of all spiral galaxies may contain bars. These bars affect their parent galaxies by fueling star formation.

Name: Irregular Galaxy UGC 12682
Description: An irregular galaxy called UGC 12682 glows warmly against the dark backdrop of the universe. Located approximately 70 million light-years away, UGC 12682 is distorted and oddly structured, with bright pockets of star formation.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 6956
Description: Against an inky black backdrop, the blue swirls of spiral galaxy NGC 6956 stand out radiantly. NGC 6956 is a barred spiral galaxy, a common type of spiral galaxy with a bar-shaped structure of stars in its center.

Name: GOODS South Field

Name: Galaxy Behind Star Cluster NGC 6752
Description: This image shows stars in a small part of the globular cluster NGC 6752. Near the bottom appears a background galaxy, much farther away, that astronomers found while studying this image. It's a dwarf galaxy that is nearly as old as the universe.

Name: Spirograph Nebula IC 418
Description: A few thousand years ago, a red giant star ejected its outer layers into space to form the planetary nebula IC 418, also known as the Spirograph Nebula. At nebula's center is the star's hot core, whose radiation causes the surrounding gas to glow.

Name: Spiral Galaxy Messier 81
Description: The arms of the "grand design" spiral galaxy M81 are filled with young, bluish, hot stars. The greenish regions in the image are bright, gaseous clouds where new stars are forming.

Name: Center of the Crab Nebula
Description: At the center of the Crab Nebula sits a stellar remnant called a neutron star that has about the same mass as the Sun compressed into a sphere only a few miles across. Spinning 30 times a second, the neutron star shoots out beams of energy that make it look like it's pulsating.

Name: Galaxy Behind Star Cluster NGC 6752
Description: This image shows stars in a small part of the globular cluster NGC 6752. Near the bottom appears a background galaxy, much farther away, that astronomers found while studying this image. It's a dwarf galaxy that is nearly as old as the universe.

Name: Asteroid Photobombing a Spiral Galaxy
Description: This image of the barred spiral galaxy UGC 12158 looks like someone took a white marking pen to it. The streaks are a foreground asteroid moving through Hubble's field-of-view, photobombing the observation of the galaxy.

Name: Diffuse Galaxy NGC 1052-DF2
Description: NGC 1052-DF2, or DF2, is an unusual "see-through" galaxy. The giant cosmic cotton ball is so diffuse and its ancient stars so spread out that distant galaxies in the background can be seen through it.

Name: Hubble Ultra Deep Field
Description: This image of the Hubble Ultra Deep Field includes infrared observations that allowed Hubble to peer deeper into the universe than it ever had before. The faintest and reddest objects in the image are galaxies that formed 600 million years after the Big Bang.

Name: Beta Pictoris Disk
Description: In 1984, Beta Pictoris was the very first star discovered to be surrounded by a bright disk of light-scattering dust and debris. Planets are thought to form in such disks, and astronomers have discovered two planets orbiting Beta Pictoris.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 1309
Description: Looking like a child's pinwheel ready to be set spinning by a gentle breeze, this dramatic spiral galaxy is home to multiple notable stellar explosions, called supernovae, including SN 2002fk and SN 2012Z.

Name: Galaxy Behind Star Cluster NGC 6752
Description: This image shows stars in a small part of the globular cluster NGC 6752. Near the bottom appears a background galaxy, much farther away, that astronomers found while studying this image. It's a dwarf galaxy that is nearly as old as the universe.

Name: Diffuse Galaxy NGC 1052-DF2
Description: NGC 1052-DF2, or DF2, is an unusual "see-through" galaxy. The giant cosmic cotton ball is so diffuse and its ancient stars so spread out that distant galaxies in the background can be seen through it.

Name: Omega Centauri
Description: Omega Centauri consists of roughly 10 million stars that are gravitationally bound. The cluster is about 10 times as massive as other big globular clusters – almost as massive as a small galaxy.

Name: 30 Doradus Nebula
Description: Glowing hydrogen clouds and dark filamentary dust structures are visible in this close-up view of a star-birth region called the 30 Doradus Nebula. The giant stellar factory lies 170,000 light-years away inside the Large Magellanic Cloud.

Name: Interacting Galaxies Arp 295
Description: One of the galaxies from galactic group Arp 295 is visible in this image, along with part of the 250,000-light-year-long bridge of stars and gas that stretches between two of the galaxies.

Name: Globular Cluster Messier 15
Description: A spectacular swarm of stars, M15 is one of the densest globular clusters ever discovered, with very hot blue stars and cooler orange stars becoming more concentrated toward its bright core. It is host to an intermediate-mass black hole at its core.

Name: Galaxy Behind Star Cluster NGC 6752
Description: This image shows stars in a small part of the globular cluster NGC 6752. Near the bottom appears a background galaxy, much farther away, that astronomers found while studying this image. It's a dwarf galaxy that is nearly as old as the universe.

Name: Uranus
Description: Hubble observed the "ice giant" planet Uranus at the same time as the New Horizons spacecraft. Knowing what the clouds on Uranus looked like from Hubble helped researchers with interpretations of the New Horizons data.

Name: Pinwheel Galaxy
Description: The Pinwheel galaxy has a pancake-like shape that we view face-on. This perspective shows off the spiral structure that gives the galaxy its nickname.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 1309
Description: Looking like a child's pinwheel ready to be set spinning by a gentle breeze, this dramatic spiral galaxy is home to multiple notable stellar explosions, called supernovae, including SN 2002fk and SN 2012Z.

Name: Neptune's Storm
Description: Three billion miles (5 billion km) away on the farthest known major planet in our solar system, an ominous, dark storm ― once big enough to stretch across the Atlantic Ocean ― shrank out of existence on Neptune.

Name: Cat's Eye Nebula
Description: NGC 6543, nicknamed the "Cat's Eye Nebula," has a surprisingly intricate structure and is one of the most complex planetary nebulae ever seen. It's estimated to be 1,000 years old.

Name: Interacting Galaxy AM 0702-601
Description: AM 0702 consists of a couple of detached galaxies, far apart and probably just beginning to interact. The first signs of the gravitational interaction are visible in the galaxy on the left, where the outer structure of the spiral arms is starting to expand.

Name: Reflection Nebula IC 349
Description: IC 349 is a reflection nebula in the Pleiades star cluster (often called the "Seven Sisters"). The eerie, wispy tendrils of an interstellar cloud are being destroyed by one of the brightest stars in the star cluster.

Name: Ring Nebula
Description: This is a close-up, visible-light view of Messier 57, better known as the Ring Nebula, the glowing remains of a sun-like star. The tiny white dot in the center is the star's hot core, called a white dwarf.

Name: Aligned Spiral Galaxies
Description: In this rare alignment between two spiral galaxies, the outer rim of a small, foreground galaxy is silhouetted in front of a larger background galaxy. Tentacles of dust extend beyond the small galaxy's disk of starlight.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 1559
Description: This magnificent barred spiral galaxy is NGC 1559. This picture is composed of a whopping 10 different Hubble images, from ultraviolet through visible light and into the near-infrared spectrum.

Name: Planetary Nebula NGC 2438
Description: NGC 2438 is a planetary nebula, formed after the death of a Sun-like star. The medium-sized star expelled its outer layers of gas into space as it died, leaving behind a white-dwarf core.

Name: GOODS South Field
Description: More than 12 billion years of cosmic history are shown in this panoramic view of thousands of galaxies in various stages of assembly. The view covers a portion of the southern field of a galaxy census called the Great Observatories Origins Deep Survey (GOODS).

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 1309
Description: Looking like a child's pinwheel ready to be set spinning by a gentle breeze, this dramatic spiral galaxy is home to multiple notable stellar explosions, called supernovae, including SN 2002fk and SN 2012Z.

Name: Supernova Remnant DEM L316A
Description: These rippling wisps of ionized gas, named DEM L316A, are the remnants of a long-dead star that ended its life in an explosion called a supernova. It is located within one of our Milky Way Galaxy’s closest galactic neighbors: the Large Magellanic Cloud.

Name: Binary Asteroid System 288P
Description: Two asteroids orbiting each other as a pair, collectively known as 2006 VW139/288P, have comet-like features. These include a bright halo of material, called a coma, and a long tail of dust.

Name: Flame Nebula
Description: The Flame Nebula, also called NGC 2024, is a large star-forming region. This image focuses on the dark, dusty heart of the nebula where a star cluster resides, mostly hidden from view.

Name: GOODS South Field
Description: More than 12 billion years of cosmic history are shown in this panoramic view of thousands of galaxies in various stages of assembly. The view covers a portion of the southern field of a galaxy census called the Great Observatories Origins Deep Survey (GOODS).

Name: Dual Nebulae NGC 248
Description: This image captures two festive-looking nebulae, situated so as to appear as one. They reside in the Small Magellanic Cloud, a dwarf galaxy that is a satellite of our Milky Way galaxy. The nebulae, together, are called NGC 248.

Name: Einstein Ring Gravitational Lens (SDSS J073728.45+321618.5)
Description: Light from a distant galaxy was deflected on its way to Earth by the gravitational field of a massive object along its path that distorted and maginfied the galaxy’s light into the arcs we see here.

Name: Globular Cluster Messier 80
Description: This stellar swarm is one of the densest of the 147 known globular star clusters in the Milky Way galaxy. M80, also called NGC 6093, contains hundreds of thousands of stars, all held together by their mutual gravitational attraction.

Name: Jellyfish Galaxy JO206
Description: The jellyfish galaxy JO206 showcases a colorful star-forming disk surrounded by a pale, luminous cloud of dust. The tendrils of jellyfish galaxies are formed by the interaction between galaxies and galaxy clusters.

Name: GOODS South Field
Description: More than 12 billion years of cosmic history are shown in this panoramic view of thousands of galaxies in various stages of assembly. The view covers a portion of the southern field of a galaxy census called the Great Observatories Origins Deep Survey (GOODS).

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 1300
Description: The core of this large spiral shows its own extraordinary and distinct spiral structure that is about 3,300 light-years long. Only galaxies with large-scale bars appear to have these a spiral within a spiral disks.

Name: Arp’s Loop
Description: Arp’s loop is a wispy bridge of gas strung among three colliding galaxies, M81, M82, and NGC 3077. The blue blobs are stars grouped together in interstellar space.

Name: Dual Nebulae NGC 248
Description: This image captures two festive-looking nebulae, situated so as to appear as one. They reside in the Small Magellanic Cloud, a dwarf galaxy that is a satellite of our Milky Way galaxy. The nebulae, together, are called NGC 248.

Name: Saturn
Description: This image of Saturn heralds the start of the planet's "spoke season" surrounding its equinox, when enigmatic features appear across its rings. The suspected culprit for the spokes is the planet's variable magnetic field.

Name: Spiral Galaxy ESO 243-49
Description: This edge-on galaxy, called ESO 243-49, appears to host a medium-sized black hole that might have come from a cannibalized dwarf galaxy. As massive as 20,000 Suns, the black hole lies above the galactic plane, an unusual location that suggests it originated somewhere else.

Name: Spiral Galaxy UGC 2885
Description: Located about 232 million light-years away, the galaxy UGC 2885 is about 2.5 times wider than our home galaxy, the Milky Way – and it contains 10 times as many stars!

Name: Compact Galaxy ESO 185-IG013
Description: ESO 185-IG013 is a luminous blue compact galaxy. These nearby galaxies show intense bursts of star formation and are unusually blue in visible light.

Name: Galactic Center
Description: Peering deep into the heart of our Milky Way galaxy reveals a tapestry of more than half a million stars. Except for a few blue foreground stars, the rest are part of the Milky Way's nuclear star cluster, the most massive and densest star cluster in our galaxy.

Name: Active Asteroid P/2013 P5
Description: This body in the asteroid belt, designated P/2013 P5, was first discovered as an unusually fuzzy-looking object. This image reveals a never-before-seen set of six comet-like tails radiating from the asteroid.

Name: Spiral Galaxy ESO 243-49
Description: This edge-on galaxy, called ESO 243-49, appears to host a medium-sized black hole that might have come from a cannibalized dwarf galaxy. As massive as 20,000 Suns, the black hole lies above the galactic plane, an unusual location that suggests it originated somewhere else.

Name: Planetary Nebula Hubble 12
Description: This bipolar planetary nebula known as PN Hb 12 (a.k.a. Hubble 12), reminiscent of a butterfly or an hourglass, formed as a Sun-like star approached the end of its life and puffed its outer layers into the surrounding space.

Name: Active Galaxy Z 229-15
Description: Z 229-15 is an interesting celestial object called a Seyfert galaxy. This means that although it hosts an extremely bright and energetic center, the rest of the galaxy remains visible.

Name: Flame Nebula
Description: The Flame Nebula, also called NGC 2024, is a large star-forming region. This image focuses on the dark, dusty heart of the nebula where a star cluster resides, mostly hidden from view.

Name: Hubble Ultra Deep Field
Description: This view of nearly 10,000 galaxies is the deepest visible-light image of the cosmos. Called the Hubble Ultra Deep Field, this galaxy-studded view represents a "deep" core sample of the universe, cutting across billions of light-years.

Name: Elliptical Galaxy NGC 1132
Description: The large elliptical galaxy NGC 1132 likely formed from a group of galaxies that merged together. The galaxy is dubbed a "fossil group" because it contains enormous concentrations of dark matter, comparable to the dark matter found in an entire group of galaxies.

Name: Ring Nebula
Description: This is a close-up, visible-light view of Messier 57, better known as the Ring Nebula, the glowing remains of a Sun-like star. The white dot in the center of the planetary nebula is the star's hot core, called a white dwarf.

Name: 30 Doradus Nebula
Description: This is the inner part of the 30 Doradus Nebula, a turbulent star-birth region in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a satellite galaxy of our Milky Way. The bright cluster of stars at left is known as R136.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 2566
Description: A prominent bar of stars stretches across the center of this spiral galaxy, NGC 2566, and spiral arms emerge from each end of the bar. Because it appears tilted from our perspective, its disk takes the appearance of a cosmic eye.

Name: Surfboard Galaxy
Description: Messier 108 is one of the largest and brightest members of the Ursa Major galaxy cluster. It is called the Surfboard galaxy because, when viewed with a telescope, it is seen nearly edge-on with no apparent bulge or pronounced core.

Name: GOODS South Field

Name: Dual Nebulae NGC 248
Description: This image captures two festive-looking nebulae, situated so as to appear as one. They reside in the Small Magellanic Cloud, a dwarf galaxy that is a satellite of our Milky Way galaxy. The nebulae, together, are called NGC 248.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 1300
Description: The core of this large spiral shows its own extraordinary and distinct spiral structure that is about 3,300 light-years long. Only galaxies with large-scale bars appear to have these a spiral within a spiral disks.

Name: 30 Doradus Nebula
Description: Glowing hydrogen clouds and dark filamentary dust structures are visible in this close-up view of a star-birth region called the 30 Doradus Nebula. The giant stellar factory lies 170,000 light-years away inside the Large Magellanic Cloud.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 1015
Description: NGC 1015 is a barred spiral galaxy, so called because the higher concentration of stars near the galaxy's center forms a bar or rod through the center.

Name: Egg Nebula
Description: In the Egg Nebula, shells of dust form concentric rings around an aging star, resembling the layers of an onion. A thick dust belt, running almost vertically through the center, blocks light from the central star while twin beams of light radiate from the star.

Name: Dual Nebulae NGC 248
Description: This image captures two festive-looking nebulae, situated so as to appear as one. They reside in the Small Magellanic Cloud, a dwarf galaxy that is a satellite of our Milky Way galaxy. The nebulae, together, are called NGC 248.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 1309
Description: Looking like a child's pinwheel ready to be set spinning by a gentle breeze, this dramatic spiral galaxy is home to multiple notable stellar explosions, called supernovae, including SN 2002fk and SN 2012Z.

Name: Spiral Galaxy UGC 10043
Description: Spiral galaxy UGC 10043 is one of the somewhat rare spiral galaxies that we see edge-on. This edge-on viewpoint makes the galaxy’s disk appear as a sharp line through space.

Name: Galaxy Cluster MACS J0416.1-2403
Description: Massive galaxy cluster MACS J0416.1-2403 weighs as much as a million billion suns. The cluster's gravitational field magnifies and distorts the light from galaxies far behind it, a phenomenon called gravitational lensing.

Name: Galaxy NGC 300
Description: NGC 300 is a spiral galaxy similar to our own Milky Way galaxy. Some of the bright blue specks in this image are young, massive stars called blue supergiants, and they are among the brightest stars seen in spiral galaxies.

Name: Galaxy Cluster Abell 370
Description: The galaxy cluster Abell 370 contains several hundred galaxies tied together by the mutual pull of gravity. Entangled among the galaxies are arcs of blue light, actually distorted and magnified images of remote galaxies behind the cluster.

Name: Spiral Galaxy UGC 5460
Description: This image reveals UGC 5460’s central bar of stars, winding spiral arms, and bright blue star clusters. Also captured in the upper left-hand corner is a far closer object: a star just 577 light-years away in our own galaxy.

Name: Interacting Galaxies Arp 298
Description: Arp 298 is made up of the two interacting galaxies NGC 7469 and IC 5283. The larger NGC 7469 hosts an active, supermassive black hole and a bright ring of star clusters.

Name: Mysterious Object He 2-90
Description: He 2-90 is an enigma. In this Hubble image, it looks like a young, dust-shrouded star with narrow jets. It's classified as a planetary nebula, the glowing remains of a dying star. But it may be neither. Astronomers now suspect He 2-90 is a pair of aging stars masquerading as a single youngster.

Name: Flame Nebula
Description: The Flame Nebula, also called NGC 2024, is a large star-forming region. This image focuses on the dark, dusty heart of the nebula where a star cluster resides, mostly hidden from view.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 2566
Description: A prominent bar of stars stretches across the center of this spiral galaxy, NGC 2566, and spiral arms emerge from each end of the bar. Because it appears tilted from our perspective, its disk takes the appearance of a cosmic eye.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 3949
Description: Like our Milky Way, the galaxy NGC 3949 has a disk full of young, blue stars peppered with pink star-birth regions. In contrast to the blue disk, the galaxy's bright center is made up of mostly older stars and appears more yellow.

Name: White Dwarf Stein 2051 B
Description: The white dwarf star Stein 2051 B and the smaller star below it appear to be close neighbors, but they reside far away from each other. After first imaging this star on October 1, 2013, Hubble returned to it one year later on the same day in 2014.

Name: Proxima Centauri
Description: The red dwarf star Proxima Centauri, part of the Alpha Centauri triple-star system, is the closest star to our Sun.

Name: Globular Cluster 47 Tucanae
Description: The ancient globular cluster 47 Tucanae is a dense swarm of up to a million stars, and this view captures a close-up of thousands of them. The large, bright stars in the image are red giants near the end of their lives.

Name: Beta Pictoris Disk
Description: The star Beta Pictoris has primary and secondary dust disks. The fainter secondary disk extends at least 24 billion miles (39 billion km) from the star and is tilted 4 to 5 degrees from the primary disk. It may be evidence of a planet in a similarly inclined orbit.

Description: These colorful stars reside at the heart of our Milky Way galaxy, about 26,000 light-years from Earth. Aging red giant stars coexist with their more plentiful younger cousins, the smaller, white, Sun-like stars, in this crowded region of our galaxy's central hub.

Name: Butterfly Nebula
Description: This Hubble image shows NGC 6302, nicknamed the Butterfly Nebula. The "wings" are regions of heated gas that are tearing across space at more than 600,000 miles (965,600 km) an hour.

Name: Interacting Galaxies Arp-Madore 608-333
Description: The two interacting galaxies making up the pair known as Arp-Madore 608-333 appear serene and unperturbed, but the two are subtly warping one another through a mutual gravitational interaction that is disrupting and distorting both galaxies.

Name: Disturbed Spiral Galaxy NGC 3718
Description: NGC 3718 is a disturbed spiral galaxy with a warped shape that looks like a plump letter “s” from Earth, with a thread of dark dust snaking through it. Hubble’s view shows the dust lane in detail as it sweeps by the core of the galaxy and curves into the surrounding gas.

Name: Galaxy Hercules A
Description: At the center of this image sits a large galaxy called Hercules A that harbors a supermassive black hole more than a thousand times as massive as the one in the Milky Way's center. Radio observations reveal large jets shooting away from the galaxy's core.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 986
Description: Barred spiral galaxies like NGC 986 are spiral galaxies with a central bar-shaped structure composed of stars. Young blue stars are dotted amongst the galaxy’s arms and the core of the galaxy is also aglow with star formation.

Name: Open Cluster KMHK 1231
Description: Open cluster KMHK 1231 is a group of stars loosely bound by gravity. This cluster in the Large Magellanic Cloud is surrounded by a crimson nebula of gas and dust extending across the image, where new stars may someday form.

Name: Open Cluster NGC 1858
Description: The stars within the young open cluster NGC 1858 are at different phases of evolution, making it a complex collection. The glowing emission nebula also suggests that star formation recently occurred.

Name: Supernova Remnant LMC N 63A
Description: This violent and chaotic-looking mass of gas is a nearby supernova remnant called N 63A. It is the remains of a massive star that exploded, spewing its gaseous layers out into an already turbulent region.

Name: Galaxy Cluster Abell 2667
Description: While looking at galaxy cluster Abell 2667, astronomers found an odd-looking spiral galaxy (in the upper left corner of the image) that is plowing through the cluster and being ripped apart by the galaxy cluster's gravitational field and harsh environment.

Name: Comet ISON
Description: Comet ISON was inside Mars' orbit and 177 million miles (25 million km) from Earth when this photograph was taken. The tail forms as dust particles are pushed away from the comet's nucleus by the pressure of sunlight.

Name: Interacting Galaxies Arp 140
Description: A barred spiral galaxy and a lenticular galaxy come together to create this interacting pair known as Arp 140. The lenticular galaxy, NGC 274, is visible on the right side of this new image, and the barred spiral, NGC 275, is at left.

Name: Galaxy Cluster Abell 2667
Description: An odd-looking spiral galaxy (upper left) is being ripped apart by a galaxy cluster's gravitational field and harsh environment. As it speeds through, it rams into the hot gas that permeates the cluster and its gas and stars are pulled away cluster's gravity.

Description: This glittering bauble called M92 is one of the brightest globular clusters in the Milky Way. It is very tightly packed with stars, containing some 330,000 stars in total.

Name: Uranus

Name: Needle's Eye Galaxy
Description: A portion of Caldwell 62, or the Needle's Eye Galaxy, shows clusters of stars and gas. The Needle's Eye is a dwarf spiral galaxy located about 11 million light-years away.

Name: Comet 2I/Borisov
Description: Hubble captured an image of Comet 2I/Borisov when it was 260 million miles (418 million km) from Earth. This was the second known interstellar object to have passed through our solar system.

Name: Open Cluster R136

Description: A partially obscured, newborn star near the center of this image is shooting twin jets into the surrounding gas and dust. The shocks from the collision light up patches of nebulosity collectively called Herbig-Haro 24.

Name: Ultra-Bright Galaxies J114329.52
Description: A jumble of misshapen-looking galaxies is punctuated by arcs, streaks, and smeared rings. These unusual features are the stretched shapes of the universe's brightest infrared galaxies, magnified and distorted by natural cosmic lenses.

Name: Dense Core CB 130-3
Description: CB 130-3 is an object known as a dense core, a compact agglomeration of gas and dust. Dense cores like this are the birthplaces of stars. A compact object teetering on the brink of becoming a star is embedded deep within CB 130-3.

Name: R Aquarii
Description: The binary star system called R Aquarii undergoes violent eruptions that blast out huge filaments of glowing gas, weaving a spiral pattern among the stars.

Name: Spiral Galaxy IC 4709
Description: Spiral galaxy IC 4709, located around 240 million light-years away, has a faint halo and swirling disk filled with stars and dust bands. The compact region at its core holds an active galactic nucleus.

Name: Galaxy Cluster 0024+1654
Description: The light from a distant galaxy, nearly 10 billion light-years away, was magnified into blue arcs and streaks by the gravity of galaxy cluster 0024+1654. The cluster's gravity acts as a lens, bending and amplifying light from the background galaxy.

Name: Globular Cluster Messier 79
Description: The globular star cluster M79 contains about 150,000 stars packed into an area measuring only 118 light-years across. Its stars are some of the oldest in our galaxy.

Name: White Dwarf Stein 2051 B
Description: The white dwarf star Stein 2051 B and the smaller star below it appear to be close neighbors, but actually reside far away from each other. Stein 2051 B is 17 light-years from Earth; the other star is about 5,000 light-years away.

Description: In a nearby galaxy called the Small Magellanic Cloud, a massive star exploded as a supernova and dissipated its interior into a spectacular display of colorful filaments. The supernova remnant, known as E0102, is the greenish-blue field of debris just below center.

Name: Interacting Galaxy Markarian 231
Description: A bright, starlike glow emanates from the center of interacting galaxy Markarian 231, the nearest quasar at 581 million light-years away. Quasars are powered by a central black hole that heats the gas around it to unleash tremendous energy.

Name: Supernova Remnant 0454-67.2
Description: This dark, tangled web is an object named SNR 0454-67.2. It formed in a very violent fashion — it is a supernova remnant, created after a massive star ended its life in a cataclysmic explosion and threw its constituent material out into surrounding space.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 6951
Description: The intermediate spiral galaxy NGC 6951 intrigues scientists with its stellar history. It had its highest rates of star formation about 800 million years ago, then sat quietly for 300 million years before beginning to birth stars again.

Name: Emission Nebula N44
Description: N44 is a complex nebula filled with glowing hydrogen gas, dark lanes of dust, and many stars of different ages. The dark, starry gap, about 250 light-years wide, is called a “superbubble.” Its presence is something of a mystery.

Name: Ring Nebula
Description: About a light-year across, the Ring Nebula is formed by a dying star floating in a blue haze of hot gas at its center. This image reveals elongated, dark clumps of material embedded in the gas at the edge of the nebula.

Name: Interacting Galaxy NGC 7714
Description: The disrupted galaxy NGC 7714 displays a striking smoke-ring-like structure. The golden loop is made of Sun-like stars that have been pulled deep into space by the gravity of a nearby galaxy that lies just out of view.

Name: Supernova Remnant E0102
Description: In a nearby galaxy called the Small Magellanic Cloud, a massive star exploded as a supernova and dissipated its interior into a spectacular display of colorful filaments. The supernova remnant, known as E0102, is the greenish-blue field of debris just below center.

Name: Cartwheel Galaxy
Description: The Cartwheel galaxy's unusual appearance was created by a nearly head-on collision with a smaller galaxy. Its spoke-like structures are wisps of material connecting the galaxy's nucleus to an outer ring of young stars.

Name: Spiral Galaxy Messier 74
Description: M74, also called NGC 628, is a stunning example of a "grand-design" spiral galaxy that is viewed from Earth nearly face-on. Its perfectly symmetrical spiral arms emanate from the central nucleus and are dotted with clusters of young stars.

Name: Hubble Ultra Deep Field
Description: This view of nearly 10,000 galaxies is the deepest visible-light image of the cosmos. Called the Hubble Ultra Deep Field, this galaxy-studded view represents a "deep" core sample of the universe, cutting across billions of light-years.

Name: Lenticular Galaxy NGC 1266
Description: This enigmatic post-starburst galaxy has a bright center and a face that hints at spiral structure, yet it holds no discernable spiral arms.

Name: Galaxy Cluster MACS 0329-0211
Description: The gravity of this massive galaxy cluster acts as a lens, magnifying and distorting the light from a distant galaxy into an arc curving above a giant elliptical galaxy (upper right).

Name: Galaxy Cluster CLG-0016+16
Description: Several massive elliptical galaxies appear to sit in a line at the center of this enormous galaxy cluster. Numerous spiral, lenticular, and smaller elliptical galaxies dot the space surrounding the giant ellipticals.

Name: Reflection Nebula N30B
Description: A unique, peanut-shaped cocoon of dust surrounds a cluster of young, hot stars in this image. This reflection nebula, named N30B, is embedded in a much larger nebula called DEM L 106. The wispy filaments of DEM L 106 fill much of the image.

Name: Planetary Nebula NGC 3918
Description: NGC 3918, also known as "The Southerner," shows a roughly spherical outer envelope, but an elongated inner balloon inflated by a fast wind from its hot central star, which is starting to break out of its spherical envelope.

Name: Galaxy Cluster Abell 68
Description: The immense gravity of massive galaxy cluster Abell 68, creates a natural lens in space, distorting, brightening, and magnifying the light coming from very distant background galaxies.

Name: Jellyfish Galaxy JW100
Description: The streams of star-forming gas dripping from the disk of the galaxy JW100 resemble dangling tentacles, leading astronomers to refer to it as a ‘jellyfish’ galaxy.

Name: R Aquarii
Description: The binary star system called R Aquarii undergoes violent eruptions that blast out huge filaments of glowing gas, weaving a spiral pattern among the stars.

Description: A barred spiral like NGC 7541 is a galaxy with whirling, pinwheeling arms, and a bright center that is intersected by a bar of gas and stars. NGC 7541 also has a higher-than-usual star formation rate.

Description: This massive, young stellar grouping, called R136, is only a few million years old and resides in the 30 Doradus Nebula, a turbulent star-birth region in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a satellite galaxy of our Milky Way.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 2442
Description: The spectacular galaxy NGC 2442 is nicknamed the Meathook Galaxy, owing to its extremely asymmetrical and irregular shape. This galaxy was host to a supernova explosion, known as SN 2015F, that was created by a white dwarf star.

Name: Hubble Ultra Deep Field
Description: This view of nearly 10,000 galaxies is the deepest visible-light image of the cosmos. Called the Hubble Ultra Deep Field, this galaxy-studded view represents a "deep" core sample of the universe, cutting across billions of light-years.

Name: Irregular Galaxy I Zwicky 18
Description: This galaxy's youthful appearance resembles galaxies typically found in the early universe. However, Hubble found faint, older stars within it, suggesting that the galaxy may have formed at the same time as most other galaxies.

Name: Stars in the Galactic Core
Description: These colorful stars reside at the heart of our Milky Way galaxy, about 26,000 light-years from Earth. Aging red giant stars coexist with their more plentiful younger cousins, the smaller, white, Sun-like stars, in this crowded region of our galaxy's central hub.

Name: Dwarf Galaxy NGC 1569
Description: The nearby dwarf galaxy NGC 1569 is a hotbed of vigorous star birth and is one of the closest "starburst" galaxies to us. The galaxy's "star factories" are manufacturing brilliant blue star clusters.

Name: Pencil Nebula
Description: Thousands of years ago, a star exploded and left behind these cosmic remnants, called NGC 2736 – or the "Pencil" Nebula for its appearance. It's located about 815 light-years away.

Name: Grand Design Spiral NGC 3631
Description: The “arms” of grand design spiral galaxies appear to wind around and into the galaxy’s nucleus, as in NGC 3631. Dark dust lanes and bright star-forming regions reside along the inner part of the spiral arms.

Name: Interacting Galaxies Arp-Madore 417-391
Description: The two galaxies that make up Arp-Madore 417-391 were distorted by gravity and twisted into a colossal ring, leaving their cores nestled side by side.

Name: Orion Nebula

Description: Extending from this active galaxy are bizarre, greenish knots of gas and dust glowing from the light of high-energy particles, blasted by powerful ultraviolet radiation from a supermassive black hole at the galaxy's center.

Name: Globular Cluster NGC 1850
Description: This 100 million-year-old globular cluster is a spherical collection of densely packed stars held together by gravity. Unlike most globular clusters, however, the stars of NGC 1850 are relatively young. Globular clusters with young stars such are not present in our own Milky Way galaxy.

Name: Ultra-Bright Galaxies J231356.64
Description: A jumble of misshapen-looking galaxies is punctuated by arcs, streaks, and smeared rings. These unusual features are the stretched shapes of the universe's brightest infrared galaxies, magnified and distorted by natural cosmic lenses.

Name: Interacting Galaxy NGC 520
Description: NGC 520 is the product of a collision between two disk galaxies that started 300 million years ago. It shows the middle stages of the merging process: the disks of the parent galaxies have merged together, but their centers haven't merged yet.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 1559
Description: This magnificent barred spiral galaxy is NGC 1559. This picture is composed of a whopping 10 different Hubble images, from ultraviolet through visible light and into the near-infrared spectrum.

Name: Galaxy Cluster El Gordo
Description: This galaxy cluster, cataloged as ACT-CL J0102-4915 and nicknamed "El Gordo" ("the fat one" in Spanish), contains several hundred galaxies swarming around under the collective gravitational pull. The total mass of the cluster is estimated to weigh as much as 3 million billion stars like our Sun.

Name: Galaxy NGC 7714
Description: The disrupted galaxy NGC 7714 displays a striking smoke-ring-like structure. The golden loop is made of Sun-like stars that have been pulled deep into space, far from the galaxy's center, by the gravity of a nearby galaxy that lies just out of view.

Name: Orion Nebula
Description: The Orion Nebula, a turbulent stellar nursery, is a perfect laboratory to study how stars are born because it is just 1,500 light-years away, a relatively short distance within our galaxy.

Name: Lenticular Galaxy NGC 612
Description: Lenticular galaxies like NGC 612 have a central bulge and disk much like spiral galaxies, but lack the characteristic arms. They typically have older star populations and little ongoing star formation.

Name: Star Cluster Messier 67
Description: M67 is a collection of over 500 stars that are loosely gravitationally bound, known as an open cluster. M67 is one of the oldest known open clusters at approximately four billion years of age ― about the same as our Sun.

Name: Stars in the Galactic Core
Description: These colorful stars reside at the heart of our Milky Way galaxy, about 26,000 light-years from Earth. Aging red giant stars coexist with their more plentiful younger cousins, the smaller, white, Sun-like stars, in this crowded region of our galaxy's central hub.

Name: 30 Doradus Nebula
Description: This massive, young stellar grouping, called R136, is only a few million years old and resides in the 30 Doradus Nebula, a turbulent star-birth region in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a satellite galaxy of our Milky Way.

Name: Fomalhaut and Fomalhaut b
Description: This image shows the debris disk around the star Fomalhaut. These disks often give rise to planets. Fomalhaut b, originally thought to be a planet when observed in 2015, was later discovered to be a rarely-seen collision between icy objects in the disk.

Name: Colliding Galaxies NGC 1410 and 1409
Description: An intergalactic "pipeline" of material flows between two battered galaxies, NGC 1410 (left) and NGC 1409 (right), that bumped into each other about 100 million years ago.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 3430
Description: The spiral galaxy NGC 3430 lies 100 million light-years from Earth. This fine example of a galactic spiral holds a bright core from which a pinwheel array of arms appears to radiate outward. Dark dust lanes and bright star-forming regions help define these spiral arms.

Name: Star Clusters in the Tarantula Nebula
Description: The Tarantula Nebula is an enormous star-forming region located 170,000 light-years from Earth. The collection of stars in the core of the nebula, shown here, is made up of two individual star clusters that differ in age by about a million years.

Name: Lenticular Galaxy NGC 5283

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 3021

Name: The Squid Galaxy
Description: This majestic spiral galaxy has an intensely active core. Its nickname, the Squid Galaxy, comes from the extended, filamentary structure that curls around the galaxy’s disk like the tentacles of a squid.

Name: Interacting Galaxies Arp 147
Description: Arp 147 consists of a pair of interacting galaxies. The left-most galaxy in this image appears nearly edge-on to our line of sight and features a smooth ring of starlight. The right-most galaxy exhibits a clumpy, blue ring of intense star formation.

Name: Star Clusters in the Tarantula Nebula
Description: The Tarantula Nebula is an enormous star-forming region located 170,000 light-years from Earth. The collection of stars in the core of the nebula, shown here, is made up of two individual star clusters that differ in age by about a million years.

Name: Flame Nebula
Description: The Flame Nebula, also called NGC 2024, is a large star-forming region. This image focuses on the dark, dusty heart of the nebula where a star cluster resides, mostly hidden from view.

Name: Galaxy Field DSF2237b
Description: Contained in this galaxy field, known as DSF2237b, are star-forming galaxies up to 11 billion light-years away. Nearly every dot of light in this image is a galaxy (with the exception of the objects with "crosshairs", which are stars in our own Milky Way "photobombing" this image).

Name: Mars

Name: Globular Cluster 47 Tucanae
Description: This image shows the core of the globular star cluster 47 Tucanae. The entire cluster contains about a million stars, with many packed tightly in the core.

Description: This red bubble is made of gas that is being shocked by the expanding blast wave from a supernova explosion. Called SNR 0509-67.5, the bubble is 23 light-years across and is expanding at more than 11 million miles (18 million km) per hour.

Name: Asteroid P/2013 R3
Description: This image shows an asteroid called P/2013 R3 as it was breaking apart. The asteroid's fragments were slowly drifting away from each other and had tails of dust pushed back by the pressure of sunlight.

Name: Galaxy Cluster Abell 370

Name: 30 Doradus Nebula
Description: Glowing hydrogen clouds and dark filamentary dust structures are visible in this close-up view of a star-birth region called the 30 Doradus Nebula. The giant stellar factory lies 170,000 light-years away inside the Large Magellanic Cloud.

Name: Star Cluster NGC 290
Description: This image features a cluster of stars called NGC 290. The star cluster resides in the Small Magellanic Cloud, one of the small galaxies orbiting our Milky Way galaxy.

Name: Dwarf Galaxy Pisces A
Description: This image captures the glow of new stars in the small, ancient dwarf galaxy Pisces A, which contains about 10 million stars. Astronomers estimate that less than 100 million years ago, Pisces A doubled its star-formation rate.

Name: Elliptical Galaxy NGC 4150
Description: This image captures the ancient elliptical galaxy NGC 4150, located about 44 million light-years away. It shows streamers of dust and gas wrapped around the galaxy's core. Closer views of the core reveal clumps of young, blue stars less than a billion years old.

Name: Interacting Galaxy NGC 6670
Description: NGC 6670 is a gorgeous pair of interacting, overlapping, edge-on galaxies resembling a leaping dolphin.

Name: Galaxy Cluster Abell 2744
Description: Abell 2744 contains several hundred galaxies and might be a pile-up of at least four smaller galaxy clusters. Abell 2744's strong gravitational field acts as a lens, distorting and magnifying the light of nearly 3,000 distant background galaxies.

Name: Nebula NGC 281
Description: The dark knots of gas and dust in this image are called "Bok globules," and they are absorbing light in the center of the nearby nebula and star-forming region called NGC 281.

Name: Interacting Galaxy 2MASX J09133888-1019196
Description: These two interacting galaxies are disturbed by gravitational interaction. Their wide separation ― approximately 130,000 light-years ― suggests that the galaxies are just beginning to merge.

Name: SN2013ge in Galaxy NGC 3287
Description: Images of the spiral galaxy NGC 3287 show Supernova 2013ge fading over time, revealing the steady source of ultraviolet light astronomers have identified as its binary companion star.

Name: Orion Nebula
Description: The Orion Nebula is the nearest star-forming region to Earth. Massive, young stars are shaping the nebula with their winds and radiation. Pillars of dense gas may be the homes of budding stars. The bright central region is the home of the four heftiest stars in the nebula.

Name: Herbig-Haro Object HH111
Description: A pair of 12 light-year-long jets of gas are blasted into space from a young system of three stars. The jet is seen in visible light, and its dusty disk and stars are seen in infrared light.

Description: The little-known nebula IRAS 05437+2502 billows out among the bright stars and dark dust clouds that surround it. Unlike many astronomical targets, this object has not been studied in detail and its exact nature is unclear.

Name: Hubble Ultra Deep Field
Description: This image of the Hubble Ultra Deep Field includes infrared observations that allowed Hubble to peer deeper into the universe than it ever had before. The faintest and reddest objects in the image are galaxies that formed 600 million years after the big bang.

Name: Interacting Galaxy IRAS 21101
Description: The gravitational interaction between these two galaxies is disturbing their shapes. The lower galaxy has a bizarre structure and a tidal tail emerges from the main body of the upper galaxy. The several bright stars in this image are within our own galaxy.

Name: Reflection Nebula Messier 78
Description: This colorful image was taken in infrared light and features a small part of M78, a reflection nebula created when light from a star is scattered or reflected off a nearby dust cloud.

Name: Irregular Galaxy NGC 7250
Description: The irregular galaxy NGC 7250 is home to bright bursts of star formation and recorded supernova explosions. It shares this image with the bright star TYC 3203-450-1, which appears so much brighter because it is around 7,500 times closer to us than NGC 7250.

Description: Einstein rings like this form when two galaxies are almost perfectly aligned, one behind the other, and the gravitational field of the closer galaxy bends and magnifies the light from the more distant galaxy into bright arcs around itself.

Name: Supernova Refsdal
Description: This massive cluster of galaxies is MACS J1149.6+2223. In this image, light from a distant supernova appears in four different places. The multiple supernova images are created as the exploding star's light is bent and magnified by the powerful gravity of a large galaxy in the cluster.

Name: Globular Cluster 47 Tucanae
Description: This image shows the core of the globular star cluster 47 Tucanae. The entire cluster contains about a million stars, with many packed tightly in the core.

Description: The Helix Nebula's intricate form was created by a torrential gush of gases escaping from a dying star. This planetary nebula offers a dizzying look down what is actually a trillion-mile-long tunnel of glowing gases.

Name: Jellyfish Galaxy JO204

Name: Dwarf Planet 2007 OR10
Description: This image reveals a moon orbiting the dwarf planet 2007 OR10, the third-largest known dwarf planet behind Pluto and Eris. It's located in the Kuiper Belt, a realm of icy debris left over from the solar system's formation.

Name: Dwarf Galaxy Henize 2-10
Description: The dwarf starburst galaxy Henize 2-10 sparkles in this view. The bright region at the center, surrounded by pink clouds and dark dust lanes, is the location of the galaxy's massive black hole and active stellar nurseries.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 1275
Description: A dusty spiral galaxy appears to be rotating on-edge as it slides through the larger and brighter galaxy, NGC 1275. These galaxies are believed to be colliding at a speed of 6 million miles (9.6 million km) per hour!

Name: Galaxy Cluster IDCS J1426.5+3508
Description: The light we observe from this rare, extremely massive young galaxy cluster, IDCS 1426, left the cluster when the universe was less than a third of its current age.

Name: Beehive Cluster
Description: Messier 44, or the "Beehive Cluster," swarms with activity as its name would suggest. This open cluster of around 1,000 stars, loosely connected by gravity, is one of the closest such clusters to Earth.

Name: Interacting Galaxy AM 1054-325
Description: Galaxy AM 1054-325 has been distorted into an S-shape from a normal pancake-like spiral shape by the gravitational pull of a neighboring galaxy. This string-of-pearls star formation may have been more common in the early universe.

Name: Star Cluster NGC 265
Description: This image displays a cluster of stars called NGC 265. The cluster resides in the Small Magellanic Cloud, one of the small galaxies orbiting our Milky Way galaxy.

Name: Active Galaxy SDSS 2201+11

Name: Interacting Galaxy NGC 34
Description: NGC 34 looks more like an otherworldly creature from the deep oceans than a galaxy. This image shows the galaxy's bright center, a result of a merging event between two spiral galaxies that has created a burst of new star formation.

Name: Elliptical Galaxy NGC 1600
Description: The huge elliptical galaxy NGC 1600 is located 209 million light-years from Earth. The black hole that lurks at the center of the galaxy is one of the most massive black holes ever detected and 10 times more massive than expected for a galaxy of its size.

Name: Bow Tie Nebula
Description: This hazy image captures a portion of the planetary nebula Caldwell 2, or NGC 40. A shell of gas is expanding outward from the nebula’s central star, which has reached the final stage of its life.

Name: Irregular Galaxy NGC 7292
Description: This galaxy, NGC 7292, is irregular, meaning that it lacks the distinct spiral arms or elliptical shape of some galaxies. Unusually, its core is stretched out into a distinct bar, a feature seen in many spiral galaxies, and this galaxy is also remarkably faint.

Name: Interacting Galaxies NGC 2207 and IC 2163
Description: This image shows two interacting galaxies. The larger and more massive galaxy on the left is NGC 2207, and the smaller one on the right is IC 2163. Strong tidal forces from NGC 2207 have distorted the shape of IC 2163.

Name: Elliptical Galaxy NGC 4589
Description: This image shows an elliptical galaxy with dark, wispy dust lanes, the signature of a recent galaxy merger. The dust is the only relic of a smaller galaxy that was consumed by the larger elliptical galaxy.

Name: Globular Cluster Caldwell 73
Description: C73, or NGC 1851, may be a remnant of two star clusters that collided within a dwarf galaxy that once hosted them both. Unlike many globular clusters, C73 hosts stellar populations with different ages.

Name: Herbig-Haro Object HH111
Description: A pair of 12 light-year-long jets of gas are blasted into space from a young system of three stars. The jet is seen in visible light, and its dusty disk and stars are seen in infrared light.

Name: Pegasus Dwarf Galaxy
Description: The Pegasus Dwarf spheroidal galaxy is a mini-galaxy in orbit around the Milky Way's neighbor, the Andromeda Galaxy. Dwarf spheroidal galaxies are the dimmest and least massive galaxies known.

Name: Galaxy Pair NGC 6090
Description: NGC 6090 is a pair of spiral galaxies with overlapping central regions and two long tidal tails made of material ripped out of the galaxies by gravitational interactions. The two visible cores are approximately 10,000 light-years apart.

Description: These wispy clouds of glowing gas make up a nebula known as N44C. It is part of the larger N44 complex, which includes young, hot, massive stars, other nebulae, and a "superbubble" blown out by multiple supernova explosions.

Name: Irregular Galaxy I Zwicky 18

Name: Galaxy Cluster Abell 2744
Description: Abell 2744 contains several hundred galaxies and might be a pile-up of at least four smaller galaxy clusters. Abell 2744's strong gravitational field acts as a lens, distorting and magnifying the light of nearly 3,000 distant background galaxies.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 3717
Description: The spiral galaxy NGC 3717 is not captured perfectly edge-on in this image; the nearer part of the galaxy is tilted ever so slightly down, and the far side tilted up. This angle offers a view across the disk and the central bulge (of which only one side is visible).

Name: Reflection Nebula N30B
Description: A unique, peanut-shaped cocoon of dust surrounds a cluster of young, hot stars in this image. This reflection nebula, named N30B, is embedded in a much larger nebula called DEM L 106. The wispy filaments of DEM L 106 fill much of the image.

Name: Galaxy Cluster Abell 68
Description: The immense gravity of massive galaxy cluster Abell 68, creates a natural lens in space, distorting, brightening and magnifying the light coming from very distant background galaxies.

Name: HH 45 in Running Man Nebula
Description: Herbig-Haro objects like HH 45 are rarely seen nebulae that occur when hot gas ejected by a newborn star collides with the gas and dust around it, creating bright shock waves.

Name: Globular Cluster 47 Tucanae
Description: This image of the heart of the giant globular star cluster 47 Tucanae reveals the glow of 200,000 stars. Young white dwarfs ― the burned-out relics of stars that have used up their nuclear fuel, cooled down, and lost most of their mass ― are beginning to migrate outward.

Name: Jellyfish Galaxy JO201
Description: As jellyfish galaxies like JO201 move through space, gas is slowly stripped away, forming trails illuminated by clumps of star formation. These blue tendrils are visible below the core of this galaxy, giving it a jellyfish-like appearance.

Name: Planetary Nebula NGC 2371
Description: This image captures the planetary nebula NGC 2371, the glowing remains of a Sun-like star. The remnant star visible at the center of NGC 2371 is the super-hot core of the former red giant, now stripped of its outer layers.

Name: Asteroid P/2013 R3
Description: This image shows an asteroid called P/2013 R3 as it was breaking apart. The asteroid's fragments were slowly drifting away from each other and had tails of dust pushed back by the pressure of sunlight.

Description: The eXtreme Deep Field, or XDF, was assembled by combining 10 years of photographs taken of a patch of sky at the center of the original Hubble Ultra Deep Field.

Name: Interacting Galaxy Markarian 273
Description: Mrk 273 is a galaxy with a bizarre structure that somewhat resembles a toothbrush. It has an intense region of starburst, where 60 solar masses of new stars are born each year.

Name: Interacting Galaxy NGC 5256
Description: NGC 5256, also known as Markarian 266, is an example of two disk galaxies that are about to merge. Each galaxy contains an active galactic nucleus, evidence that the chaos is allowing gas to fall into the regions around central black holes.

Name: Minkowski’s Object
Description: This striking pair is an elliptical galaxy NGC 541 and an unusual star-forming, irregular dwarf galaxy known as Minkowski’s Object (the bluish object to the lower left of NGC 541). A radio jet from NGC 541 likely caused the star-formation in Minkowski’s Object.

Name: V838 Monocerotis Light Echo
Description: This image captures a light echo from the star V838 Monocerotis. After the star brightened temporarily, light from that eruption began propagating outward through a dusty cloud around the star. The light reflects or "echoes" off the dust and then travels to Earth.

Name: Saturn and its Moons
Description: This image captures the moons Mimas, Enceladus, and Dione as they begin their race across Saturn's disk. The planet's rings are tilted nearly edge-on toward the Sun, an event that occurs once every 15 years.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 2525
Description: Located about 70 million light-years away, this spiral galaxy is known as NGC 2525. The bright blue-white burst of light at the left of the galaxy shows a star's explosive death in a supernova.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 3521
Description: The spiral galaxy NGC 3521 has a soft, woolly appearance. This galaxy belongs to a class known as flocculent spirals, in which fluffy patches of stars and dust are scattered throughout the disk.

Name: Dwarf Galaxy NGC 4449
Description: Hundreds of thousands of vibrant blue and red stars blaze in this dwarf galaxy located some 12.5 million light-years away.

Name: Galaxy Cluster Cl 0024+17
Description: In this image of the galaxy cluster Cl 0024+17, blue streaks are images of very distant galaxies that are behind the cluster. The distant galaxies appear distorted because their light is bent and magnified by the cluster's gravity.

Name: Planetary Nebula NGC 2440
Description: NGC 2440 is a planetary nebula with a chaotic structure, created when a dying star ejected its outer layers. Its central star is one of the hottest known, with a surface temperature around 360,000 degrees Fahrenheit (200,000 degrees Celsius).

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 3021
Description: Spiral galaxy NGC 3021 is home to Cepheid variable stars. These stars pulsate at a rate that is closely related to their intrinsic brightness. Astronomers use this information to calculate a galaxy’s distance.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 2217
Description: The magnificent central bar of NGC 2217 (also known as Arp-Madore 0619-271) shines bright in this barred spiral galaxy, which is a similar size to our own Milky Way.

Name: Elliptical Galaxy Messier 87
Description: This image of the giant galaxy M87 shows a 3,000-light-year-long jet of plasma blasting from the galaxy's 6.5-billion-solar-mass central black hole. The jet seems to cause stars to erupt along its trajectory.

Name: Dumbbell Nebula
Description: This image captures a small part of the Dumbbell Nebula, which resides more than 1,200 light-years away. Known as a planetary nebula, it is the result of an old star that has shed its outer layers in a glowing display of color. It was the first planetary nebula ever discovered.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 3021

Name: Helix Nebula
Description: The Helix Nebula's intricate form was created by a torrential gush of gases escaping from a dying star. This planetary nebula offers a dizzying look down what is actually a trillion-mile-long tunnel of glowing gases.

Name: Interacting Galaxy IC 2810
Description: IC 2810 is a disk galaxy viewed nearly edge-on. It is slightly disturbed by gravitational interaction with a smaller, dusty companion (located below it). The larger galaxy shows blue knots of star formation.

Name: Galaxy Cluster Abell 2744
Description: Abell 2744 contains several hundred galaxies and might be a pile-up of at least four smaller galaxy clusters. Abell 2744's strong gravitational field acts as a lens, distorting and magnifying the light of nearly 3,000 distant background galaxies.

Name: Interacting Galaxies Arp 148
Description: Arp 148 is the aftermath of an encounter between two galaxies, resulting in a ring-shaped galaxy and an elongated companion. The shapes and arrangement of the galaxies suggest that this is a snapshot of an ongoing collision.

Name: Galaxy Cluster RXC J0949.8+1707
Description: The numerous fuzzy blobs and glowing shapes scattered across this image make up a galaxy cluster named RXC J0949.8+1707. Located to the upper right of the frame sits an especially beautiful and interesting barred spiral galaxy, seen face-on.

Name: Supernova Refsdal
Description: This massive cluster of galaxies is MACS J1149.6+2223. In this image, light from a distant supernova appears in four different places. The multiple supernova images are created as the exploding star's light is bent and magnified by the powerful gravity of a large galaxy in the cluster.

Name: Spiral Galaxy Messier 74
Description: Messier 74, also called NGC 628, is a stunning example of a "grand-design" spiral galaxy that is viewed from Earth nearly face-on. Its perfectly symmetrical spiral arms emanate from the central nucleus and are dotted with clusters of young stars.

Name: Hubble Ultra Deep Field

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 3147

Name: Star Cluster Westerlund 2
Description: This image captures a giant cluster of about 3,000 stars called Westerlund 2. The cluster resides inside a vibrant stellar breeding ground known as Gum 29, located 20,000 light-years away in the constellation Carina.

Name: Cleopatra's Eye
Description: Cleopatra’s Eye, or NGC 1535, is a planetary nebula with a dimmer outer region surrounding a brighter inner center. The dying star exhaled its outer layers into space as the core turned into a white dwarf star.

Name: Dwarf Galaxy Andromeda III
Description: Andromeda III is a faint, spheroidal collection of old, reddish stars, one of at least 13 dwarf satellite galaxies in orbit around the Andromeda galaxy.

Name: Ultra-Bright Galaxies J022633.98
Description: A jumble of misshapen-looking galaxies is punctuated by arcs, streaks, and smeared rings. These unusual features are the stretched shapes of the universe's brightest infrared galaxies, magnified and distorted by natural cosmic lenses.

Name: Emission Nebula NGC 261
Description: The ionized gas blazing from within this diffuse region marks NGC 261 as an emission nebula. It is home to numerous stars hot enough to irradiate surrounding hydrogen gas, causing the cloud to emit a pinkish-red glow.

Name: Hickson Compact Group 40

Name: Aurora at Jupiter's North Pole
Description: A curtain of glowing gas, called an aurora, wraps around Jupiter's north pole like a lasso. Aurorae are produced when high-energy electrons race along the planet's magnetic field and excite atmospheric gases, causing them to glow.

Name: Planetary Nebula NGC 2818
Description: The spectacular structure of the planetary nebula NGC 2818 contains the outer layers of a dying star that were expelled into interstellar space. Our own Sun will undergo a similar process, but not for another 5 billion years or so.
