Description: Chains of star formation appear in a galaxy in ultraviolet light. Brilliant knots of hot, blue stars like these form along the jets of active black holes found in the centers of giant elliptical galaxies.

Description: While it looks like the spiral galaxy NGC 105 is plunging edge-on into a neighboring galaxy, this is just a circumstance of perspective. NGC 105’s elongated neighbor is actually far more distant.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 976
Description: Despite its tranquil appearance, the spiral galaxy NGC 976 has played host to one of the most violent astronomical phenomena known: a supernova explosion. These violent events take place at the end of the lives of massive stars and can outshine entire galaxies for a short period.

Name: Star Cluster Westerlund 2

Name: Comet 3/I ATLAS
Description: After the interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS was first discovered and observed in July of 2025, it was later observed once again as it moved through our solar system. This image was taken by Hubble when the comet was 178 million miles (286 million kilometers) from Earth.

Name: Interacting Galaxy NGC 3447
Description: This pair of interacting galaxies is called NGC 3447. The two are strongly distorted by the gravitational forces between them, twisting them into the unusual shapes seen here. Astronomers are unsure what each looked like before they began to tear one another apart.

Name: Galaxy Cluster MACS J0416.1-2403
Description: Amid the bright light of its member galaxies, the galaxy cluster MACS J0416.1-2403 also emits a soft glow of "intracluster light," produced by stars that are not part of any individual galaxy.

Name: Mars
Description: Hubble captured this image of Mars soon before the planet made its closest approach to Earth in 2007. White clouds cover the north polar region. The long, dark feature to the lower left of center is the canyon system Valles Marineris.

Name: Interacting Galaxies Arp 86
Description: Arp 86 is a peculiar pair of interacting galaxies, composed of NGC 7753, the large spiral galaxy, and NGC 7752, its smaller companion. The gravitational dance between the two will eventually result in NGC 7752 being tossed out into intergalactic space or entirely engulfed by its larger neighbor.

Name: Irregular Galaxy NGC 7250
Description: The irregular galaxy NGC 7250 is home to bright bursts of star formation and recorded supernova explosions. It shares this image with the bright star TYC 3203-450-1, which appears so much brighter because it is around 7,500 times closer to us than NGC 7250.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 4455
Description: This smattering of celestial sequins is a spiral galaxy named NGC 4455, though it doesn't resemble the more-common "grand design" spiral shape at first glance. The galaxy is about 45 million light-years away.

Name: Supernova Wilson in CANDELS Survey
Description: In this image of the Cosmic Assembly Near-infrared Deep Extragalactic Legacy Survey (CANDELS), astronomers found a supernova called SN UDS10Wil, nicknamed SN Wilson. It exploded over 10 billion years ago.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 4237
Description: NGC 4237 is classified as a flocculent spiral galaxy. This means that its spiral arms are not clearly distinguishable from each other, but are instead patchy and discontinuous. This gives the galaxy a tuft-like appearance, somewhat resembling fluffy cotton.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 1068
Description: Hydrogen clouds at the center of barred spiral galaxy NGC 1068 are glowing because they are caught in a "searchlight" of radiation beamed out of the galaxy's black hole, which is larger and more active than the black hole in the heart of our galaxy.

Name: Nebula and Star Cluster NGC 3603
Description: In NGC 3603, a glittering cluster of stars is surrounded by clouds of gas and dust. The cluster contains some of the most massive stars known. These huge stars live fast and die young, ultimately ending their lives in supernova explosions.

Name: Spiral Galaxy Messier 106
Description: A striking feature of M106 is its extra pair of arms. Most spiral galaxies only have one pair of arms, but M106 has an extra set, seen here as red wisps of gas. Unlike the other arms, these two extra arms are made up of hot gas rather than stars.

Name: LRLL 54361 Light Echo
Description: A pulse of light emanates from the protostellar object LRLL 54361, a mysterious infant star that behaves like a police strobe light. The extent and shape of the scattered light changes substantially over a 25.34-day period.

Name: Irregular Galaxy I Zwicky 18
Description: This galaxy's youthful appearance resembles galaxies typically found in the early universe. However, Hubble found faint, older stars within it, suggesting that the galaxy may have formed at the same time as most other galaxies.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 4380
Description: The galaxy NGC 4380 looks straight out of a science fiction film, swirling like a gaping portal to another dimension. In the grand scheme of things, though, it is actually quite ordinary. Spiral galaxies like NGC 4380 are common in the universe.

Name: Andromeda Galaxy Halo
Description: This image captures the light from 300,000 stars (and a star cluster) in the Andromeda galaxy's halo, a vast spherical cloud of stars surrounding the galaxy's bright disk. Also embedded in the image are many background galaxies that are much farther away.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 3021
Description: Spiral galaxy NGC 3021 is home to Cepheid variable stars. These stars pulsate at a rate that is closely related to their intrinsic brightness. Astronomers use this information to calculate a galaxy’s distance.

Name: The Grasshopper Galaxies

Name: Supernova Remnant Cassiopeia A
Description: The tattered remains of a supernova explosion known as Cassiopeia A is located in the Milky Way some 10,000 light-years away from Earth.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 4535
Description: The galaxy NGC 4535’s young star clusters dot its spiral arms. Glowing-pink clouds surround many of these bright-blue star groupings. These clouds are a sign that the galaxy is home to especially young, hot, and massive stars.

Name: Spiral Galaxy Messier 81

Name: Dwarf Galaxy UGCA 307
Description: Appearing as just a small patch of stars, UGCA 307 is a diminutive dwarf galaxy without a defined structure, resembling nothing more than a hazy patch of passing cloud.

Name: Jellyfish Galaxy JW100
Description: The streams of star-forming gas dripping from the disk of the galaxy JW100 bear a resemblance to dangling tentacles, leading astronomers to refer to it as a ‘jellyfish’ galaxy.

Name: Supernova 1987A
Description: This image shows the remnant of Supernova 1987A, a stellar explosion in a nearby galaxy that astronomers witnessed in 1987. A shock wave of material unleashed by the stellar blast is slamming into a surrounding ring of gas, causing it to glow.

Name: Intermediate Spiral Galaxy NGC 4654
Description: Intermediate spiral galaxy NGC 4654 interacted gravitationally with a companion galaxy about 500 million years ago that stripped gas along its edge, limiting star formation in that region and causing the asymmetrical distribution of the galaxy’s stars.

Name: Heart of Messier 82
Description: This image features the star-powered heart of the starburst galaxy M82, home to brilliant stars whose light is shaded by sculptural clouds made of clumps and streaks of dust and gas. The galaxy forms stars 10 times faster than our Milky Way Galaxy.

Description: The Flame Nebula or NGC 2024 is a large star-forming region in the constellation Orion that lies about 1,400 light-years from Earth.

Name: Blue Snowball Nebula
Description: Caldwell 22 (C22), nicknamed the Blue Snowball Nebula, is a planetary nebula located about 2,500 light-years from Earth. Nebulae like these represent a stage in evolution that stars like our Sun undergo when they run out of fuel.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 4571
Description: This cosmic portrait shows a stunning view of the majestic spiral galaxy NGC 4571, which lies approximately 60 million light-years from Earth. NGC 4571 is part of the Virgo cluster, which contains more than a thousand galaxies.

Name: Comet Wirtanen
Description: In this image, the nucleus of comet 46P/Wirtanen is hidden in the center of a fuzzy glow from the comet's coma. The coma is a cloud of gas and dust that the comet has ejected as it is heated by the Sun during its passage through the inner solar system.

Name: Asteroid P/2013 R3
Description: This image shows an asteroid called P/2013 R3 as it was breaking apart. The asteroid's fragments were slowly drifting away from each other and had tails of dust pushed back by the pressure of sunlight.

Name: Gravitational Lens SDSS J1004+4112
Description: The five star-like, blue-white points of light near the center of the image are the light from a single distant quasar, the bright core of a galaxy 10 billion light-years away. The quasar is magnified and replicated by the galaxy cluster 7 billion light-years distant.

Name: Star-Forming Nebula NGC 604
Description: This festively colorful nebula, called NGC 604, is one of the largest known regions of star birth in the nearby Messier 33, the Triangulum Galaxy. The bright stars in NGC 604 are extremely young, having formed a mere 3 million years ago.

Name: Merging Galaxies SDSSCGB 10189
Description: These three galaxies, together known as SDSSCGB 10189, are set on a collision course and will eventually merge into a single larger galaxy, distorting one another’s spiral structures through mutual gravitational interaction.

Name: Supernova Refsdal
Description: This massive cluster of galaxies is MACS J1149.6+2223. In this image, light from a distant supernova appears in four different places. The multiple supernova images are created as the exploding star's light is bent and magnified by the powerful gravity of a large galaxy in the cluster.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 4911
Description: Spiral galaxy NGC 4911 contains rich lanes of dust and gas near its center, silhouetted against glowing newborn star clusters and pink clouds of hydrogen. The galaxy's outer spiral arms are being distorted by forces from a companion galaxy, NGC 4911A (upper right).

Name: Andromeda Galaxy
Description: Over 100 million stars are on display in this portion of the Andromeda galaxy, located over 2 million light-years away. This portrait of our galactic neighbor uses 7,398 exposures taken over 411 individual pointings of the telescope.

Name: Star-Forming Nebula NGC 604

Name: Omega Centauri
Description: Omega Centauri consists of roughly 10 million stars that are gravitationally bound. The cluster is about 10 times as massive as other big globular clusters – almost as massive as a small galaxy.

Name: Spiral Galaxy Messier 81
Description: The arms of the "grand design" spiral galaxy M81 are filled with young, bluish, hot stars. The greenish regions in the image are bright, gaseous clouds where new stars are forming.

Name: LRLL 54361 Light Echo
Description: A pulse of light emanates from the protostellar object LRLL 54361, a mysterious infant star that behaves like a police strobe light. The extent and shape of the scattered light changes substantially over a 25.34-day period.

Name: Galaxy Cluster Abell 370
Description: The galaxy cluster Abell 370 contains several hundred galaxies tied together by the mutual pull of gravity. Entangled among the galaxies are arcs of blue light, actually magnified and distorted images of remote galaxies behind the cluster.

Name: 30 Doradus Nebula
Description: Glowing hydrogen clouds and dark filamentary dust structures are visible in this close-up infrared view of a star-birth region called the 30 Doradus Nebula. The giant stellar factory lies 170,000 light-years away inside the Large Magellanic Cloud.

Name: Hubble Ultra Deep Field
Description: This view of nearly 10,000 galaxies is the deepest visible-light image of the cosmos. Called the Hubble Ultra Deep Field, this galaxy-studded view represents a "deep" core sample of the universe, cutting across billions of light-years.

Name: Andromeda Galaxy Halo
Description: This image captures the light from 300,000 stars (and a star cluster) in the Andromeda galaxy's halo, a vast spherical cloud of stars surrounding the galaxy's bright disk. Also embedded in the image are many background galaxies that are much farther away.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 4911
Description: Spiral galaxy NGC 4911 contains rich lanes of dust and gas near its center, silhouetted against glowing newborn star clusters and pink clouds of hydrogen. The galaxy's outer spiral arms are being distorted by forces from a companion galaxy, NGC 4911A (upper right).

Name: Spiral Galaxy Caldwell 5
Description: This image of spiral galaxy IC 342, also known as C5, shows a sparkling, face-on view of the center of the galaxy. Intertwined tendrils of dust in spectacular arms wrap around a brilliant core of hot gas and stars.

Name: Globular Cluster Messier 15
Description: Nestled among the stars of M15 is an astronomical oddity. The pinkish object to the upper left of the cluster's core is a gas cloud surrounding a dying star. Known as Kuestner 648, this was the first planetary nebula found in a globular cluster.

Name: Vega's Circumstellar Disk
Description: The summer star Vega is encircled by a nearly 100-billion-mile-diameter disk of debris, known as a circumstellar disk, that's far more smooth than those we see in many other young star systems.

Name: Interacting Galaxies Arp 273
Description: Arp 273 is of a pair of interacting galaxies that form a shape resembling a rose. The larger of the spiral galaxies, known as UGC 1810, has a disk that is distorted by the gravitational pull of the galaxy below it, known as UGC 1813.

Name: Spiral Galaxy Messier 106
Description: A striking feature of M106 is its extra pair of arms. Most spiral galaxies only have one pair of arms, but M106 has an extra set, seen here as red wisps of gas. Unlike the other arms, these two extra arms are made up of hot gas rather than stars.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 3021
Description: Spiral galaxy NGC 3021 is home to Cepheid variable stars. These stars pulsate at a rate that is closely related to their intrinsic brightness. Astronomers use this information to calculate a galaxy’s distance.

Name: V838 Monocerotis Light Echo
Description: This image captures a light echo from the star V838 Monocerotis. After the star brightened temporarily, light from that eruption began propagating outward through a dusty cloud around the star. The light reflects or "echoes" off the dust and then travels to Earth.

Name: Star Cluster Hodge 301
Description: Hodge 301 (lower right corner) is the most active starburst region in the local universe. This cluster of massive stars is part of the Tarantula Nebula. Many of the stars have exploded as supernovae, unleashing material that plows into the nebula and creates the filaments and sheets to the left.

Name: Hubble Deep Field
Description: Called the Hubble Deep Field, this image captures several hundred galaxies that had never been seen before. Some galaxies are near and some are very far. Their various shapes and colors provide clues about the evolution of the universe.

Description: The dwarf galaxy NGC 4214 is ablaze with young stars and gas clouds. This image captures intricate patterns of glowing hydrogen shaped during the star-birthing process, cavities blown clear of gas by stellar winds, and bright stellar clusters.

Name: Andromeda Galaxy Tendril
Description: Swaths of ionized gas glow in a tendril of the Milky Way's neighboring galaxy, Andromeda. These regions, which are common in spiral and irregular galaxies, often indicate the presence of recent star formation.

Description: NGC 5331 is a pair of interacting galaxies. It glows very brightly in infrared light, with about 100 billion times the luminosity of the Sun.

Name: Interacting Galaxy VV 283
Description: VV 283 looks like a single peculiar galaxy, but is in fact a pair of merging galaxies. A tidal tail swirls out from a messy central region and splits into two branches. The upward twisting branch is brightened by luminous blue star knots.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 105
Description: While it looks like the spiral galaxy NGC 105 is plunging edge-on into a neighboring galaxy, this is just a circumstance of perspective. NGC 105’s elongated neighbor is actually far more distant.

Name: Elliptical Galaxy Messier 87
Description: This image of the giant galaxy M87 shows a 3,000-light-year-long jet of plasma blasting from the galaxy's 6.5-billion-solar-mass central black hole. The jet seems to cause stars to erupt along its trajectory.

Description: The eXtreme Deep Field, or XDF, was assembled by combining 10 years of photographs taken of a small patch of sky. About 5,500 galaxies appear in the XDF!

Description: This image of the heart of the giant globular star cluster 47 Tucanae reveals the glow of 200,000 stars. Young white dwarfs ― the burned-out relics of stars that have used up their nuclear fuel, cooled down, and lost most of their mass ― are beginning to migrate outward.

Name: Dwarf Galaxy Leo A
Description: This image features the nearby dwarf irregular galaxy Leo A. Astronomers study dwarf galaxies like Leo A because they are numerous and may offer clues to how galaxies grow and evolve.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 2976
Description: This picture shows the inner region of NGC 2976, located roughly 11 million light-years away in the constellation Ursa Major. Despite the lack of well-defined arms visible in this image, NGC 2976 is a spiral galaxy.

Name: Globular Cluster Caldwell 73
Description: C73, or NGC 1851, may be a remnant of two star clusters that collided within a dwarf galaxy that once hosted them both. Unlike many globular clusters, C73 hosts stellar populations with different ages.

Name: Galaxy Cluster Abell 370
Description: The galaxy cluster Abell 370 contains several hundred galaxies tied together by the mutual pull of gravity. Entangled among the galaxies are arcs of blue light, actually distorted and magnified images of remote galaxies behind the cluster.

Name: Rosette Nebula
Description: Hubble captured a small portion of the Rosette Nebula, which is a huge star-forming region spanning 100 light-years across and located 5,200 light-years away.

Name: Hubble Ultra Deep Field
Description: This view of nearly 10,000 galaxies is the deepest visible-light image of the cosmos. Called the Hubble Ultra Deep Field, this galaxy-studded view represents a "deep" core sample of the universe, cutting across billions of light-years.

Name: Irregular Galaxy I Zwicky 18
Description: This image captures the irregular dwarf galaxy I Zwicky 18 and a companion galaxy to its upper right. The two galaxies are interacting, triggering star formation in I Zwicky 18.

Name: Elliptical Galaxy NGC 4458
Description: The elliptical galaxy NGC 4458 is a member of the Virgo cluster, the nearest large galaxy cluster to Earth. Comprised of over 2,000 galaxies, the Virgo cluster is located about 54 million light-years away.

Name: Spiral Galaxy UGC 9391
Description: This spiral galaxy, UGC 9391, contains two types of stars that astronomers use to calculate accurate distances to galaxies and refine the measurement for how fast the universe expands with time, called the Hubble constant.

Name: Reflection Nebula NGC 1333
Description: This ethereal Hubble view shows NGC 1333, a nearby star-forming region. Glowing gases and pitch-black dust are stirred up and blown around by several hundred newly forming stars embedded within this dark cloud.

Name: Mars
Description: Mars was approximately 61 million miles (98 million km) from Earth when Hubble captured this image. Thin water-ice clouds that are apparent in ultraviolet light give the Red Planet a frosty appearance.

Name: Nebula and Star Cluster NGC 3603
Description: In NGC 3603, thousands of sparkling, young stars are nestled within a giant nebula. This stellar "jewel box" is one of the most massive young star clusters in our Milky Way galaxy.

Name: Spiral Galaxy Messier 74
Description: Messier 74, also called NGC 628, is a stunning example of a "grand-design" spiral galaxy that is viewed from Earth nearly face-on. Its perfectly symmetrical spiral arms emanate from the central nucleus and are dotted with clusters of young stars.

Name: Star Cluster Messier 35
Description: The young open cluster M35 is home to some 400 stars. M35 contains numerous hot blue stars, as well as some cooler and older orange and red giant stars.

Name: Reflection Nebula NGC 1333
Description: This ethereal Hubble view shows NGC 1333, a nearby star-forming region. Glowing gases and pitch-black dust are stirred up and blown around by several hundred newly forming stars embedded within this dark cloud.

Name: Triangulum Galaxy
Description: This mosaic captures the nearby Triangulum galaxy. Striking areas of star birth glow bright blue throughout the galaxy.

Name: Stephan's Quintet
Description: This close-up shows four of the five galaxies that make up Stephan's Quintet. The image reveals bright, blue clusters of stars, born from the violent interactions between some of the member galaxies.

Name: Galaxy Pair Arp 40
Description: Arp 40 is a curious pair of spiral galaxies some 800 million light-years away. The smaller galaxy is superimposed on the larger one, which is a type of active galaxy called a Seyfert galaxy.

Name: Reflection Nebula NGC 1333
Description: This ethereal Hubble view shows NGC 1333, a nearby star-forming region. Glowing gases and pitch-black dust are stirred up and blown around by several hundred newly forming stars embedded within this dark cloud.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 3568
Description: This image captures a side-on view of NGC 3568, a barred spiral galaxy. In 2014, the light from a supernova explosion in NGC 3568 reached Earth – a sudden flare of light caused by the titanic explosion accompanying the death of a massive star.

Name: Asteroid Ceres
Description: The largest known asteroid, Ceres, is approximately 590 miles (949 km) across, about the size of Texas. It resides with tens of thousands of other asteroids in the main asteroid belt.

Name: Spiral Galaxy Messier 81
Description: The arms of the "grand design" spiral galaxy M81 are filled with young, bluish, hot stars. The greenish regions in the image are bright, gaseous clouds where new stars are forming.

Name: Pinwheel Galaxy
Description: This image of Messier 100, also called the Pinwheel Galaxy, was one of the first images taken by Hubble after the completion of its first servicing mission, which installed a new-and-improved camera and additional instruments.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 3568
Description: This image captures a side-on view of NGC 3568, a barred spiral galaxy. In 2014, the light from a supernova explosion in NGC 3568 reached Earth – a sudden flare of light caused by the titanic explosion accompanying the death of a massive star.

Name: Spiral Galaxy NGC 2835
Description: The twisting patterns created by the multiple spiral arms of NGC 2835, a stunning barred spiral galaxy, create the illusion of an eye. A supermassive black hole with a mass millions of times that of our Sun is known to nestle in the very center of NGC 2835.
